title: Ranking NFL contenders by backup QB situations: Mac Jones, Davis Mills headline best insurance policies
summary: No one wants to think of their starting QBs going down, but these NFL contenders have solid backups
full_text:
A quality NFL backup quarterback doesn't exactly garner the headlines of an All-Pro-caliber starter. It shouldn't. That said, the value cannot be overlooked. If a franchise's starter goes down for a game, or two, or six, the season could go in the toilet in an instant if they don't have someone who can come in and keep things afloat momentarily. So, while the last thing anyone wants to think about is the established starter missing time, it's good to have a quality insurance plan.
Take last season, for example. A number of backup quarterbacks rose to the occasion, and their successes drove the playoff picture. A key reason why the Houston Texans overcame C.J. Stroud's absence after a concussion in Week 9 was due to backup Davis Mills thriving when his number was called. Mills went 3-0 over his stretch as the starter, which helped Houston mount a playoff berth. In the NFC, Mac Jones led the San Francisco 49ers to a 5-3 record as the starter while Brock Purdy was sidelined, and that helped them stay in the hunt for the No. 1 seed in the conference until Week 18.
Of course, maybe the greatest recent example of having a top backup is Nick Foles in 2017, as he stepped in for an injured Carson Wentz and led the Philadelphia Eagles to a Super Bowl LII title.
With all that in mind, we're going to look at a slew of contenders and size up what their backup quarterback situation looks like and rank them. To draw a line in the sand for what "contender" actually means, we're looking at clubs that have odds to win Super Bowl LXI of +2500 or shorter at DraftKings Sportsbook, which gives us 16 teams in total.
Starter : Josh Allen Backups : Kyle Allen , Shane Buechele
Kyle Allen inked a two-year, $4.1 million deal to be the primary backup to Josh Allen, while 2021 undrafted free agent Shane Buechele is the third-stringer. Allen, who has been in the NFL since 2018, has starting experience (19 total starts), but hasn't started a game since Week 13 of the 2022 season while a member of the Houston Texans. In that game, he completed just 51.3% of his passes, tossed two interceptions, and recorded two fumbles (one lost). For his career, the 30-year-old is 7-12 as a starter, while completing 62.5% of his passes with an 82.1 passer rating. While maybe no quarterback can compare to Josh Allen, it would be a Grand Canyon-sized difference in the event they need to hand the keys over to Kyle Allen.
Starter : Jared Goff Backups : Teddy Bridgewater , Luke Altmyer (UDFA)
Not that long ago, Teddy Bridgewater was coaching high school football. After resigning from his post at Miami Northwestern Senior High School in August of last year, he signed on to be a backup for the Buccaneers and did see some action in Week 12 last season against the Rams . There, Bridgewater completed 53.3% of his throws for just 62 yards. The last time he started a game came back in Week 17 of the 2022 season as a member of the Dolphins . Now, Bridgewater is back in Detroit (where he served as a backup from 2023 to 2024) with the Lions and will likely serve as the top option behind Jared Goff, with undrafted rookie Luke Altmyer also in the fold. While Bridgewater has 65 regular-season starts under his belt and is above .500 (33-32) over that run, it's fair to wonder how much he truly has in the tank as he'll turn 34 during the 2026 season.
Starter : Justin Herbert Backups : Trey Lance , DJ Uiagalelei
Justin Herbert has been remarkably durable over the course of his career, considering the volume of hits he takes. Since entering the NFL in 2020, Herbert has taken the most hits (615) and the most sacks (225) in the league. That includes 129 quarterback hits last season, which was tied for the second-most in the last 20 years. While L.A. has invested in the offensive line and was simply dealt a bad hand with injuries to Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt last season, you'd think they'd pursue a better backup than they currently have in Trey Lance. Lance does have the pedigree of being a former No. 3 overall pick, but he's never lived up to that billing. With the Chargers already in playoff position and deciding to rest their starters, Lance got the nod in Week 18 last season and didn't seize the opportunity. He completed 45.5% of his passes for 136 yards passing and an interception, which resulted in a 43.4 passer rating.
Starter : Dak Prescott Backups : Joe Milton, Sam Howell
The Cowboys have two solid options behind Dak Prescott, which could give them a puncher's chance if No. 4 were sidelined at any point. Joe Milton, who was acquired during the 2025 offseason, has a cannon for an arm and has shown some flashes over his two seasons in the NFL. He technically doesn't have a start under his belt, but played 95.3% of the offensive snaps in a Week 18 game in 2024 while a member of the Patriots . There, he completed 22 of his 29 passes (75.9%) for 241 yards and a touchdown. He also rushed for a touchdown. Meanwhile, Sam Howell, who signed a one-year, $2.5 million contract this offseason, has legitimate starting experience. He started all 17 games for the Commanders in 2023. While he did throw for 3,946 yards and 21 touchdowns, he owned a 4-13 record and registered a league-leading 21 interceptions, so it wasn't exactly a lights-out campaign. Still, there's a solid blend of experience and talent between the two.
Starter : Jordan Love Backups : Tyrod Taylor , Kyle McCord , Kyron Drones (UDFA)
Green Bay had one of the better backups in the NFL last season in Malik Willis , but he's now off in Miami and slated to be the starter for the Dolphins. That led to several new faces coming in behind Jordan Love. Tyrod Taylor is the wily veteran of the group as he'll turn 37 in August, while Kyle McCord was signed to a futures contract this winter after the 2025 sixth-rounder spent his rookie season in Philadelphia. Then, there's undrafted rookie Kyron Drones out of Virginia Tech. McCord has yet to appear in a regular-season game, so Taylor is the backup with the most experience. He started four games for the Jets last season. While he was 1-3 over that stretch, it did include some solid play at times. His best statistical start in 2025 came in a Week 3 loss to the Buccaneers, where he completed 26 of his 36 passes for 197 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Taylor shouldn't be looked at as a backup that can take over for half a season, but might be able to tread water for a game or two, while McCord is more of a developmental wild card.
Starter : Bo Nix Backups : Jarrett Stidham , Sam Ehlinger
Jarrett Stidham remains Denver's top backup, and the Broncos had to turn to the veteran for the AFC Championship after Bo Nix suffered a season-ending ankle injury in the divisional round. Stidham couldn't rise to the occasion and pull off the upset, falling to the Patriots in a tightly contested 10-7 defeat. He completed 17 of his 31 throws for 133 yards, a touchdown, an interception and a fumble. Still, Stidham is a solid backup who has drawn plenty of praise from Sean Payton over his tenure in Denver. That was evident in the two-year, $12 million extension he signed in March of 2025 that included $7 million guaranteed. As for Sam Ehlinger, he re-signed with Denver this offseason on a one-year deal and has NFL starting experience as well. In 2022, he started three games for the Colts (0-3) and completed 63.4% of his passes with a 76.1 passer rating. That's not going to knock anyone's socks off, but at least the third-stringer has seen live reps.
Starter : Matthew Stafford Backups : Ty Simpson (R), Stetson Bennett , Matthew Caldwell (UDFA)
It's admittedly hard to place the Rams backup QBs on this list. Typically, when we're talking about contenders, there isn't a first-round quarterback waiting in the wings, but that's what we have here in Los Angeles. Ty Simpson being plucked by the Rams with the No. 13 overall pick was one of the stunners of the 2026 NFL Draft , but a prudent move for the organization with Stafford in his age-38…
author: Tyler Sullivan

title: Ranking the NFL's top 10 running back duos ahead of 2026 season
summary: Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson Jr. take the top spot, but Jahmyr Gibbs, Derrick Henry and Christian McCaffrey make this ranking loaded with star power
full_text:
What's better than one good running back? Well, two good running backs, of course. And it's with that idea in mind that we present to you the top 10 running back duos for the 2026 season. Weighing individual stardom, balanced backfields, and recent production against projection made it easier said than done. In some cases, one superstar was enough. In others, injury returns or breakout projections helped duos stand out.
So without further ado, here's the list for 2026.
Honorable Mentions: J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey , Broncos ; Saquon Barkley and Tank Bigsby , Eagles ; Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason , Vikings ; Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle , Steelers ; Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell , Buccaneers
This one is certainly a projection, but look at the context. New Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel can put running backs in a position to succeed, especially in open space on the perimeter. Hampton missed a bunch of last season due to injury, but when he was out there, he was very good at running to the perimeter of the formation. He makes for a great fit with McDaniel. Mitchell is a true home-run hitter. He's not just going to step in and be De'Von Achane , but if he can provide even a modicum of the big-play potential that Achane brings on an every-snap basis, that'll help raise this duo's ceiling considerably.
Cook comes off his best-career season, having registered a personal-best (by a lot) 309 carries for a league-leading 1,621 yards, along with 12 touchdowns. He also contributed in the passing game with 33 receptions for 291 yards and two scores. He got up to a 56% snap rate, another career high, with both Davis and Ty Johnson rotating in behind him. Johnson actually played more snaps than Davis did last year, but he's getting up there in age at this point and Davis' underlying metrics like success rate and yards both before and after contact improved last season, so we're betting that under a new head coach, he can take over a larger role this year than the one he had under Sean McDermott. (Joe Brady was the offensive coordinator last year but things can still change when you move into the top job.)
McCaffrey is so good that it doesn't matter whether you put Kaelon Black or Jordan James or Isaac Guerendo or Patrick Taylor or me or you or anyone else -- the 49ers still deserve to be on this list. CMC is the most versatile back in the league, so effective as a receiver that even in a season where he averages just 3.9 yards per carry, he can still be one of the most effective weapons in the league. He racked up an incredible 102 catches for 924 yards and seven touchdowns a year ago, and this is a guy who has led the league in rushing before. In Kyle Shanahan's offense, McCaffrey is a threat to dice the defense on every single play -- especially because he's liable to be out there for something like 80% of the snaps or more.
Love is one of the best running back prospects in recent years. In his two seasons as Notre Dame's starter, he ran for 2,497 yards at an average of 6.9 yards per carry, totaling 35 touchdowns on the ground. And he was an extremely effective receiver, racking up 55 catches for 517 yards and five additional scores. And he did all that while splitting carries with Jadarian Price . Allgeier has a 1,000-yard rushing season under his belt and is also experienced at backing up a top running back prospect from his days in Atlanta. He probably wasn't thrilled to see the Cards draft a running back so high after he signed with them in free agency, but he can take comfort in the fact that he's once again in one of the top duos in the league.
All Williams does is score touchdowns. In three seasons as the starter, he has 36 scores on the ground and another eight through the air. He's averaged at least 4.8 yards per carry in two of those three seasons, and he actually led the league in rush yards per game in 2023. He ceded some time down the stretch of last season to Corum, who didn't do much as a rookie but came on as an effective change of pace in Year 2. He averaged 5.1 yards a pop on his 145 carries in 2025. He doesn't contribute much as a receiver (22 targets in two years), but the Rams don't throw much to their running backs anyway, so that's not necessarily a bug. With Sean McVay calling the plays, these guys will be in position to succeed every single week.
Swift is coming off arguably the most effective season of his career at age 26. He averaged 4.9 yards per carry and posted a 54.7% rushing success rate, stark improvements over the 3.8 yards per carry and 43.9% success rate he posted during his first year in Chicago. Monangai proved to be an effective power complement to Swift's, well, swiftness. He averaged 4.6 yards per carry and also topped a 50% success rate with his runs, per Pro-Football-Reference. This duo isn't quite what Johnson had in Detroit in Jahmyr Gibbs and David Montgomery , but it's a highly effective one nonetheless.
It would have been hard to imagine this duo landing anywhere on this list midway through last season, when Stevenson faced fumbling issues and Henderson could barely get on the field. But then Stevenson went out with an injury, Henderson blew up in his absence, and Stevenson played the best football of his career once he returned. Now these guys look like a pairing that can each do a little bit of everything, including hit on big plays both on the ground and through the air. If Henderson's pass blocking improves, then they can be truly interchangeable three-down backs. And considering that blocking was considered a strength of Henderson's coming out of Ohio State, the safe bet is on him getting there. The Pats have a really good duo here.
This isn't your typical thunder and lightning running back duo. Sure, Henry is a hulking beast of a back who can power his way through everyone in his path and stiff-arm anyone into the ground, but he's also one of the fastest backs in the league when he hits a crease, and he can take it to the house from anywhere on the field. Even in a season where Lamar Jackson was alternately injured and ineffective (for him), Henry still ran for 1,595 yards at 5.2 yards per carry. And while Hill looks like he's a jitterbug back who will shake you up in space, his best skill is actually pass protection, where he is one of the best in the NFL. He's an effective receiver as well, which makes him a strong complement to Henry.
This isn't exactly the most balanced duo considering Pacheco's ineffectiveness since his 2024 leg injury, but Gibbs is just that good. If he's not the best back in the league, it's only because a guy in the No. 1 pairing on our list also exists. Gibbs has topped 5.0 yards per carry in each of his three NFL seasons, racking up 49 total touchdowns along the way. He finally took over the true lead role in the backfield last season and fully exploded as a receiver, picking up more catches (77) than he had targets in either of his first two years in the NFL. Dan Campbell has already alluded to even more work for Gibbs this season, so all the Lions need is for Pacheco to do some short-yardage work and keep the chains moving when he gives the superstar a break.
As mentioned above, Bijan Robinson is arguably the best running back in football. Like Gibbs, he totally exploded last season, electrifying the field with 1,478 yards and seven touchdowns while stepping into the largest receiving role of his career with 79 catches for 820 yards and four scores. He can do everything there is to do on the field, and seemingly do it with relative ease. Brian Robinson Jr. ran for at least 733 yards in each of his first three NFL seasons before landing in San Francisco last year, where he still managed to get to 400 despite playing only 17% of the offensive snaps. In a larger role behind Bijan, he could do more with his opportunities.

title: Offseason moves the Cardinals should be optimistic about
summary: The Arizona Cardinals had plenty of action on the team’s “transactions” page. From the first day of the free agency period to now, the roster has had a ton of turnover. New head coach Mike LaFleur had a honey-do list of what he needed GM Monti Ossenfort to accomplish. And Ossenfort did a great job […]
full_text: OT Paris Johnson Jr. #70 and TE Trey McBride #85 (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals had plenty of action on the team’s “transactions” page. From the first day of the free agency period to now, the roster has had a ton of turnover. New head coach Mike LaFleur had a honey-do list of what he needed GM Monti Ossenfort to accomplish. And Ossenfort did a great job bringing in capable bodies and getting rid of the athletes who weren’t getting the job done. RELATED: WHO IS POISED TO BREAKOUT IN 2026? Admit it: this year’s roster has improved over last year’s. Admittedly, after losing 14 games, it doesn’t take much to make changes and proclaim it’s “a new conqueror.” If you review all the deletions and additions, the Cardinals fanbase should have some bigger expectations going forward. Here are three reasons for optimism for 2026: Getting younger Quite a few players found their groove once they hit 30-years old. Some even played into their 40s. K Adam Vinatieri was 46 when he called it quits. QB Tom Brady was one year younger. QB/K George Blanda made it to 48 years old and was kicking game-winning field goals. Warren Moon, Jerry Rice, and Vinny Testaverde found success past the 4-0 mark. A male is at his athletic peak at age 26. And teams want to remain in that range. The Cardinals have three players who are just 21 years old. 17 roster members are 22 or 23. A dozen are 30+, with five of that number just now 30. The new long snapper, Casey Kreiter, is the senior member of the roster, being 35 years old. This is a very young ballclub. Some may point to the fact that it makes this squad inexperienced and prone to mistakes. Which is true. Sometimes. The New England Patriots went from 4-13-0 to 13-4-0 in one year, and they are the NFL’s youngest team. So, there goes that statement stating youth cannot win games. This year, the pinnacle is being shined on this new offense that LaFleur has brought over from the Los Angeles Rams. LaFleur is a disciple of the San Francisco 49ers as well. Expect the success that these two clubs have had to become the norm in the desert. This new offense will feature RB Jeremiyah Love (age 21), TE Tip Reiman (24), WR Devin Duvernay (28), OG Chase Bisontis (22), C Hjalte Froholdt (29), WR Reggie Virgil (22), RB Tyler Allgeier (26), Marv Harrison (23), TE Elijah Higgins (25), OT Paris Johnson (25), TE Trey McBride (26), WR Michael Wilson (26), and rookie QB Carson Beck (23). The defense has its own story with CB Will Johnson (age 23), LB Jordan Burch (24), DT Walter Nolen (22), CB Denzel Burke (23), LB Cody Simon (24), CB Max Melton (24), LB Baron Browning (27), CB Garrett Williams (25), LB Zaven Collins (27), EDGE Josh Sweat (29), and S Budda Baker (30). This is a promising young core for not only the upcoming 2026 season, but the foundation for years to come. Clearing up the QB situation Not long after LaFleur was hired, the decision was made on what to do with QB Kyler Murray, who had spent a good many games on IR in 2025. A day to before the Cardinals report, and there is not yet a resolution to Jacoby Brissett’s contract situation. AZ and Brissett (who is his own agent) have been actively negotiating for the last several months and agree he’s due a raise. No consensus yet on the number. https://t.co/GwHgf03Rlq — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 21, 2026 During his downtime, backup Jacoby Brissett took over, and the offense came alive. WR Michael Wilson and TE Trey McBride had tremendous seasons despite both starting running backs being out and a very suspect offensive line effort. Yes, Brissett only won one game, but in seven games, Arizona was winning late in the fourth quarter, and somehow the defense managed to allow the other team to take victory away. he’s representing himself and still dragging this out? either he knows his number or he doesn’t — Sofie 🧡 🌟 (@sophie_mae947) July 21, 2026 LaFleur didn’t want the distraction of a QB battle, and the decision was made to cut bait with Murray. Then, the head coach announced that Brissett was his starter going forward. Unfortunately, Brissett has since held out of team activities, wanting his contract to be restructured with more years added and his salary elevated. "It's fun to play football." Gardner Minshew doesn't know how much he'll play QB for the #AZCardinals , but he's working to find out. https://t.co/wN0ypxugcT — Darren Urban (@Cardschatter) May 27, 2026 So, now instead of Murray vs. Brissett for the starting nod, it just could become Gardner Minshew or rookie Carson Beck vs. Brissett instead. Which either should become a lot less fireworks. The hiring of OC Nathaniel Hackett It has been established that LaFleur is an offensive-minded head coach. He was previously the OC with the Rams, who had a very successful offensive showing. LaFleur came off the coaching tree of both Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan. The Cardinals will follow this trail. The Cardinals are hiring Nathaniel Hackett as their offensive coordinator, sources tell The Insiders. Hackett, 46, was the offensive coordinator for three seasons under Matt LaFleur in Green Bay. Now, he teams up with Mike LaFleur in Arizona. pic.twitter.com/y0yM9gUltQ — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) February 4, 2026 Despite being the offensive coordinator, LaFleur did not call plays in LA – McVay did. LaFleur did call plays for one game in 2025 when McVay was out sick. Coming to Arizona, LaFleur has stated that he will become the Cardinals’ play caller. But he had to reach out to somebody who had experience at the NFL level as his offensive confidant. And that somebody had to be a coach that LaFleur knew and could instantly trust. A lot of head coaches call plays for either their offense or defense, and that’s fine. In fact, it is quite remarkable. With as much that is going on in a game, it is enough to keep tabs on the comings and goings of a live contest, much less have the added duties of calling plays. But some head coaches, such as Andy Reid of the Kansas City Chiefs, do. Hackett was the OC for LaFleur’s brother Matt with the Green Bay Packers from 2019 to 2021. During those years, Green Bay’s offense was ranked: #15 (2019), #1 (2020), and #10 (2021). The hiring is legit. Hackett’s has called plays before, so that is always an option and a fallback. Plus, his history doesn’t suggest a power running team approach but rather is geared towards a lot of tight end usage, which is right up LaFleur’s way of thinking. At least Hackett has been there. #Cardinals HC Mike LaFleur on hiring Nathaniel Hackett as his Offensive Coordinator: “He’s been very successful and is very highly thought of, especially in our profession. I wanted him and nobody else. And he’s here.” (📽️ @PHNX_Cardinals ) pic.twitter.com/ZLhqn2FlRw — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) February 18, 2026 LaFleur came out and stated that his only choice for OC was Hackett. This means that as LaFleur is making his way and grooming the offense, he has talent already in the offensive room with Hackett at the ready for advice with a bevy of experience. Hackett has involvement with play calling, but LaFleur has stated that he will be Arizona’s play caller going forward. It is a job that he has had in the past, and he has stated he really enjoys that aspect of coaching.

title: Falcons training camp 2026: Quarterback battle important for present, critical for future
summary: The Atlanta Falcons have had a quarterback problem for years, a statement blindingly obvious to anyone who has been an Atlanta Falcons fan over the past few seasons. Since 2022, when the Falcons hastily traded Matt Ryan to Indianapolis in the wake of a failed effort to trade for Deshaun Watson, they’ve started Marcus Mariota, […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Atlanta, GA, USA; Atlanta Falcons quarterbacks Tua Tagovailoa (1) and Michael Penix Jr. (9) on the field during Minicamp. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | Dale Zanine-Imagn Images The Atlanta Falcons have had a quarterback problem for years, a statement blindingly obvious to anyone who has been an Atlanta Falcons fan over the past few seasons. Since 2022, when the Falcons hastily traded Matt Ryan to Indianapolis in the wake of a failed effort to trade for Deshaun Watson, they’ve started Marcus Mariota, Desmond Ridder, Taylor Heinicke, Kirk Cousins, and Michael Penix Jr.; that’s more than one starter per season. In fact, they’ve had two different quarterbacks starting for the team in each of those four years, and they have not had one true franchise guy at any point in that span. Penix could still be that player, but it’s hardly a given. We enter 2026 with Penix recovering from ACL surgery, one of many such surgeries in his college and now NFL career, and with very little on-field to suggest he’s a potentially elite quarterback. He’s competing with Tua Tagovailoa, who is coming off a dismal season with the Dolphins where he was benched, and has dealt with scary concussions throughout his career. The only guys behind them are big-armed undrafted free agent Jack Strand and journeyman backup Trevor Siemien, so there’s very little chance of a Cinderella story if Tua and Penix don’t pan out. That makes the quarterback battle crucial on two fronts. It’s obviously important for this year, because the better player needs to have the reins of an offense richly veined with playmakers to help these Falcons shake off eight straight losing seasons and recapture hope and competence. But it’s also important for next year, because any outcome outside of Penix seizing this job and excelling will likely have the Falcons looking to draft, sign, or trade for a potential franchise option. Why it matters in 2026 The Falcons don’t want to continue to squander their talent. Bijan Robinson was the league’s most productive running back last year, leading the NFL in yards from scrimmage, but was stuck on a team that had a frequently anemic passing attack and blew far too many games. Drake London and Kyle Pitts are game-changing talents who have dealt with streaky, inconsistent passers throughout their careers. Jahan Dotson, Zachariah Branch, and Austin Hooper offer real talent—and in the case of Branch, really intriguing potential—but could see their production blunted if the quarterback position isn’t effectively settled. A great quarterback would have a passing attack with this many weapons humming. A good quarterback would have it looking capable, at minimum. As we’ve seen over the years, promising but inconsistent quarterbacks and shaky ones alike have conspired to make it look elite for shining moments and disappointing for long stretches. The Falcons badly need to figure out whether Tua or Penix is the right fit for these weapons and this passing attack. At his best, Tua can deliver timely, very accurate passes in the short-to-intermediate areas of the field, a skill set that plays well with the YAC capabilities of Bijan, Brian Robinson, London, and Branch, as well as Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees’ screen designs. Penix has been more inconsistent across the board in his brief career, but his ability to attack defenses deep opens up potentially devastating big plays for London, Pitts, and Dotson. There are significant stylistic differences here that might come into play if this ends up being a very close battle, but the likelier outcome is simply that one of these quarterbacks is more healthy and effective this summer and wins the battle outright well before preseason wraps. At the moment, my money would be on Tua, who had a head start as the healthy player earlier this summer and should be able to reliably pepper his supporting cast with short-to-intermediate passes the way Kirk Cousins did at his best last year. Whoever wins, however, will need to be good enough to at least partially unlock this passing game’s significant potential, lest their backup catapult past them midseason. Why it matters in 2027 and beyond Let’s say Tua grabs the starting job and lands somewhere between his 2024 and 2025 seasons, finishing with something like 13 games played and a 68% completion percentage. It’s more or less a given that Tua will miss some time given that he has appeared in 17 games just once in his career. The hope would be that he could exceed the two-year averages of about 2,750 yards, 20 touchdowns, and 12 interceptions he managed in Miami. If that’s the case, will the Falcons sign up for a long-term deal with Tua? I would say it’s very unlikely, though they could go for a two-year, incentive-laden deal if Tua plays well in those 13 games and they don’t like the options they survey in the draft and across the league. Barring a spectacular, fully healthy seasons from Tua, the Falcons are not going to sign on to make him their quarterback for the next 3-5 years; the likelier outcome is that Tua’s second career is spent picking up quality short-term deals as a stopgap or low-end starter in Atlanta or elsewhere. There’s a narrow band in which Tua becomes Atlanta’s long-term starter under Stefanski, in other words. If he seizes the job I’ll be rooting very hard for him to become the guy he was in 2022 and 2023, when he put up 54 touchdowns against 22 interceptions and led the league in passing yards on season, because it would be great for the Falcons if he could recapture his best years and stay healthy. But given the past couple of seasons and his significant injury history, it’s not a strong bet that Tua will leave 2026 as the unquestioned or even likely starter in 2027. Penix is in a different boat. If he doesn’t win the job, the Falcons could very well dangle him for trade in 2026 or 2027, banking on a team that misses out on a rookie quarterback being willing to bet on the arm talent and their own ability to maximize his ability and adding to their war chest of draft picks. Barring a trade, though, Penix would be Tua insurance with starting experience and evident talent, which is a valuable thing to have. If he can’t beat out Tua, however, I’d say his long-term future with the Falcons is very much in doubt heading into the final year of his rookie deal (his contract does, however, have the fifth year option). It’s a different story if he does win the job, which I’ve continually said unlocks the best-case scenario for Atlanta. Penix starting, staying healthy, and playing well does not entirely dispel the long haul concern about his injury history—nothing can do that, really—but it would give the Falcons the confidence to go into 2027 with him as the starter. Atlanta will always want a quality insurance policy for Penix, but if he can blossom in Stefanski’s offense, the Falcons will not need to invest early round draft capital or massive dollars in his replacement and can build the offense around what he does best with confidence. That frees them up to augment the roster in 2027 without limitations, especially if they finish as a playoff team or borderline playoff team, and could accelerate their path to becoming a perennial postseason contender. The fifth year option gives them flexibility for 2028 to ensure he stays healthy if they’re hesitant to commit to longer than that, as well. Of course, that also is an ideal outcome that can’t be said to be likely at the moment. We have seen glimpses of tantalizing talent from Penix, but not enough to believe he’s going to become a franchise quarterback yet. We also know that another significant ACL injury adds a cautionary note for a team hoping to rely on him as a franchise player, and that Penix is both older for a quarterback entering his third year (26) and already in the third year of his rookie deal. If Penix does surpass Tua but does not show signs of a significant growth, which is obviously a real…

title: Beatdown roundtable: favorite almost-signing in Ravens history
summary: Baltimore Beatdown is all about Almost Ravens this week! In addition to our reader-driven bracket narrowing down the biggest near-acquisitions in team history, our staff will also be providing their opinions on their favorite moves the Ravens almost pulled off. Today, we’re focusing on trades: The Ravens’ near-signing of future Hall of Fame linebacker Bobby […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - FEBRUARY 09: Darius Slay Jr. #2 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts during Super Bowl LIX against the Kansas City Chiefs at Caesars Superdome on February 09, 2025, in New Orleans, Louisiana. The Eagles defeated the Chiefs 40-22. (Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baltimore Beatdown is all about Almost Ravens this week! In addition to our reader-driven bracket narrowing down the biggest near-acquisitions in team history, our staff will also be providing their opinions on their favorite moves the Ravens almost pulled off. Today, we’re focusing on trades: The Ravens’ near-signing of future Hall of Fame linebacker Bobby Wagner in 2022 is a really interesting one. Wagner himself had a solid year in Los Angeles with another second-team All-Pro berth and may have stayed in Baltimore for a few years. And the Ravens likely would not have traded for Roquan Smith during the regular season and signed him to a long-term extension that has not aged well. Smith has been great in Baltimore, but it’s fair to wonder if a more moderate price for Wagner plus the second-round pick the Ravens sent to Chicago would have been a better allocation of resources. – Nikhil Mehta My favorite player the Ravens almost signed is Darius Slay. While Slay was on the backend of his NFL journey in 2023-24, he was still playing well and likely would have been a great fit in Baltimore. Placing him alongside Marlon Humphrey, Kyle Hamilton and company could have paid dividends. Slay likely would helped sure up the team’s secondary and alleviate some of their issues allowing big passing plays in recent seasons. He profiled as the prototypical veteran who the Ravens sign and get high-level play out of late in their career. – Frank Platko My personal favorite player the Ravens almost signed was Za’Darius Smith. When the deal with “Z” was announced, I was so thrilled for him to come back as a Raven. Looking back on it now, if Smith’s deal had stayed, with Mike Macdonald as the defensive coordinator in 2022 and 2023, he could have been an anchor for what would become one of the NFL’s most feared defenses while Macdonald was in Baltimore (once Macdonald got through his early kinks in 2022). Instead, everything went haywire. Smith back out of Baltimore’s four-year deal, then signed a three-year deal with Minnesota. He was then traded to Cleveland before the 2023 season, traded to Detroit in the middle of the 2024 season, signed with the Eagles at the start of the 2025 season, then retired after five games. I was devastated when I learned Smith had backed out with the Ravens.. – Zach Canter While not my favorite player among the bunch, Ryan Grant has to be my personal favorite “almost signing” of the Ravens, purely for the hilarity that ensued. It’s no secret that Baltimore has historically struggled to field quality wide receivers, and this was never more true than the final few years of Joe Flacco’s tenure with the team. Entering the 2018 offseason, the Ravens desperately needed wide receiver help after the Jeremy Maclin signing did not pan out the season prior. Baltimore chose to bring in two veteran free agents ahead of the draft in John Brown and Ryan Grant. Brown, a speedster coming from Arizona, was given a modest one-year deal worth up to $6.5 million with incentives. Grant, on the other hand, was oddly given a four-year, $29 million deal despite totaling just 985 receiving yards in his first four seasons with Washington. Fans were rightfully puzzled by the signing. As with Maxx Crosby though, a failed physical nixed the deal, which ultimately led to the team signing a much more accomplished veteran wide receiver in Michael Crabtree, who had just been released by the Raiders. Grant fizzled out, playing just two more seasons in the NFL, ultimately proving the Ravens right for backing out of the deal due to health concerns, but the decision to give him such a contract in the first place baffles me to this day. – Dustin Cox Who is the biggest Almost-Raven in franchise history? | Baltimore Beatdown

title: 2026 AFC North Positional Rankings: Cornerback
summary: During this year’s free agency cycle and 2026 NFL draft, all four AFC North teams made significant moves to add talent to their rosters. While more additions are still possible over the next few months, everyone’s core players are mostly set ahead of the 2026 season. How do the different positional groups in the division […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - NOVEMBER 30: Denzel Ward #21 of the Cleveland Browns warms up prior to a game against the San Francisco 49ers at Huntington Bank Field on November 30, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images During this year’s free agency cycle and 2026 NFL draft, all four AFC North teams made significant moves to add talent to their rosters. While more additions are still possible over the next few months, everyone’s core players are mostly set ahead of the 2026 season. How do the different positional groups in the division stack up to one another? Let’s rank the AFC North squads by position, continuing with cornerback. 1. Pittsburgh Steelers Starters: Joey Porter Jr., Jamal Dean, Jalen Ramsey Depth: Asante Samuel Jr., Daylen Everette, Brandin Echols The Steelers are returning Joey Porter Jr. and Jalen Ramsey as primary cornerbacks while making two notable additions this offseason. Veteran Jamal Dean was inked to a three-year contract after playing seven years in Tampa Bay, where he established himself as a reliable and consistent player. Although he’s never earned Pro Bowl or All-Pro recognition, Dean was PFF’s No. 3 graded cornerback in 2026 with three interceptions and two passes defended. Porter has become a high-level coverage player through three seasons and has the potential to make a jump to stardom status in Year 4. A potential X-factor is Asante Samuel Jr., who the Steelers also signed after he was medically cleared to return from a spinal injury, 2. Baltimore Ravens Starters : Nate Wiggins, Chidobe Awuzie, Marlon Humphrey Depth: T.J. Tampa, Chandler Rivers, Bilhal Kone The Ravens re-signed Chidobe Awuzie this offseason to return as a starter alongside Marlon Humphrey and Nate Wiggins, after the veteran had a solid 2026 campaign with the team. Humphrey and Wiggins were among the most targeted cornerbacks in the league last season and allowed their fair share of production. Wiggins flashed high-level potential throughout the year despite some struggles, though, racking up 14 pass breakups and three interceptions. Humphrey was PFF’s 105th-graded cornerback and allowed a 90.9 passer rating when targeted. Humphrey is in need of a big bounce-back season entering his age-30 campaign, while Wiggins still possesses star potential entering Year 3. The Ravens have a plethora of young cornerbacks far down the depth chart who will battle it out for the final roster spots in this group. 3. Cleveland Browns Starters: Denzel Ward, Tyson Campbell, Myles Harden Depth: Anthony Kendall, Dom Jones, Myles Bryant Denzel Ward remains one of the top cornerbacks in the NFL at 19 years old despite some durability issues in recent seasons. He’s made five Pro Bowls in eight career seasons, including three consecutive. After trading for Tyson Campbell in the middle of last season from the Jacksonville Jaguars, he will return as a starter alongside Ward. In 12 games with the Browns, Campbell recorded 12 pass breakups, 53 tackles, one interception and a forced fumble as well. Myles Harden is the team’s primary nickel corner entering his third career season. Harden started five games last season after playing only four in his rookie campaign. His PFF grade of 48.7 ranked 108th among all cornerbacks. At 24 years old, Harden could take a step forward this year and help solidify this group. 4. Cincinnati Bengals Starters: Dax Hill, DJ Turner II, Jalen Davis Depth: Tacario Davis, Josh Newton, Ja’Sir Taylor The Bengals lost Cam Taylor-Britt in free agency but are returning two other starters at cornerback. DJ Turner is coming off a career-best third season in the NFL, where he recorded 18 pass breakups, two interceptions and was PFF’s No. 19 graded player at the position (73.3). At 25 years old, Turner could be primed to take another step forward. His former Michigan teammate, Dax Hill, started all 17 games and played over 1,000 defensive snaps in 2025. Since being drafted in 2022, Hill has floated between being a safety and nickel cornerback but will likely play exclusively on the outside now. Jalen Davis is slotted to step into the starting slot role having only three total starts in eight career seasons. Davis played a career-high 270 defensive snaps last season. The Bengals drafted Tacario Davis out of Washington in the third round this year, an intriguing 6-foot-4 prospect who should see playing time right away.

full_text: Bills quarterback Josh Allen talks with offensive coordinator Joe Brady during drills on day three of the Buffalo Bills training camp. | Shawn Dowd/Rochester Democrat and Chronicle / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. Can you feel it? Buffalo Bills training camp is about to begin, and with that comes a return to on-field football. If it feels to you as though this has been a painfully long offseason, you’re not alone. With change at the top of the Bills’ coaching structure, we’ve been left trying to fill a void in meaningfully discussing what the team will do on the field under the direction of first time head coach Joe Brady and first time NFL defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. This summer, those two men are front and center as fans and those who cover the Bills try and catch a glimpse of the team’s new look. Well, that chance comes now by way of seven morning session at St. John Fisher University. It’s a pared-down schedule between July 29 and August 7 at Fisher, at which point they’ll head back to One Bills Drive to finish training camp in front of season ticket holders during the Return of the Blue & Red practice. Getting into that event has proven nearly impossible because of the new stadium (prompting a second, equally difficult, ticketed event open to the general public on August 18), but tickets for training camp are at a premium unlike any season before simply because of the shorter schedule. So this week we’re asking Rumblers a simple question… Are you going to Buffalo Bills training camp this summer? Are you still in limbo and hoping to secure tickets for a practice? Sound off in The Feed poll and in the comments section below!

title: Parker Brothers Tailgate Menu for the Buffalo Bills 2026 season
summary: Tailgating has become synonymous with the Buffalo Bills and their passionately loyal fanbase, football fans from every walk of life who routinely show up exuding energy regardless of the location of the game or the temperature outside to fervently support their team. And I’m writing the Parker Brothers Tailgate menu because I’ve been friends with […]
full_text: Tailgating has become synonymous with the Buffalo Bills and their passionately loyal fanbase, football fans from every walk of life who routinely show up exuding energy regardless of the location of the game or the temperature outside to fervently support their team. And I’m writing the Parker Brothers Tailgate menu because I’ve been friends with Rory and Ray since Kindergarten and have remained close friends with these brothers through a lot with the Bills over the years. It’s a bond that has always extended beyond Bills tailgates, but as we’ve gotten older, the Bills tailgates have become our central meeting ground, a guaranteed place to reconvene every fall and winter. And I sincerely cherish the yearly regathering with these two. I’m sure you know the exact feeling of camaraderie with your tailgating group. What started as a nano-tailgate with a deep fryer for wings and fries has gradually morphed into a full-scale tailgating operation, often feeding 50-plus patrons thanks to multiple flat tops, cooking apparatuses, and condiments galore. I cannot recommend the Parker Brothers Tailgate enough. And here is their menu for the 2026 Bills season. (Rory and Ray will be situated in the new “white” lot — behind Prohibition 2020 — for the 2026 campaign, and they welcome you to join them.) Week 2 – September 17: Detroit Lions, 8:15pm — Birria tacos This was a new menu item in 2025, and it went over like gangbusters. And who hasn’t experienced the birria taco craze at their local Mexican restaurant or taqueria? Well the Parkers are bringing that succulent experience to the grand opening of the new Highmark Stadium. Slow-cooked, marinated beef, melted Oaxacan cheese, and a consomé that knocks your socks off the moment you take your first bite. Birria tacos will hit the spot on a momentous evening in Orchard Park with weather that should still feel like summer… before literal and figurative fireworks inside the new stadium. Week 3 – September 27: Los Angeles Chargers — No tailgate (wedding in Lake George) For the first time I can remember, Rory and Ray will not be at a Bills tailgate, working tirelessly to feed the masses before unwinding while watching their Bills play. Family wedding in the Adirondacks will keep them away for this one, but trust me, they’ll be back with more energy than ever after their own bye week. Week 4 – October 4: New England Patriots, 1pm — Stingers What wings are to Buffalo, stinger subs are to the Parkers tailgate. Well, stingers and garbage plates. Every year, the stinger tailgate attracts more friends and random passers-by than any other because of the Parkers’ attention to detail with their stinger construction. Thick chicken fingers, dipped in country sweet sauce, combined with perfectly cooked shredded beef, with any combination of lettuce, cheese, onions, banana peppers, and mayo on a fresh sub roll that can be toasted if you’d like (highly recommend it). All ahead of a colossal showdown with the defending AFC champs in the House That Josh Built. Week 8 – November 1: Baltimore Ravens, 1pm — Surprise, Surprise Despite the pestering of my Parker Brothers sources, this tailgate remains a mystery. All I could manage to coax from said source was this, and it’s awesomely cryptic, it’s actually making me hungry right now: “This tailgate has never been done before, maybe never again,” and “I’ll go out on a limb and say no one has ever tried it ever.” ….as if you needed more encouragement to get to Bills-Ravens. Week 11 – November 22: Miami Dolphins, 1pm — Turkey 2 Ways Have you ever had deep-fried turkey? If the answer is no, this is one glorious sliver of life you have yet to experience. The Parkers call this Turkey 2 Ways because you can get a few slices of classically cooked Thanksgiving turkey. And if that’s your jam, I respect that. I recommend a taste of the Parkers deep-fried version that of course features a crunchy exterior and impossibly juicy meat as the focal point around mashed potatoes, corn, and everything else you’ll eventually eat on Thanksgiving with your family. Week 12 – November 26: Kansas City Chiefs, 8:20pm — Cheesesteaks Why aren’t the Parkers doing a Thanksgiving tailgate on Thanksgiving night? Well, they figured the tryptophan would probably be overwhelming at this stage of Thanksgiving, so they’re venturing away from all the food you’ve likely eaten in the hours leading up to this perennial enormous regular-season battle between the Bills and Chiefs. And the Parkers Cheesesteaks could hold their own on any corner on the streets of Philadelphia. Trust me. Ask for extra cheese. Thank me later. Week 15 – December 19: Chicago Bears — Italian beef A cousin of the Cheesesteaks, I actually slightly prefer the Italian beef — my last name should be a dead giveaway I’d have this take. Of course, this menu item from Rory and Ray is a nod to one of Chicago’s most revered culinary offerings, which just so happens to be the city’s version of the beef on weck. The spicy giardiniera — finely diced peppers, carrots, celery — elevate this sandwich into the stratosphere. And the warm, seasoned roast beef will warm your insides ahead of this super-fun AFC-NFC showdown between two of the best improvisational quarterbacks in the NFL. Week 18 – January 10: New York Jets, TBD — Smash burgers I adore smash burgers, and every time I eat one, I wonder… how and why were we not always eating burgers this way… two patties, pressed thin, with ample amounts of melted cheese to hold them together? And the Parkers have perfected the on-site smash burger… Ray is normally on the flat-top, precisely flattening each patty before loading with cheese. Rory’s responsibilities come in the made-to-order building of your burger. And he will walk you through the process once your patties are ready to be assembled between two buns. Because the Parkers have gotten so good with the presentation — and taste — of their smash burgers, this is an exquisite cap to the Bills 2026 regular season at this tailgate. Playoffs — TBD Among the menu items the Parkers have done in the past that would be possible during a Bills playoff run: Garbage Plates (unequivocally my favorite, thanks in large part to Mrs. Parker’s meat sauce) Hibachi (a gigantic undertaking but Michelin-star worthy) Burritos (made to your exact specifications, Chipotle-style) Breakfast (bacon, sausage, eggs, all sizzling on the griddle) Deep-fried everything (bring anything you want, the Parkers will deep fry right in front of your eyes) Spaghetti and meatballs (I never knew I needed this Italian classic before a football game, until I went to a Parker Tailgate) What is your tailgate scene like? Are you already planned out with specific menu items? Leave a comment explaining everything in detail!

full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 06: Levi Wallace #39 of the Buffalo Bills reacts during the fourth quarter against the New England Patriots at Highmark Stadium on December 06, 2021 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Levi Wallace went from undrafted free agent from Alabama to key No. 2 cornerback during the Buffalo Bills rise to prominence early in the Josh Allen era, and now he’s decided to hang up his cleats. The four-year Bills cornerback recently told ESPN Tucson he was officially retired: “I’ve been retired for a while, honestly,” Wallace said on ESPN Tucson’s “Spears & Ali” Tuesday morning. “People are making a big deal out of it because I officially announced it. Mentally, I’ve been done, so I’m doing other stuff and venturing out and seeing what else is out there. I have to, in a sense, reinvent myself and realize, ‘What is it that I really want do besides football, a sport I’ve been playing since I was 5 years old?’ I’ve enjoyed it. I’m excited for what next season holds.” A former walk-on at Nick Saban’s Alabama program, Wallace didn’t hear his name called in the 2018 NFL Draft after a three-interception, 15 pass breakup 2017 in which the Crimson Tide won the national title. He made an immediate impact in Buffalo with three PBUs and 37 tackles in seven contests as a rookie before he moved into a full-time role in his second season in which he appeared in all 16 regular season games. Wallace snagged two interceptions per season in 2019, 2020, and 2021 and knocked away 30 passes in his four seasons with the Bills during the regular season. He played on over 75% of the defensive snaps in both 2019 and 2021, clearly emerging as a reliable cornerback in Sean McDermott’s defense because of his zone savviness and natural ball skills. After his Bills career, Wallace, now 31, spent two seasons with the Broncos and finished his regular-season career in Pittsburgh. He got injured in camp with the Jaguars in 2025.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis
summary: The Buffalo Bills have long searched for a top-notch combination of defensive linemen. With respect to the discussion surrounding the wide receiver group, if you’re a longtime fan of this franchise—and, if you’re reading this, I’m assuming that you are—you know that it seems like the Bills have been rebuilding their defensive line for nearly […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 28: Phidarian Mathis #72 of the Buffalo Bills reacts after a tackle in the fourth quarter of the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Highmark Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have long searched for a top-notch combination of defensive linemen. With respect to the discussion surrounding the wide receiver group, if you’re a longtime fan of this franchise—and, if you’re reading this, I’m assuming that you are—you know that it seems like the Bills have been rebuilding their defensive line for nearly as long as I-86 has been under construction. While general manager Brandon Beane has made some big swings during his tenure, bringing in former first-round draft picks like Von Miller, Leonard Floyd, Joey Bosa, and Star Lotulelei, no one can say that the Bills haven’t tried to field a star-studded defensive line. Whether it was because of scheme, unfortunate injuries, or acquiring players who were already on the back nine of their careers, those moves haven’t exactly panned out the way the Bills hoped. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a defensive lineman the Bills added last season who might not have been a first-round pick for his former franchise, but he performed like a solid contributor in limited action with Buffalo. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Phidarian Mathis Number: 72 Position: DT Height/Weight: 6’4” 312 lbs. Age: 28 (29 on 4/26/2027) Experience/Draft: 5; selected by the Washington Commanders in the second round (No. 47 overall) of the 2022 NFL Draft College: Alabama Acquired: Signed with Buffalo’s practice squad on 9/10/2025 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Mathis re-signed with Buffalo this offseason, inking a one-year contract worth $1.195 million overall. That total also stands as his cap hit if he makes the 53-man roster. If Buffalo releases him before Week One, they’ll carry just $25,000 in dead cap this year. If he makes the roster for the first week, his whole base salary—$1.145 million—becomes fully guaranteed thanks to his status as a vested veteran. 2025 Recap: Mathis spent the preseason with the New York Jets, the same team with which he ended the 2024 season. He appeared in two preseason games with the Jets, notching three total tackles. However, Mathis was waived by the Jets before their preseason finale, as the team traded for Harrison Phillips and Jowon Briggs, leading to Mathis’ exit. He went unclaimed on waivers, but signed with Buffalo’s practice squad after the first week of the season. Mathis remained on the practice squad without a call-up until Week Five, when he was active for Buffalo’s 23-20 loss to the New England Patriots. Mathis made two tackles on 17 defensive snaps in that game. He was elevated once more in a Week Nine win over the Kansas City Chiefs before he was signed to the active roster on November 5. Mathis played the following week, a game where the Bills were embarrassed by the Miami Dolphins, but he missed the next three weeks due to a shoulder injury. Once he was healthy, he sat two more weeks as a healthy scratch before returning to play against the Cleveland Browns. He played in Buffalo’s final three regular season games, bringing his season tackle total to 13 across 120 defensive snaps. He also played six snaps on defense against the Jacksonville Jaguars, logging zero tackles in the victory. Mathis was a healthy scratch the following week in Buffalo’s 33-30 loss to the Denver Broncos. Positional outlook: Mathis is one of eight defensive tackles listed on the current roster. Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, Zion Logue, Zane Durant, T.J. Sanders, Tommy Akingbesote, and DeWayne Carter are the others. Landon Jackson and Kody Huisman are listed at defensive end, but they will likely play as down linemen just like the defensive tackles. Mathis, Walker, Carter, and Logue all figure to compete at the nose in Buffalo’s new defense. 2026 Offseason: Mathis is healthy and has participated in OTAs. 2026 Season outlook: Mathis is exactly what Buffalo needs in the middle of their new-look defensive line. He can eat space up front, he’s a strong run defender, and he can keep blockers from moving to the linebackers at the second level of Buffalo’s defense. Should he start? No, he likely will suit up as a rotational piece if he makes the club. As a team transitioning to an odd-front look, the Bills need all the space-eating linemen they can find, and Mathis has experience in a system similar to Jim Leonhard’s from his time in college at Alabama. In his senior year with the Crimson Tide, Mathis had 51 tackles, 12 tackles for loss, and 9 sacks. This guy is no slouch, but his professional output hasn’t come close to matching that one college season, as he has just 38 tackles and 2 tackles for loss in his pro career. If Mathis is going to make the 2026 Bills, he doesn’t have to be the same player he was at Alabama, but it would certainly be nice if he could show flashes of being that guy. All Buffalo needs him to do is control his gap, collapse the pocket, and stuff a run or three. The Bills don’t have many natural nose tackles on the roster, and they really don’t have any who have made much of a name for themselves outside of die-hard fandoms. Mathis is by no means a lock for the roster, as he’s likely to find himself in a battle with Carter and Logue for the right to back up Deone Walker. If he plays the way he did last season—and hopefully even a bit better—then I think he’ll be someone who not only makes the team, but plays around 40% of the snaps throughut the season. He’s not going to be the star along the defensive line, but he has all the traits to be someone who overperforms his contract. I expect Phidarian Mathis to be one of Buffalo’s top rotational pieces up front this season barring a poor preseason or an injury. He earned the opportunity through his play last season, and I think he’s one of the players whose shot at the roster is helped by the scheme change this year.

The Titans defeated the Panthers 30-3. (Photo by Brian A. Westerholt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #51. Geoff Hangartner Geoff Hangartner is about as offensive lineman as they come. He played college football at Texas A&M, where he never missed a game, though he did get in trouble for drinking in driving. He was picked by the Panthers in the fifth round in 2004 and took a role as a backup center and special teams player. He was thrust into a starting role in year two due to injury and played well. Still, he was demoted back to a bench role for year three and was only called upon when injuries hit. He split time as a starter and reserve in his fourth season before departing for Buffalo in free agency in 2009. The Panthers apparently realized what they had and re-signed Hangartner after the Bills let him go in order to go younger on the offensive line. He slid in at right tackle and was an integral part of a strong offensive line that helped Cam Newton win rookie of the year honors. He seemed poised to hold down that spot for a while but went from starting guard to training camp cut before the 2013 season, once again as the victim of a team making a youth push on the offensive line. He ended up making a few cameos as an injury replacement that season before retiring. Hangartner was the quintessential underappreciated interior lineman that never wowed anyone but also more than held is own. It seemed like he was always a target for replacement, but he always showed up and played well whenever the team was forced to rely on him. And he was a passable kickoff returner in a pinch. He returned three kickoffs during the 2007 season, one of which set up a game winning drive against the Seahawks. Not bad for a 300 pounder.

title: Panthers Training Camp Roundup: Nic Scourton is out for the season
summary: Good evening Panthers fans! We’re into training camp and a lot of information is floating around the internet. I’m here to try and highlight some pieces I think fans want to know about and just help you keep up with all the happenings in general! This is not an all encompassing piece, so if there’s […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Charlotte, NC, USA; Carolina Panthers running back Jonathan Brooks (25) walks off the field during the first day of mini camp at Bank of America Stadium practice facility. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images Good evening Panthers fans! We’re into training camp and a lot of information is floating around the internet. I’m here to try and highlight some pieces I think fans want to know about and just help you keep up with all the happenings in general! This is not an all encompassing piece, so if there’s something that happened that you find interesting/exciting, feel free to share below! Nic Scourton is out for the season One day into training camp, and the Panthers have lost their first casualty for the season, and it was their promising young 2025 2nd round pick, EDGE Nic Scourton. Scourton appeared primed to have a big role on this front seven opposite Jaelen Phillips, but we’re going to have to wait til 2027 as Scourton went down with what appeared to be a severe knee injury early in the day. Speculation was it was very serious due to how he and the players around him reacted, and sure enough, its a torn ACL. Horrible news for the Panthers, sending best wishes to Nic on a speedy and healthy recovery. Other tidbits Running back Jonathon Brooks practiced in training camp for the first time in his career ( shout-out to Mike Kaye for that factoid ). While I know many fans have been skeptical of his health, he appears primed to have a significant role in the offense if this direction continues. The Panthers have officially announced rookie first round pick Monroe Freeling will be starting at right tackle to start the year given the medical issue keeping Taylor Moton out. Initially, Freeling was set to enter a competition with Rasheed Walker at left tackle, but the team quickly created a new plan for Moton’s absence. Dave Canales said OL Brady Christensen “looked good” in his first training camp action back with the team. Christensen is coming off a torn Achilles last season, but he may be needed sooner than later if the Panthers injury luck continues. Canales also said he’s optimistic that Jaycee Horn will return in the next couple weeks from his foot injury, which was a laceration requiring stitches. Good news for an otherwise heavy amount of injury news this off-season. Tetairoa McMillan and LB Trevin Wallace are fully practicing after being limited in OTAs . I doubt I have to go into how important McMillan is, but Wallace is returning from an injury and is expected to be the 2nd linebacker starting alongside Devin Lloyd on the interior. What are you all looking for/seeing from the Panthers during training camp, Panthers fans? Comment down below!

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: Jan 10, 2009; Charlotte, NC, USA; Carolina Panthers fullback Brad Hoover (45) runs as Arizona Cardinals cornerback Ralph Brown (20)defends in the Cardinals 33-13 victory against the Panthers at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Bob Donnan-Imagn Imagescor Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #52. Brad Hoover Fullbacks are a relic of a bygone era of NFL football. For the Panthers, one of their fans’ favorite players from the early aughts happened to be one. Brad Hoover was the epitome of a local product, hailing from High Point, NC and attending Western Carolina. Following the 2000 NFL Draft, the Panthers signed Hoover as an undrafted free agent. His rookie season was actually the most usage he got, carrying the ball 89 times for 290 yards and a touchdown. The 2004 season was another memorable one for Hoover. Starting running backs Stephen Davis and DeShaun Foster both suffered season ending injuries early in the year (as did wide receiver Steve Smith, it was a rough year all around). The defending NFC Champions had eight different running backs carry the ball that year, including a good chunk by Hoover, who was second on the team in rushing attempts that year behind only Nick Goings. Hoover played several snaps at running back for the first time since his college days and led the way for Goings the back half of the year. Once Goings was established as the starter for the last eight games, the Panthers went 6-2. Unfortunately, those aforementioned injuries to key players led to a 1-7 start, and the team missed the playoffs. Hoover would play all ten of his NFL seasons in Carolina, endearing him to the fanbase, many of whom were familiar with him from his college and high school days in the region. His willingness to do the dirty work to spring big plays was constantly on full display, and the fans rewarded his efforts with loud chants of “HOOOOOOOOV” any time he touched the football. Fullbacks never break any statistical records, and Hoover’s career stats are considered paltry by most standards (he finished with less than a thousand career rushing yards). Still, his impact was felt by the fans as well as the opposing defenders as he blew open holes for some of the best rushing attacks the franchise has ever seen. Though his position is often overlooked, fans of the Panthers knew just how important Hoover was to that 2003 Super Bowl run. As one of the unsung heroes of the Panthers ground and pound offense of the early 2000s, Hoover earned the No. 52 spot on our countdown.

title: Ranking Ryan Poles’ draft picks from 2022 and 2023
summary: Ryan Poles concluded his fifth draft as the general manager of the Bears in April, headlining the class with Oregon safety Dillon Thieneman. It’s exciting to imagine what could come from his haul in the 2026 NFL Draft, especially seeing the success Chicago had from their rookie class in 2025. The general belief within the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 23: Darnell Wright #58 of the Chicago Bears lines up before a play during an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Soldier Field on November 23, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ryan Poles concluded his fifth draft as the general manager of the Bears in April, headlining the class with Oregon safety Dillon Thieneman. It’s exciting to imagine what could come from his haul in the 2026 NFL Draft, especially seeing the success Chicago had from their rookie class in 2025. The general belief within the NFL scouting community is that it takes three years to evaluate whether a draft pick was good or not. This coincidences with the fifth-year option deadline, and it gives players a long enough runway period to get acclimated into the league while putting some accountability on the table once contract extensions become a possibility. As of this writing, two of Poles’ draft classes as general manager of the Bears have concluded at least three NFL seasons: the 2022 and 2023 classes. There’s a possibility some of these rankings change as the years progress, but there’s enough film and data on these players to know who the good picks were. These rankings will factor in peak production, longevity, and draft status. For example on the latter: a player who fizzled out as a third-round pick would be ranked lower than a seventh-round pick who fizzled out due to the higher expectations that come with the earlier draft selection. Without further ado, here’s my ranking of all 21 draft picks the Bears made in those two years. 21. Velus Jones Jr. Originally drafted as a wide receiver in the third round of the 2022 NFL Draft, Velus Jones Jr. only ever caught 12 passes for the Bears. He eventually made the change to running back to improve his chances of making the 53-man roster with a better group of weapons in 2024. His pre-draft specialty as a returner didn’t pan out, as he fumbled four times in 27 games before the Bears released him midway through his third year in Chicago. 20. Zacch Pickens Zacch Pickens didn’t even make it to his third year with the Bears, as he ended up a roster cut before the start of the 2025 season, which would’ve been Year 3 in his stint. Their 2023 third-round pick didn’t make much of an impact in two years, tallying just 1.5 sacks and 39 tackles. The only reason Pickens isn’t in last place is because he didn’t actively cost the Bears games like Jones did. 19. Tyler Scott Hand up: I really liked the Tyler Scott pick at the time it was made. The speedster from Cincinnati entered the NFL as a fourth-round pick in 2023 and caught 17 passes for 168 yards as a rookie. He only caught one pass the entire 2024 season, though, and he didn’t offer much value as a special teams defender. The Bears ended up releasing him before the 2025 season, too. 18. Travis Bell One of Ryan Poles’ “favorite human beings” , Travis Bell was a seventh-round pick in 2022 at defensive tackle but never played a regular season snap with the Bears. He bounced around a few NFL practice squads but most recently won a UFL championship with the Louisville Kings this past season. 17. Trestan Ebner Part of Baylor’s one-two punch in the backfield including Abram Smith, Trestan Ebner was the speedster of the two, and despite being less heralded in the pre-draft process, was the only one drafted. Unfortunately, he only played one season with the Bears, averaging just 2.3 yards per carry on 24 rushing attempts. Chicago waived him before the 2023 season, and he never signed with another team. 16. Zachary Thomas One of the three sixth-round picks the Bears made in 2022, Zachary Thomas also never played a snap for the team. He got waived before the start of the regular season and made the practice squad, but he ended up claimed by the Rams in November of that year. Even though he never played for Chicago, the fact that he stuck around the league for a while longer ranks him above Ebner. 15. Trenton Gill The Bears got two years out of Trenton Gill as their punter, but the results were never great. In both of his years, he finished outside of the top 20 in the NFL in both yards per punt and percentage of punts inside the 20-yard line. He ended up released after Chicago drafted Tory Taylor in 2024. Gill played more than the average seventh-round pick, but the production wasn’t up to par for what you’d hope from using a draft pick on a special teamer. 14. Ja’Tyre Carter Ja’Tyre Carter ended up starting two games at guard for the Bears in 2023, but his other 11 appearances with the team were as a backup on special teams. He’s currently on a futures deal with the Panthers, so he’s still in the NFL. For a seventh-round pick, you can do worse than someone who’s remained in the league for five years, even if it’s not with the team who drafted him. 13. Kendall Williamson A seventh-round pick in 2023, Kendall Williamson spent his rookie year on the Bears’ practice squad. However, they didn’t sign him to a futures deal at the end of the regular season, so he became a free agent without ever suiting up for the team. The reason he’s higher than others on this list is because of what he’s done outside of Chicago; he appeared in all 17 games with the Chargers last year, serving as a backup safety and special teams contributor. 12. Doug Kramer Doug Kramer is the highest ranked of his fellow 2022 sixth-round picks, though that’s not necessarily a high bar. He spent 2024 as a primary backup offensive lineman for the Bears, subbing in as a fullback in some instances. He most notably fumbled a handoff on the goal line in Chicago’s loss to the Commanders that year — you know the one — though that’s more the coaching staff’s fault than anything. Kramer gets some credit for having some staying power with the team, as he was on the Bears for the most part of three years. 11. Roschon Johnson The first player on this list who’s still on the Bears, Roschon Johnson showed some encouraging flashes in his second NFL season, rushing for six touchdowns on just 55 carries in 2024. With the addition of Kyle Monangai last offseason, though, Johnson took a step back in his offensive role, carrying the ball just twice in 2025. He’s Chicago’s third-string running back and projects as a special teamer heading into 2026. 10. Noah Sewell Noah Sewell is also still on the Bears’ roster, and he even started in nine games for them in 2025 when T.J. Edwards went down with injury. The results weren’t pretty, though; among 81 qualified linebackers, he ranked just No. 78 with a 64.7 PFN LB Impact Score last year. Sewell has been a serviceable backup and special teamer, though he faces more competition for a roster spot going into 2026. 9. Dominique Robinson Though he never took that giant leap Bears fans had hoped from him as a developmental edge rusher, Dominique Robinson has made out well for himself as a raw fifth-round pick from Miami (OH) in 2022. He spent four years with the Bears and played in 46 games, tallying 68 tackles and 3.5 sacks. He signed a one-year, $4 million deal with the Texans this offseason. 8. Terell Smith If Terell Smith hadn’t missed the 2025 season due to injury, he’d probably rank higher on this list. He looked the part of great cornerback depth through his first two seasons with the Bears, playing in 26 games and starting in six of them. Heading into the final year of his rookie deal, he’s allowed a passer rating of just 76.9 when targeted in his NFL career thus far. 7. Elijah Hicks The first player on this list to earn a second contract with the Bears, Elijah Hicks has been a staple on their special teams units each of the last four years. He’s combined for 122 tackles in that time and has even stepped in as a replacement on defense when needed, having started 15 games for Chicago. He came back on a one-year, $2.6 million deal this offseason. 6. Tyrique Stevenson It’s tough to tell where to rank Tyrique Stevenson, because…

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Safety
summary: The Chicago Bears carried four safeties last year, and if that trend continues, then there’s not much drama at this position this season. Roster Locks The Bears paid Coby Bryant $40 million over three years to man one safety spot, so he’ll essentially replace Kevin Byard III, who not only played at an All-Pro level […]
full_text: Nov 2, 2025; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Chicago Bears safety Elijah Hicks (22) celebrates during the second quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | Katie Stratman-Imagn Images The Chicago Bears carried four safeties last year, and if that trend continues, then there’s not much drama at this position this season. Roster Locks The Bears paid Coby Bryant $40 million over three years to man one safety spot, so he’ll essentially replace Kevin Byard III, who not only played at an All-Pro level but was also the captain of the defense both years in the Windy City. The 27-year-old Bryant is an ascending talent who brings more versatility, and he quickly embraced a leadership role. “He’s one of those guys, he knows what good football and bad football looks like,” head coach Ben Johnson recently said about Bryant. “He just came from a Super Bowl-winning team. There’s a premium on that experience. I think that easily resonates with all the guys in the locker room. I think there’s an instant amount of respect that he’s garnered because of that.” The 25th overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft brought Oregon safety Dillon Thieneman to Chicago, and while he started the offseason working with the second string, he didn’t stay with the twos very long. “Thieneman worked his way into first-team reps during mandatory minicamp while spending the spring learning Dennis Allen’s defense,” ESPN’s Courtney Cronin recently reported . “Thieneman has been a sponge, particularly with his teammates in the secondary, and soaked up as much knowledge as he could from fellow safeties Coby Bryant and Elijah Hicks, the latter of whom will push him for playing time.” Hicks has carved out a nice career for himself after being a part of Ryan Poles’ first draft class. The former seventh-round pick inked a one-year, $2.6 million deal, and he’ll be a core special teamer while backing up at safety. The Bears also signed Cam Lewis in free agency (2 years/$6M), and he has experience at safety, nickel, and special teams. Lewis missed some of the offseason workouts with an injury, but as long as he’s healthy, he’s a lock. A Good Bet To Make It I think four is plenty at safety with how the roster is constructed, so the other three will be fighting for a spot or two on the practice squad. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad Gervarrius Owens spent last year on Chicago’s practice squad, after previous stints with the Giants, Titans, and Vikings. Anthony Johnson Jr. missed the 2025 season with an injury, but in 2024, he played in 9 games with the Giants, and as a seventh-round pick in 2023 by the Packers, he appeared in 12 games with 4 starts for Green Bay. Skyler Thomas is a 2026 UDFA out of Oregon State, where he averaged 80 tackles a season over his last two years there. Do you see any surprises at safety for the Bears in 2026?
