title: Projecting The Top 3 Offensive Training Camp Battles For The Chicago Bears
summary: They say that the offseason always feels shorter when your favorite team makes the playoffs. For the Chicago Bears and their fans, I’m not sure they would share the same sentiment. Although the offseason was technically shortened by two weeks due to a pair of playoff games, the feeling of getting back and challenging for […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 08: Braxton Jones #70 and Colston Loveland #84 of the Chicago Bears in action against the Minnesota Vikings at Soldier Field on September 08, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images They say that the offseason always feels shorter when your favorite team makes the playoffs. For the Chicago Bears and their fans, I’m not sure they would share the same sentiment. Although the offseason was technically shortened by two weeks due to a pair of playoff games, the feeling of getting back and challenging for a Super Bowl has been a topic of discussion for the better part of seven months. Although the regular season is still just over six weeks away, fans can finally turn their focus to the start of training camp and how this roster will shake out. In just one season, head coach Ben Johnson re-shaped the offense and transformed a Bottom 10 unit into a Top 10 product. For the first time in a decade, the sole focus hasn’t been on the quarterback. Although former No. 1 overall pick Caleb Williams does need to take another step forward in 2026, there’s far more excitement surrounding this unit than anxious energy. Even with high hopes, there are a few camp battles worth keeping an eye on, and that’s what we’ll dive into now. Here are the Top 3 Training Camp battles on the offensive side of the ball. Left Tackle This feels familiar, doesn’t it? It might be hard to believe, but despite having one of the league’s best offensive lines, left tackle continues to be a question mark for this team. Going back to the Bears’ playoff opener against the Green Bay Packers in the Wild Card round, it felt like they had their starting five for the next two-plus seasons. Then, a ruptured patellar tendon to Ozzy Trapilo and a surprise retirement a month later from Drew Dalman, and all of a sudden, that elite offensive line had two open holes in its starting lineup. We’ll dive into both spots, but let’s start at left tackle. Like last year, this will be a multi-week, multi-name competition. The only real saving grace is that this should be a more straightforward competition with two primary names to watch. The veteran Braxton Jones comes in as the odds-on favorite, and assuming he’s healthy, there’s reason to believe he should win the competition pretty handily. That said, former Cleveland Browns first-round pick Jedrick Wills Jr. is an x-factor, pending health. At his best, he’s still young (and talented) enough to make a splash and win the job. The biggest question will be health, which has been the story so far in his NFL career. There’s an outside chance that one of Theo Benedet or Kiran Amegadjie could compete for the starting job. Still, considering the team’s decision in the Divisional Round last year to keep Benedet on the bench for Joe Thuney moving positions, it seems like he’s going to be more of the overall swing offensive lineman, versus being in the conversation to start at left tackle. Amegadjie might still have the talent to develop into a useful player. Still, his continued lack of availability has hurt not only his chances to make an impact but, one could argue, his standing in the roster bubble heading into training camp and the preseason. When all is said and done, fans should expect a healthy Jones to win the job, but if he falters, keep an eye on Wills. No matter how it plays out, simply getting average play would be a massive win for 2026 while Trapilo gets back to full health. Center Center seems like a spot that, no matter how hard the Bears try to fix it, remains a question mark almost every season. When Chicago inked Dalman to a lucrative three-year deal, it’s hard to imagine there were any concerns about him retiring heading into 2026. It’s impossible to fault a player for looking out for their long-term health, but it still came as a shock to everyone around the league. Luckily, the Bears were able to act swiftly, trading for veteran Garrett Bradbury and supplementing that low-cost move with a second-round selection of Logan Jones. Similar to the battle at left tackle, Bradbury appears to be the clear favorite heading into camp. Head coach Ben Johnson has made it clear on multiple occasions that he values a veteran center, and even if Bradbury has been a below-average player for most of his career, the experience factor is something fans should not discount. In terms of scheme fit, Bradbury fits well with his athleticism and overall experience. The ceiling isn’t anything to write home about, but ultimately, they could do a lot worse if he ends up starting for the majority of the upcoming season. Jones, on the other hand, is a seasoned player coming from Iowa. Despite his lack of NFL experience, there’s hope within the organization that he’ll hit the ground running at the professional level. He’s got plenty of starting experience (35 starts in three seasons), and for better or for worse, he’s one of the older prospects that came out of April’s draft (he’ll turn 25 in mid-October). While he might not have the same ceiling as former Iowa standout Tyler Linderbaum, the floor appears to be extremely safe with plenty of room to grow into a quality NFL center. It will be interesting to see how this battle plays out, as the inherent advantage will go to the veteran out of the gate. That said, if Jones proves that he can lead the offense and take charge pre-snap, his overall play, even as a rookie, might be enough to win him the job heading into Week 1. If not, don’t be surprised to see Jones inserted into the starting lineup at some point during the first few months of the season. After all, this coaching staff has shown that they aren’t afraid to mix things up when the time is right. Running Back 3 Even if this battle isn’t as exciting as ones where a starting job is up for grabs, how they choose to handle the third running back spot is absolutely worth keeping an eye on. Some believe that Roschon Johnson, who is going into a contract year, will be the “favorite” for the role. Others, like me, look at Johnson’s history of limited availability and see this as a great opportunity to move in a different direction. It’s still unclear how many names the Bears will keep on the final 53-man roster, but three seems like a safe bet to start. Barring an injury to D’Andre Swift or Kyle Monangai, the top two on the depth chart are as set as they can be. Similar to last season, fans should expect a running back-by-committee approach, with Swift seeing more snaps than Monangai. Even so, we’ve seen how injuries happen, and for that reason, the third running back on the roster is an important one. With Eric Bieniemy off to Kansas City for a second stint, Johnson dipped back into his time in Miami, pulling Eric Studesville in for another stretch in Chicago. The 59-year-old running backs coach spent nine years in Miami, gaining experience from head coaches Adam Gase and Mike McDaniel. Only time will tell how much influence he has in Chicago for Johnson’s offense, but anything taken away from McDaniel’s prolific rushing attack would be an added value to the Bears. Assuming they keep just three players, this competition will come down to four names, including Johnson, Brittain Brown, Salvon Ahmed, and undrafted rookie Coleman Bennett. For my money, this should be a wide-open race, and whoever wins the job will need to strike a balance between contributing on offense and having a noticeable role on special teams. Each player brings something different to the competition, but upside and versatility will be key. For that, I’d deem Ahmed as the early favorite for the job, assuming he can stay healthy.

title: Dan Pitcher may not be in Cincinnati after the 2026 season: Why that’s a good thing
summary: If you want to use a measurement of success for the Bengals in 2026, consider one that doesn’t pertain to wins and losses and how far they go in the playoffs. In addition to that, consider it from offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher’s perspective. Pitcher is an up-and-coming head coaching candidate in the NFL. That means […]
full_text: Oct 8, 2023; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Cincinnati Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-USA TODAY Sports If you want to use a measurement of success for the Bengals in 2026, consider one that doesn’t pertain to wins and losses and how far they go in the playoffs. In addition to that, consider it from offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher’s perspective. Pitcher is an up-and-coming head coaching candidate in the NFL. That means he may be a head coach as early as next year. If you’re a Bengals’ fan, yes, that would mean he wouldn’t be the Bengals’ offensive coordinator in 2027. However, if Pitcher is going to be an attractive head coaching candidate come mid-January, that’s a good thing. That probably means the Bengals’ offense would have been very good in the regular season. Jourdan Rodrigue, who is a tremendous national NFL writer for The Athletic and a regular guest on the NFL Daily podcast with Gregg Rosenthal, recently named a breakout candidate on the coaching staffs of the 32 teams in the NFL . For the Bengals, she mentioned Dan Pitcher. “Pitcher has drawn interest from other teams for both head coach and offensive coordinator positions,” Rodrigue wrote. “With Cincinnati clearly swinging for the fences after an active offseason in hopes of maximizing quarterback Joe Burrow’s prime, Pitcher could receive an even larger spotlight. Senior writer Paul Dehner Jr. also mentioned tight ends coach and run game coordinator James Casey, who he says is ‘beloved’ in the building and has a big role in setting up the run-pass marriage for the rest of the offense.” Here’s another thing that interests me. If the Bengals’ offense is great this season, Pitcher isn’t going to just get interviews from teams that are desperate, a la Cleveland and Las Vegas. He’s going to attract interviews from teams that actually need head coaches and recognize what Pitcher has done with Joe Burrow and the Bengals’ offense. There’s a real chance Pitcher may not be on the Bengals’ coaching staff in 2027. That might not sit well with Bengals fans, but it would be a product of the Bengals being really good on offense this season, and that would probably result in a postseason berth. If Pitcher is also getting interviews for head coaching jobs while the Bengals are in a playoff run, that would be a good thing.

title: Bengals get plenty of positive vibes in 2026 NFL season predictions
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have become a popular dark horse team for the upcoming season for analysts who aren’t banking on old narratives holding true. SB Nation’s Jarrett Bailey put together 61 predictions for the NFL season, and it would do a disservice to him to go over every single one that involves the Bengals here. […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 07: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals looks on prior to the game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Jamie Schwaberow/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have become a popular dark horse team for the upcoming season for analysts who aren’t banking on old narratives holding true. SB Nation’s Jarrett Bailey put together 61 predictions for the NFL season , and it would do a disservice to him to go over every single one that involves the Bengals here. But he had a really positive outlook for how their season will play out. We’ll talk about several of the highlights here. If things play out to Bailey’s predictions, Joe Burrow will have a career year that will help propel Cincinnati back into the playoffs. He has Burrow topping 50 touchdowns and leading the league in passing yards. We also see Ja’Marr Chase get another triple crown. This time getting 20 touchdowns. Obviously, with stats like that, it isn’t surprising some hardware also ends up with the Bengals’ stars. Burrow receives his first MVP award, and Chase gets his first Offensive Player of the Year award. Because of the offensive explosion and a slightly improved defense, Bailey sees this not only being a return to the playoffs for the Bengals, but a strong run as well. Starting with landing the No. 1 seed after winning the division for the first time since 2022. They also end up defeating the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Championship game before suffering a loss to the Dallas Cowboys in the Super Bowl. It is safe to say fans would take a season like this (minus the ending) in a heartbeat after the last three years of frustration for one reason or another. Everyone knows what the offense is capable of, and maybe this is finally the year head coach Zac Taylor lets Burrow and company go out and try to win games with some more aggression early. The defense coming together behind acquisitions like Dexter Lawrence and Bryan Cook, and Burrow ultimately staying healthy are the two biggest X-factors this team faces. If those both break Cincinnati’s way, then it is hard to believe this team isn’t bound for the postseason. And once they make it, Burrow has usually been able to put a run together. What do you think of the predictions, and what are some you have for this team?

The former Bengals quarterback, QB coach, and offensive coordinator called both players “great teammates” and noted Trumpy’s ability to play like a traditional tight end, blocking and getting open over the middle, while also running wide receiver routes. “I always say [Trumpy] was Gronk before Gronk,” Anderson said, referring to future Hall of Fame tight end Rob Gronkowski. Anderson then mentioned that Trumpy’s career yards per catch (15.4) was the best of any Bengal in the franchise’s history. Anderson also talked about Trumpy’s bold move into the broadcast booth and beautiful voice. Then the conversation shifted to Brooks, who Anderson praised for his exceptional toughness between the tackles despite his size as well as his pioneering play in the passing game. “At one point in his career, his touchdown receptions were head and shoulders ahead of every other running back in the league,” Anderson said. Watch the full interview here .

title: Bengals Ring of Honor voting gets even tougher as Willie Anderson reflects on what the honor truly means
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have done a remarkable job of celebrating the franchise’s history since launching the Ring of Honor in 2021. Now, with another loaded ballot and a growing list of deserving candidates, one of the organization’s all-time greats believes the process is becoming almost impossible. Former Bengals offensive tackle Willie Anderson recently discussed the […]
full_text: CLEVELAND - NOVEMBER 26: Offensive lineman Willie Anderson #71 of the Cincinnati Bengals on the sideline during a game against the Cleveland Browns at Cleveland Browns Stadium on November 26, 2006 in Cleveland, Ohio. The Bengals defeated the Browns 30-0. (Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have done a remarkable job of celebrating the franchise’s history since launching the Ring of Honor in 2021. Now, with another loaded ballot and a growing list of deserving candidates, one of the organization’s all-time greats believes the process is becoming almost impossible. Former Bengals offensive tackle Willie Anderson recently discussed the evolution of the Ring of Honor, sharing his thoughts on what the recognition has meant to him and why future voting decisions will only become more difficult. “You can’t put everybody in” In putting some thoughts on the team’s recent ceremony to honor their past greats, Anderson acknowledged the difficult position fans now find themselves in each summer. Congratulations to these 2 legends who gave their all to @Bengals . I still wanna use this time to say to our Bengals owners “ Please reconsider next year’s plan of only putting 1 player per year in the Ring of honor! So many men are deserving and we want them to be here to… https://t.co/8hYOSst0hb — Willie Anderson (@BigWillie7179) July 22, 2026 With modern stars such as Geno Atkins, Andrew Whitworth, A.J. Green, Carlos Dunlap and Leon Hall joining an already stacked group of former Bengals legends on the ballot, every vote inevitably leaves worthy candidates on the outside looking in. That’s exactly what Anderson expected. The Bengals have quietly built one of the NFL’s deepest collections of franchise legends. While the organization spent years without formally recognizing many of its greats, the Ring of Honor has helped bridge generations of Bengals football—from the Riverfront Stadium era all the way to today’s contenders. The honor hits differently For Anderson, being inducted into the Bengals Ring of Honor in 2022 remains one of the defining moments of his football career. Despite earning four Pro Bowl selections, three First-Team All-Pro honors and continued Hall of Fame consideration, Anderson emphasized that being celebrated by the organization and fan base carried unique meaning. It’s a recognition that comes directly from the people who watched those careers unfold every Sunday. That perspective helps explain why Anderson understands how emotional the annual vote has become. Unlike league-wide awards or Hall of Fame voting, the Bengals Ring of Honor represents something deeply personal between the franchise and its supporters. This year’s vote showed exactly how difficult it’s becoming On Wednesday, the Bengals announced that Bob Trumpy and James Brooks earned induction into the 2026 Ring of Honor after voting by season ticket members. They will officially be honored during halftime of Cincinnati’s Nov. 1 home game against the Tennessee Titans. Both players were unquestionably deserving. Trumpy remains arguably the greatest tight end in franchise history, while Brooks is one of the most explosive offensive players the Bengals have ever fielded. Yet even after those two names came off the board, several all-time Bengals remain waiting. The major issue with the club’s reluctance to put out a Ring of Honor for so many years is a logjam of deserving players having to bide their time long after their great careers ended. It has quietly forced the team to add multiple players per year (ranging from two to four, depending on the year), dimming the exclusivity aspect of a team Hall of Fame. In the unfortunate cases with Trumpy, Paul Brown and Ken Riley, their inductions were posthumous. Had the team engaged in this great endeavor earlier on, at least some of these great Bengals figures would have been able to be present to see their careers come full circle. And, while there are many more deserving names waiting, the franchise recently announced that beginning in 2027, only one individual will be inducted each year instead of two, making future ballots even more competitive. That appears to be the qualm Anderson has with the process. A good problem to have For much of the Bengals’ early history, conversations centered around why so many franchise legends weren’t receiving enough recognition. Today, the discussion has shifted—even with the issues of a late start to a Ring of Honor. Instead of wondering whether the Bengals have enough worthy candidates, fans are debating which deserving legend should go first. That’s a testament to both the organization’s rich history and the success of the Ring of Honor itself. As Willie Anderson noted, there simply isn’t enough room for everyone at once—and that’s perhaps the strongest indication yet that the Bengals have built a legacy worth celebrating for generations to come.
author: Anthony Cosenza

title: Cleveland Browns training camp 2026: TE and FB preview, who replaces David Njoku?
summary: Next up on our training camp preview is the tight end position. There are fix tight ends on the roster, but after the departure of David Njoku, all we really have confidence in is Harold Fannin, who had an outstanding rookie season. Who is the next man up, though? We also check out the team’s […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - APRIL 21: Harold Fannin Jr. #44 and run game coordinator/tight ends coach Jeff Blasko of the Cleveland Browns run a drill during a voluntary veteran minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on April 21, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Next up on our training camp preview is the tight end position. There are fix tight ends on the roster, but after the departure of David Njoku , all we really have confidence in is Harold Fannin , who had an outstanding rookie season. Who is the next man up, though? We also check out the team’s fullback candidates heading into camp. 1. Harold Fannin – Starting TE Height: 6-4 | Weight: 241 lbs | Age: 22 Experience: 2 years | College: Bowling Green Browns fans are expecting big things from Harold Fannin this year. After his impressive rookie season with 731 yards receiving, fans are predicting him to be in the 800-1,000 yard receiving range. For some of the league’s elite tight ends, that’s not too far-fetched. In fact, Travis Kelce has done it all 11 seasons he’s been in the NFL. However, David Njoku , who was viewed as an explosive receiving tight end for Cleveland, only surpassed 800 yards once in his 9 years with the team. It’s easy to jump to that being more indicative of the Browns’ quarterback situation as opposed to the talent of the tight end himself. Nonetheless, the most important part here is that Fannin is viewed as a big-time weapon for this offense. As a rookie, he showed a nice mix of acrobatic catches and the strength to generate yards after the catch that didn’t seem like they were even there. If there’s one negative on his receiving game as a rookie, it would be that, in my opinion, he sometimes dropped the easy ones. To grow his game over time, he’ll need to be a better in-line blocking tight end. It took Njoku a few years to get to that point. For now, we’ll see how Todd Monken’s offense utilizes Fannin. Will he be kept in the slot more often like he was as a rookie, with one of the other guys on the depth chart taking on a heavier blocking role? Final Roster Odds: 100% 2. Blake Whiteheart – Backup TE Height: 6-4 | Weight: 250 lbs | Age: 26 Experience: 4 years | College: Wake Forest I usually try to have a loose ranking in these previews for how the depth chart or competitions may unfold, but that isn’t true for the tight end position from the second spot onward. The backup roles after Harold Fannin are wide open. But let’s try to focus back in on Blake Whiteheart here. Whiteheart was an undrafted free agent with the Arizona Cardinals in 2023, but didn’t make their roster at the end of camp in 2024. The Browns added him, and he was off-and-on the team’s practice squad that year before being a backup tight end in 2025. He had maybe one semi-memorable catch in two years with Cleveland, having 8 catches for 55 yards and 1 touchdown. He also contributed 10 tackles on special teams last year. Final Roster Odds: 40% 3. Jack Stoll – Blocking TE Height: 6-4 | Weight: 245 lbs | Age: 28 Experience: 6 years | College: Nebraska Jack Stoll was an undrafted free agent in 2021, and spent the first three years of his career with the Philadelphia Eagles. After that, he’s tried to find a home with the Giants, Dolphins, and Saints. He is not much of a receiving tight end — last year with the Saints, he started 4 games, but had 6 catches for 46 yards and 1 touchdown. Prior to that, his highest receiving totals was in 2022, when he had 11 catches for 123 yards. Stoll has been relied on as a blocking tight end, and the expectation is that he’ll fill that same void in Cleveland. According to Pro Football Focus, Stoll was a Top-15 pass blocking tight end in 2025. It’s not unheard of for career blocking tight ends to see a bigger receiving role, but we’re assuming he won’t be the complementary receiving tight end to Harold Fannin — but he could be the lead candidate for the blocking role. Final Roster Odds: 75% 4. Joe Royer – Rookie TE Height: 6-5 | Weight: 250 lbs | Age: 24 Experience: Rookie | College: Cincinnati If there’s a top candidate for the complementary receiving tight end, it might be rookie Joe Royer . He finished out his college career with Cincinnati, but played several seasons at Ohio State, so many fans will be familiar with him. Taken in the fifth round of this year’s draft , Dane Brugler had him as the 12th-ranked tight end prospect in this year’s class. He’s expected to make his mark as a receiver, not a blocker: Royer is a smooth athlete for the position, with the impressive hands needed to easily adjust and frame the football, regardless of the placement. Although he is more of a one-speed receiver down the seam, he runs hard and has some giddy-up with the ball in his hands (only FBS tight end with multiple receptions of 60-plus yards in 2025). Though competitive as a blocker, his execution must improve for NFL coaches to trust him. DBN’s Barry Shuck also wrote a couple articles about Royer this offseason. The first tells you everything you need to know about Royer’s background , while the other pumps up the possibility of him forming an explosive duo with Fannin. Final Roster Odds: 90% 5. Carsen Ryan – Rookie FB/TE Height: 6-3 | Weight: 255 lbs | Age: 22 Experience: Rookie | College: BYU In the seventh round of the draft, the Browns selected Carsen Ryan . Two tight ends at the back of the draft? Or is there something else going on with Ryan? He was the 18th-ranked tight end in this year’s draft class by Dane Brugler . He went to BYU for his final college season in hopes of getting more reps as a receiving tight end, and it paid off. Brugler praised his all-around game and didn’t summarize any weaknesses, which begs the question: why did he fall to the 7th round? A surprising NFL combine snub, Ryan stands out in both phases as a receiver and blocker. He is an urgent, controlled route runner who feasts underneath against zone coverage, with reliable hands and some creativity after the catch. He is limited by some body stiffness and needs to do a better job with body position to win a crowd. As a blocker, he is both quick and physical with his inline duties to reach, cut off or get outside defenders. I’ve seen some labels thrown out there that Monken might consider Ryan for the fullback position, considering his former experience as a running back. But with there not being a proven candidate at tight end, he has just as good of a chance as any to ascend the depth chart, even as a 7th round pick. On the same note, since his draft status wasn’t high to begin with, Cleveland is also in a position to where they can probably stash him on the practice squad. Barry Shuck also did a nice write-up on Ryan’s background here . Final Roster Odds: 50% 6. Brenden Bates – Backup TE Height: 6-5 | Weight: 255 lbs | Age: 26 Experience: 3 years | College: Kentucky Brenden Bates has now had two stints with the Browns. He began his NFL career as an undrafted free agent in 2024 with the Bears, and then went to the Jets. Cleveland signed him at the end of 2024, and then spent half the season on the team’s practice squad before the Texans signed him. When he was waived, he then was re-signed by the Browns to their roster. With the Browns last year, Bates started 3 games and had 2 catches for 25 yards. He’s lumped into the same group as Whiteheart and Stoll, and unfortunately he likely falls third in that group, so I’m expecting him more so to play a role on the third-team offense in camp. Final Roster Odds: 25% 7. Michael Burton – Fullback Height: 6-0 | Weight: 247 lbs | Age: 34 Experience: 12 years | College: Rutgers Last, but not least, we have fullback Michael Burton on the team. If someone would’ve asked you, “Which player on the Browns’ roster has been in the league the longest,” you probably wouldn’t have guessed Burton (although that might be because you didn’t even know he was on the team). Burton has 12 years of NFL experience.…

summary: Cleveland Browns general manager Andrew Berry has received mostly positive reviews for the work he did in the offseason to address the team’s aging and injured offensive line. full_text: Aug 7, 2009; Berea, OH, USA; A general feature of a Blocking Sled at Cleveland Browns training camp. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Emmons-Imagn Images Cleveland Browns general manager Andrew Berry has received mostly positive reviews for the work he did in the offseason to address the team’s aging and injured offensive line. Sure, there have been some grumblings that Berry may have overpaid in free agency, most notably guard Zion Johnson, but no one can say that Berry did not see a need and did what he could to fix it. Teams have to look past just the upcoming season, of course, which is why Berry selected Spencer Fano, Austin Barber, and Parker Brailsford in the 2026 NFL Draft. Fano is expected to hold down the left tackle position for the next decade or so, Barber looks to have a future at either guard or tackle, and Brailsford will be looking to earn the starter’s role at center this summer. With the line mostly set for the next year or two, now could be a time to bring in a developmental player, one who has some skills but could use some polishing and some quality coaching from the likes of offensive line coach George Warhop. A player like Dodji Dahoue, who is looking for a team after not sticking with the New York Giants as an undrafted free agent. No immediate signing for former undrafted #Giants , Eastern Michigan @EMUFB offensive tackle Dodji Dahoue, per league source, but remains a good potential practice squad International Player Pathway candidate for team. Dahoue (6-foot-9, 310) born in France, raised in Washington,… https://t.co/Mw6CMcKQoF pic.twitter.com/09c1Jxh5kx — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) July 23, 2026 Dahoue is massive (6-foot-9 and 300 pounds), smart (he earned a degree in mechanical engineering at Eastern Michigan), and a quick learner, as pointed out in this story from the Eastern Michigan football team’s website : Dahoue’s path to Eastern Michigan stands out for how quickly he developed into a contributor after coming to football later than most. Born in France and raised between the Washington, D.C., area and Mali, he did not play football in high school at Lycée Liberté de Bamako, graduating at just 16 before returning to the United States in 2021. He enrolled at Santa Rosa Junior College, where he initially redshirted while learning the fundamentals of the game after briefly exploring basketball. By 2022, he broke through as the program’s Freshman of the Year, and in 2023 he served as a team captain and earned All-Nor-Cal Conference honors, showing rapid growth on the field. At Eastern Michigan, Dahoue continued that upward trajectory. He saw action in six games during the 2024 season, gaining experience at the collegiate level, before stepping into a starting role in 2025. He started five games and was establishing himself as a key piece of the lineup before a season-ending injury cut his year short. Throughout his time at EMU, Dahoue’s impact was evident in his physical presence and continued development, culminating in a unique journey from no football background to a junior college standout and Division I starter. Not your normal path to the NFL, but Dahoue was a starter his senior year before being injured, and the MAC is a respectable enough football conference that some team will likely give him a look. Could that be the Browns? Maybe. They need all the bodies they can get when it comes to the offensive line, and developmental players are not just reserved for the quarterback. So perhaps they would be open to giving Dahoue a tryout to see if he brings enough to the field to warrant a longer look. What do you think, Browns fans? Should the team bring Dahoue in for a look? Or do they have enough on their plate already when it comes to the offensive line? Let us know in the comments!

(Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images With rookies and other veterans reporting to Berea , Cleveland Browns training camp is all but officially open. There are question upon question around the roster, despite a load of lauded young talent , starting with the quarterback position . The turnover on the offensive side of the ball has been staggering. The defense has been a different story, but two huge departures did occur: DC Jim Schwartz resigned , and DE Myles Garrett was traded . The Browns are hoping that DC Mike Rutenberg can buoy the ship while depending on DE Jared Verse and the interior defensive line to replace Garrett. Veteran DT Maliek Collins is one of those key pieces , but he is coming back from a Week 13 knee injury that ended his 2025 season prematurely. That injury will linger into the start of Cleveland’s training camp, as Collins was placed on the active/PUP list: We have placed DT Maliek Collins on active/PUP 📰 » https://t.co/xSCsPeMI4U pic.twitter.com/rzqXl7iL6X — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) July 23, 2026 Details of what the active/PUP list means : Like players on IR, players are put on the active/physically unable to perform list (or PUP) at the start of training camp because of a football-related injury. The difference is these players count against the active roster limit. Players on the PUP list can participate in all team activities except practice. They can be activated at any point during camp once they are medically cleared. A player can’t be placed on the PUP list after they have practiced or played in a preseason game. Players on the active/PUP list can be moved to the reserve/PUP list during the preseason roster cutdown period. Players won’t count against the active roster limit if they’re placed on the reserve/PUP list and they must miss the first four games of the season. HC Todd Monken had noted previously that Collins’ injury could last into the start of training camp. With players reporting, we will continue to cover all injury, physical, and conditioning-related reports over the next few days.

Biggest question the Cowboys are facing How quickly can Parker’s defense get up to speed? There are a lot of changes in personnel — potentially up to seven new starters — and scheme, as they move to a 3-4 system. The pass rush has much to prove with the biggest addition being the trade for edge rusher Rashan Gary from the Green Bay Packers . The linebacker room is not particularly deep, and DeMarvion Overshown will have to prove he can stay healthy. The secondary has improved with additions in free agency (S Jalen Thompson , CB Cobie Durant ) and the draft (first-rounder S Caleb Downs ). The Cowboys do not have to have another Doomsday Defense to succeed in 2026, but the defense needs to be much improved over last season to make a difference. Three players to watch WR George Pickens : He is on the franchise tag at a cost of $27.3 million as the Cowboys want to see more from him in his second season before deciding whether to commit long term to the receiver. He set career highs in catches (93), yards (1,429) and touchdowns (nine) in his first season. The contract issue is resolved for at least this season, but how will Pickens respond? LB Malachi Lawrence : Downs has received most of the attention as the Cowboys’ first of two first-round picks (No. 11), but Lawrence, selected at No. 22, is as imperative to the defense’s success as Downs. He has to be a factor in the pass-rush department for the defense to succeed. LT Tyler Guyton : The left tackle is entering his third year, and he could hold the key to the offense. Injuries have slowed his progress, but he was better in 2025 before a high ankle injury ended his season. He has to stay healthy and perform at a high level. If he can, then the Cowboys can keep their front five in the spots they want them in, which means Tyler Smith stays at left guard. The Oxnard Iliad: Cowboys’ 0 to 99 training camp guide – Dan Rogers, Blogging the Boys Get the rundown on the Cowboys training camp roster. As the cool Pacific breeze rolls off Mandalay Beach into Oxnard, the countdown to Dallas Cowboys training camp signals the arrival of a new battle. Much like the grueling siege on the beaches of Troy, the upcoming weeks will transform the practice fields into a theater of war where hungry longshots and seasoned veterans clash in fierce, unforgiving roster battles. Every depth-chart skirmish is driven by tactical deception, where coaching staffs look to unveil their own Trojan Horse surprises, whether through a hidden-gem player or an unexpected battlefield wrinkle drawn up from their new young general. With 90 soldiers descending on the practice fields, keeping track of every fresh face can be a little difficult. That is why we have broken down the entire roster by the numbers, literally, to provide you with an ultimate cheat sheet for every single player running around this summer. From elite cornerstone pillars to the fiery undrafted rookies clawing for a spot on the practice squad, here is one thing you should know about every Cowboys’ player as the pads go on and the battles begin. Cowboys Executive Will McClay Addresses George Pickens’ Future in Dallas – Randy Gurzi, SI.com Will McClay speaks on George Pickens future. While appearing on Crown Global Media’s Doin’ Alright podcast, McClay said he’s not concerned with outside perceptions . He even said he doesn’t want anyone to tell him how to handle his checkbook, just like he wouldn’t tell anyone what to do with theirs. ”Public perception is, oh, you should sign this guy and do that. But, you know, I don’t tell you how to run your checkbook, you don’t tell me how to run mine. And it’s, you know, our businesses. And so I really, everybody’s philosophy is a little bit different. And we love George Pickens,” McClay said. “Finding a way to fill the team with 53 of the best players in today’s day and age is very, very difficult. So you go through the different contracts and the different aspects and all those different ways and you put it together. And that situation with George presented itself in a way that we could do it that way and still keep our team together. That’s the best way for me to put it.” Could McClay’s comments mean George Pickens will stay in Dallas long-term? Dallas Cowboys insider disagreed with some of my 38 roster locks, and he makes some fair points – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports Who could be some surprise cuts this offseason? LT Nate Thomas I see why Fisher isn’t treating Thomas as a lock. The likes of fourth-round rookie Drew Shelton and even Ajani Cornelius could change the math quickly in camp. But with Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer announcing to the world former first-round rookie Tyler Guyton is competing with Thomas for the starting role, that to me means Thomas is on another tier compared to other linemen. If he’s competing to start, he has to be a lock, right? To Fisher’s point, I do believe the so-called open competition at offensive tackle is more of a motivation tactic to light a fire for Guyton than anything else. Role Call: Otito Ogbonnia tasked with replacing impact DT in 2026 – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com Otito Ogbonnia will likely play a big role in 2026. How He Got Here: This should all feel very familiar for Ogbonnia, being in Texas, I mean. That’s because he hails from Katy, TX, an afternoon drive south of NTX in the Houston area. His talent in high school took him to UCLA, meaning there’s an added familiarity in that it’s also the school attended by fellow defensive linemen Kenny Clark and Jay Toia. Ogbonnia, a former fifth-round pick of the Los Angeles Chargers in 2022, was signed this offseason as a free agent to help add depth following the decision to trade another former Bruin, Osa Odighizuwa, to the San Francisco 49ers. What’s Next: Ogbonnia will walk into training camp with the express mission of proving he can be a worthy backup to Clark and All-Pro defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. That will, of course, pit him against Toia, but also Jonathan Bullard and others. Working in his favor is the fact he’s got 21 NFL starts in 40 active games under his belt, with 82 combined tackles through his first four seasons in the league. He’ll need to combine his youth with his experience to make waves in Oxnard and beyond for Christian Parker. Daily discussion question: What will we be talking about this time next week?

title: One prediction for training camp, offensive line edition
summary: Our Dallas Cowboys prediction series continues. Today, we’ll look at arguably the most important position on offense beyond quarterback – the offensive line. The offensive line is the backbone of the offense. A unit that was explosive and capable for the Cowboys in 2025 is looking to build on that success with continuity and by […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - SEPTEMBER 08: Tyler Guyton #60 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on during the first quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on September 08, 2024 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Our Dallas Cowboys prediction series continues. Today, we’ll look at arguably the most important position on offense beyond quarterback – the offensive line. The offensive line is the backbone of the offense. A unit that was explosive and capable for the Cowboys in 2025 is looking to build on that success with continuity and by continuing to develop the young talent. Tyler Booker looks like he’ll be elite soon, Tyler Smith already is, and Cooper Beebe is solid now, with future potential. It’s the tackles that are the issue. Terence Steele has his issues and one day may be replaced, but it is Tyler Guyton providing the most worry. The Cowboys invested a first-round pick on the left tackle. Guyton’s numbers were not good in 2025. He was ranked No. 71 out of 89 graded tackles last year overall by Pro Football Focus , and ranked 81st and 46th, between pass and run blocking, respectively. He also missed seven games due to injuries, so his reliability has also come into question. Guyton’s inconsistency could ultimately lead to more questions. Do the Cowboys have to play musical chairs with the left side of the line if he continues to struggle by moving Tyler Smith to tackle? Do they make the change to Nate Thomas or even Drew Shelton, possibly closing the door on Guyton’s future with the Cowboys? For Guyton, however, it is his athleticism that stands out, and ultimately what will help him get back on track at camp. Prediction: Tyler Guyton ends the talk of a competition for LT early in camp Now that Brian Schottenheimer has declared that position up for grabs between Guyton and Nate Thomas, Guyton will start to put it all together in camp and end the competition talk. Thomas, who also had his fair share of struggles last year, will be the motivational tool Guyton will use to his advantage. He will build on the strengths he has as a run blocker by improving his pass blocking, and the left tackle position will not only be his, but the left side of the offensive line will be secure. Agree or disagree? What is your one prediction for the offensive line?

title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 52
summary: It is Day 52 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Jan 7, 1979; Los Angeles, CA, USA; FILE PHOTO; Dallas Cowboys running back (33) TONY DORSETT in action against the Los Angeles Rams during the 1978 NFC Championship at Memorial Coliseum. The Cowboys defeated the Rams 28-0. Mandatory Credit: David Boss-Imagn Images © Copyright David Boss It is Day 52 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. We’re now at Day 52 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit a statement win from Roger Staubach’s final regular season. The Cowboys hosted the Los Angeles Rams in Week 7 of the 1979 season, and Dallas delivered one of its cleanest performances of the year, and looked every bit like one of the NFC’s top teams. Sunday, October 14, 1979 — 9:00 p.m. ET Texas Stadium, Irving, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 30, Los Angeles Rams 6 The Rams had been one of Dallas’ recurring NFC measuring-stick opponents throughout the 1970s, and the Cowboys had shut them out 28-0 in the previous season’s NFC Championship Game. A win here would make it two straight Dallas wins over Los Angeles and give the Cowboys another reminder that when Staubach and Tom Landry’s offense were in rhythm, they could overwhelm any opponent. The Cowboys started by leaning on their stars. Staubach connected with Tony Hill for an 18-yard touchdown in the first quarter, giving Dallas the early lead. From there, the Cowboys steadily squeezed the Rams with balance on offense and control on defense. Los Angeles managed only two Frank Corral field goals, while Dallas kept finding ways to stretch the margin. Tony Dorsett kept his strong midseason run going, rushing for 103 yards which gave the Cowboys balance, forced the Rams to defend the entire field, and helped open things up for Staubach in the passing game. Staubach was the headline in this game, throwing three touchdown passes. That performance pushed him to 137 career touchdown passes, breaking Don Meredith’s Cowboys franchise record. In a season that would eventually become his final NFL campaign, this was one more reminder that “Captain Comeback” was still operating at a high level. The Cowboys put the game away with a 17-point third quarter, turning a competitive game into a comfortable primetime win. For a team that had been built for years on postseason toughness and big-game composure, this felt like a classic Landry-era control game, run the ball, protect the quarterback, hit explosive passes, and squeeze the opponent until the scoreboard reflected the gap. By the time the fourth quarter arrived, the Rams were no longer threatening. Dallas had 403 total yards, including 201 rushing yards and 202 passing yards, while Los Angeles finished with only 158 total yards. The defensive side may have been the most impressive part. The Rams had explosive players, but Dallas kept them out of the end zone and forced three turnovers. This game belongs on the countdown because it captures the Cowboys in one of their final regular-season peaks under Staubach. They were still dangerous, still balanced, and still capable of making a playoff-caliber opponent look ordinary. #Cowboys vs #Rams 1979 Week 7 Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 30, Los Angeles Rams 6 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/eEUzpzeE4T — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 22, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game Tony Dorsett rushed for 103 yards, part of a strong midseason stretch in which he also ran for 145 yards against Minnesota the week before and 111 against St. Louis the week after. title: Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: OLB Charles Snowden
summary: Charles Snowden joined the Cowboys late into the offseason, but his pass-rushing experience could help him stick around when it really matters. Where does Snowden fit into the growing competition at outside linebacker, and how much does an impending three-game suspension hurt his chances? Background Years in NFL: 5Acquired by: Free agent (2026) Despite mid-round grades by […]
full_text: Aug 23, 2025; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Las Vegas Raiders defensive end Charles Snowden (49) against the Arizona Cardinals during a preseason NFL game at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images Charles Snowden joined the Cowboys late into the offseason, but his pass-rushing experience could help him stick around when it really matters. Where does Snowden fit into the growing competition at outside linebacker, and how much does an impending three-game suspension hurt his chances? Background Years in NFL: 5 Acquired by: Free agent (2026) Despite mid-round grades by some in 2021, Snowden went undrafted after a late-season ankle injury at Virginia limited his ability to participate in the Senior Bowl and pre-draft workouts. He signed with Chicago as a UDFA and spent most of the year on their practice squad, but did get called up for two games. For the next two years, Snowden struggled to find a home. He didn’t get a job following the Bears’ 2022 camp, then was unemployed for a few months before landing on Tampa Bay’s practice squad. Same story in 2023: didn’t make the Bucs roster or practice squad, was out for a while, then joined the Raiders’ practice squad in December. He started 2024 on Las Vegas’ practice team again, but was quickly called up and appeared in 16 games. Over the last two years in Vegas, Snowden has logged 18 starts and had a regular share in their pass-rush rotation. He had career highs in 2025 with three sacks and five tackles-for-loss, plus his first and only interception. With only two accrued seasons so far, Snowden was an exclusive rights free agent this past March and did get a minimal deal from Vegas. But the Raiders released him shortly after the draft, and Snowden sat in free agency until signing with Dallas in mid-June. On July 14th, news broke that Snowden was suspended for the first three games of 2026 because of a DUI that occurred back in 2024. The delayed punishment from the league was allegedly because it took that long for the legal process to play out. Snowden is allowed to fully participate in training camp and preseason games, not facing any restrictions until final cuts. Contract Status Years Left: 1 2026 Cap Hit: $1.1 million There is some conflicting information out there about Snowden’s deal, some having it as a one-year contract and others two years. The one-year deal makes more sense as he’d still be a restricted free agent in 2027, and turns 29 next March. The Cowboys retain some leverage, while Snowden gets a shot making more money before he hits 30. 2026 Projections Role: Backup OLB Roster Chance: 50% Dallas already had plenty of OLB options before signing Snowden. With three spots guaranteed for Rashan Gary, Donovan Ezeiruaku, and Malachi Lawrence, and a likely fourth for James Houston, there was going to be fierce competition between Sam Williams, Tyrus Wheat, Marist Liufau, and Isaiah Land for probably one last job on the 53-man roster. The Cowboys probably already knew about Snowden’s suspension before they signed him, so that shouldn’t be a major factor in their decision. If anything, it gives them a freebie on a potential depth guy for three weeks who won’t count against the 53. Snowden can compete for the next month, then Dallas can shelve him for three weeks and see how other guys fare on the field. Maybe they release someone to make room for him, or maybe injuries open a spot. Or, the Cowboys could just release him if they feel good about the rotation. Given Snowden’s experience, it’s reasonable that he could easily beat out guys like Wheat, Liufau, and Land this summer. The real competition will be with Williams, who has plenty of experience in his own right and was a standout special teamer last year. Many feel that Williams will thrive as a 3-4 OLB, so he could leave all other down-roster contenders in the dust. Still, Dallas saw something in Snowden that they made the 28-year-old a late addition to their training camp roster. At that age, and with the suspension looming, the Cowboys must feel that Snowden could be valuable during the regular season. His 6’6” frame will make him easy to spot on the field, but hopefully his play in preseason games will be what really attracts attention. title: Cowboys’ LB identified as player with the ‘most on the line’ in 2026
summary: The Athletic recently gathered their NFL reporters together to compile a list by choosing one player from each team who they believe has the most at stake entering the 2026 season. For the Dallas Cowboys, Jon Machota chose linebacker DeMarvion Overshown. Dallas Cowboys: DeMarvion Overshown, LB Three players immediately come to mind: Overshown, LT Tyler […]
full_text: The Athletic recently gathered their NFL reporters together to compile a list by choosing one player from each team who they believe has the most at stake entering the 2026 season. For the Dallas Cowboys, Jon Machota chose linebacker DeMarvion Overshown. Dallas Cowboys: DeMarvion Overshown, LB Three players immediately come to mind: Overshown, LT Tyler Guyton and WR George Pickens. Overshown gets the nod because he’s in the final year of his rookie contract. Guyton will likely have another season in Dallas even if this one doesn’t go well. Pickens is likely getting paid well by the Cowboys or another team in free agency next year. Overshown doesn’t have that type of job security. When healthy, he’s easily Dallas’ best linebacker. But significant knee injuries have caused him to miss 32 games over the last three seasons. A strong, full season likely leads to a quality new deal. But if he’s unable to stay on the field, Overshown could be left with underwhelming contract offers. — Jon Machota Of the potential Dallas Cowboys players Jon Machota could have chosen as the player with the most at stake entering the 2026 season, you can’t argue LB DeMarvion Overshown wasn’t the right choice. Not only does he have to prove he can overcome his past injury history, but also has to prove he can be a reliable starter in a contract year. If Overshown can stay healthy for the entire 2026 season, he could prove to be one of the best off-ball LBs in the entire league. He was just recently landed outside the Top 10 LBs in ESPN’s rankings, but possesses the talent to shoot up that list with a strong showing this season. Staying healthy of course will be key though. Overshown isn’t the only Cowboys player with a lot at stake this season. There is one player on the roster who might have more at stake than him, cornerback DaRon Bland, who could potentially be playing his last season in Dallas if his play doesn’t improve. Despite being the seventh highest-paid CB in the league, Bland’s play hasn’t lived up to his big-money contract recently. A lot of that probably has to do with the reoccurring foot injury that’s required surgery in back-to-back seasons. He too, like Overshown, has to prove he can overcome his concerning injury history to once again play at an All-Pro level like in 2023. It could be a toss of the coin as to which player, Bland or Overshown, has more at stake entering the 2026 season. Both have troubling injury history’s over the past few years and both could be playing to remain in Dallas beyond this year. Bland could potentially be a salary-cap casualty if his play doesn’t improve and Overshown may not receive an extension from the Cowboys. If all goes as planned, both Overshown and Bland will remain healthy for the entire season and be at their best. These two players are expected to be key members of Christian Parker’s new-look 3-4 defense, and as such, will play important roles this season. If they don’t play up to par, and could be in another disappointing season for Dallas’ defense. Who do you think has the most at stake heading into the 2026 season?

title: The other Cowboys rookie to watch during training camp
summary: Five years ago, almost, I had a theory. I believed, still do, that if not for Micah Parsons and what he did across his rookie season, then Osa Odighizuwa would have received a lot more attention. This is a bit ambitious, but maybe Odighizuwa would have even wound up as a Defensive Rookie of the […]
full_text: May 1, 2026; Frisco, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys linebacker Jaishawn Barham (55) goes through a drill during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images Five years ago, almost, I had a theory. I believed, still do, that if not for Micah Parsons and what he did across his rookie season, then Osa Odighizuwa would have received a lot more attention. This is a bit ambitious, but maybe Odighizuwa would have even wound up as a Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate. You never know. The Dallas Cowboys brand never hurts in that way. Incidentally, Odighizuwa was traded away this offseason and we are wishing him all the best (at least individually). Now coincidentally, the pick that Dallas received from the San Francisco 49ers in the trade may have helped set up his successor for being the “other” defensive rookie on the Cowboys. Jaishawn Barham is going to be important to watch during camp Caleb Downs is obviously going to absorb a majority of the headlines and attention in the way that Micah Parsons did, but this means that his version of Osa Odighizuwa is Jaishawn Barham. While Downs is a game-changer and one that we all remain incredibly thrilled about, his selection did not satisfy the biggest need on the Cowboys roster across the offseason. Jaishawn Barham’s did. Dallas was, and is still, in sore need of help at linebacker. Also coincidentally, the Cowboys struck a second trade with the 49ers this offseason for linebacker help and did so shortly before selecting Barham during the NFL draft. Dallas acquired Dee Winters from their longtime rivals so in many ways the 49ers built the Cowboys current linebacking group. With all due respect to Winters, and residually DeMarvion Overshown, Barham is going to be the player to watch throughout training camp, and a big reason for that is the versatility of being able to play traditional linebacker and having the ability to be a serious pass rusher. ESPN recently named him as a rookie to watch during training camp at large. Jaishawn Barham, LB, Dallas Cowboys An intriguing defensive shift is underway in Dallas, as new coordinator Christian Parker brings a Vic Fangio-inspired system to a roster that has endured a brutal coaching carousel. Dallas has had four defensive coordinators in the past four years: Dan Quinn, Mike Zimmer, Matt Eberflus and now Parker. That car wash, along with some bad injury luck and draft misses (and the trade of Micah Parsons) has left the Cowboys’ defense thin on young and exciting talent. Barham might change that. He started his career in college as an inside linebacker before kicking to the edge in his final season with Michigan. Dallas plans to move the third-round pick back to stack linebacker, where plenty of snaps are up for grabs in a thin room that features Dee Winters and DeMarvion Overshown. But because Barham has experience rushing the passer, he can fill the Zack Baun/Jihaad Campbell role in Dallas — an integral spot in the Eagles’ defense that Parker helped coach for the past two seasons. How often the Cowboys give Barham snaps in training camp — and where exactly he lines up — will be a sign of how the first-year coordinator intends to call defense in 2026. We have allowed ourselves, rightfully, to dream about how Christian Parker is going to utilize Caleb Downs specifically. That makes sense given Parker’s background as a defensive backs guru. But Parker obviously has a history with the Philadelphia Eagles and the way that they utilized, as ESPN notes here, both Zack Baun and Jihaad Campbell was of the “we need some of that” variety. Perhaps Barham is that answer and in some ways that is a more important question to answer than anything. Training camp is just about here and we are finally going to start getting answers to some of these questions. This is one of the more paramount ones, and hopefully the answer is one that we all like.
author: RJ Ochoa

title: The Cowboys don’t need more points, they need more early leads
summary: It’s a widely held belief that the Cowboys are not great starters. And at first glance, the numbers seem to bear that out: last year, the Cowboys had four games (24%) in which they failed to score a single point in the first quarter, and scored no more than a field goal in the first […]
full_text: It’s a widely held belief that the Cowboys are not great starters. And at first glance, the numbers seem to bear that out: last year, the Cowboys had four games (24%) in which they failed to score a single point in the first quarter, and scored no more than a field goal in the first quarter in 10 out of 17 games (59%). Those numbers sound alarming. They really aren’t. Last year, NFL teams went scoreless in the opening quarter 32% of the time and scored no more than a field goal in 52% of first quarters. The Cowboys weren’t unusually bad in the first quarter last season. In fact, by league standards they were around average. The Cowboys weren’t unusually bad in the first quarter last season. In fact, by league standards they were around average. The real issue was that those points rarely translated into an early lead. Here’s the winning percentage, by quarter, of teams that held the lead at the end of each respective quarter last year (numbers don’t add up to 272 games because some games were tied at the end of a quarter). body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 4px 6px !important; } NFL win probability when in the lead, by quarter, 2025 1. Quarter 2. Quarter 3. Quarter W/L 148 – 63 – 1 160 – 71 – 1 158 – 62 in % 70% 70% 72% Last year, teams leading after the first quarter won 70% of the time. Remarkably, that percentage barely changed as the game progressed. There’s no question that jumping out to an early lead can be a major advantage. Playing with the lead changes the game on both offense and defense. Teams playing from behind are forced to take more risks, creating mistakes that teams with the lead are then able to exploit. Playing with the lead changes the game, so let’s look at how the Cowboys have done in this department, and try to figure out what’s behind it. And we’ll start by contrasting the 2025 team with the three 12-5 teams from 2021-23. body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 4px 6px !important; } Cowboys record based on scores after Q1 Leading after Q1 Trailing after Q1 Game tied Cowboys 2021-23 27-2 7-9 2-4 Cowboys 2025 2-1 4-4-1 1-4 The difference is striking: where the 12-5 teams averaged almost 10 games per season in which they held a lead after the first quarter, the 2025 team had just three. The winning percentage when trailing or with the game tied after the first quarter for the 2025 team is 39%, that of the three 12-5 teams is only marginally better at 41%. So, the issue for the 2025 teams was not so much about catching up, but about not being able to jump out to an early lead. And there are multiple reasons for that. Ineffective Game Scripts The first 15-20 or so offensive plays are pre-planned during the week. There are many reasons why these plays may not work: sloppy execution, the opponent anticipating the plays, or the plays simply not being very good. We also know that at least part of the game script is designed to figure out the opposing defense. Rather than immediately attacking to score, this probing approach on offense is not conducive to scoring early. In any case, when these scripted plays fail to pick up first downs, the offense stalls, forcing them to play catch-up later in the game. Deferred Strategy Like most other teams, the Cowboys almost always defer possession to the second half if they win the coin toss. Deferring is usually the analytically correct decision because it maximizes the chance of consecutive possessions around halftime. But analytics always assume an average team. When you’re fielding one of the league’s worst defenses, voluntarily asking that defense to make the game’s first stop may no longer be the optimal strategy. The Cowboys won the coin toss eight times last year, and elected to receive just once, in Week 7 against Washington. Perhaps the team was still optimistic about the defense in the first half of the season, but they knew for sure that they were in dire defensive straits in the second half of the season. They won three coin tosses in the second half (Weeks 14, 15, and 18) and still elected to defer in each one. Given what we knew about the defense by December, those three decisions are worth questioning. Self-Inflicted Wounds The Cowboys frequently derailed their own opening drives through penalties, dropped passes, or costly early turnovers, putting even more pressure on an already outmatched defense. We often talk about how the offense remains largely unchanged versus last year and how that is a good thing. Last year’s Cowboys weren’t undone because they couldn’t score enough points or couldn’t come from behind. They were undone because they spent too much of the season playing from behind. The 12-win Cowboys teams didn’t succeed because they were comeback artists. They succeeded because they spent most Sundays playing with the lead. If Brian Schottenheimer wants to get this team back into the playoffs, that challenge starts with the first two drives of every game.

title: Cowboys news: Diving into the competition at offensive tackle
summary: Cowboys Depth Chart: Training camp competition awaits at offensive tackle – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram There are some things to work out at offensive tackle. Safe (4) Tyler Guyton, Terence Steele, Nate Thomas, Drew Shelton While there will be competition at left tackle and questions still exist around the long-term stability at right tackle, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 14: Tyler Guyton #60 of the Dallas Cowboys runs across the field during an NFL football game against the New York Giants at AT&T Field on September 14, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Cowboys Depth Chart: Training camp competition awaits at offensive tackle – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram There are some things to work out at offensive tackle. Safe (4) Tyler Guyton, Terence Steele, Nate Thomas, Drew Shelton While there will be competition at left tackle and questions still exist around the long-term stability at right tackle, the 53-man roster spots are safe at the top of the room. Tyler Guyton is the one with the biggest microscope on him going into training camp. The 2024 first-round pick has yet to put together a fully healthy training camp, much less a fully healthy season. After head coach Brian Schottenheimer said during OTAs that Guyton’s starting job is up for grabs , the need for progression is bigger than it has ever been for the Oklahoma product. Through two seasons, Guyton has allowed 57 quarterback pressures and eight sacks. On the other side, Terence Steele should be able to hold down his starting job at right tackle because of his strong run blocking ability. However, lapses exist in his pass protection, as he’s given up 93 quarterback pressures and 15 sacks over the past two seasons. He’s been a staple of durability since tearing his ACL in 2022, though, as he’s started every game over the past three seasons. At left tackle, 2024 seventh-round pick Nate Thomas is Guyton’s biggest threat for the starting job. After being moved from guard to tackle before training camp last season, Thomas quickly ascended up the depth chart. He is now in position to be the starting left tackle, at best, or the backup swing tackle with a strong training camp. The staff’s confidence in Thomas didn’t quite translate onto the field; across 219 pass block snaps last season, Thomas allowed 23 pressures and three sacks. The dark horse in the room is fourth-round rookie Drew Shelton . In a draft class that had an overflowing bucket of right tackle talent, the Cowboys took a day-three swing on Shelton, who primarily played left tackle at Penn State. Across 356 pass block snaps as a senior, Shelton allowed just 18 pressures and one sack. With a lack of confidence at the top of the depth chart, a path exists for Shelton to make a big impact as a rookie with a strong training camp. Myth Busting Season: 3 Dallas Cowboys storylines that training camp will reveal more about, including Caleb Downs’ role – Mauricio Rodriguez, AtoZ Sports These will certainly be some interesting things to watch. Dallas Cowboys training camp is days away, and with it comes the annual opportunity to separate fact from fiction. Every offseason, Cowboys coaches drop hints about how they plan to use certain players, and every year, some of those hints turn out to be a whole bunch of nothing. Or at the very least, nothing compared to what Cowboys fans and media make them out to be. I’m talking about when the Cowboys hinted fullback Hunter Huepke would evolve into a tight end. Or when wide receiver KaVontae Turpin was supposed to take running back snaps. And one of my favorites: when Tony Pollard was going to line up as a slot receiver. All of those storylines fizzled. But there have been many others that turn out to be true. Today, we’re looking at three storylines that I wonder if they’re true or myth. Let’s begin with the biggest name of the offseason… George Pickens as a slot receiver One of the biggest offseason talking points surrounding the Cowboys offense has been the plan to move Pickens around the formation. Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said Pickens “does not like” to stay in one spot and wants to be moved around. Last year, offensive coordinator Klayton Adams admitted the coaching staff didn’t realize how dynamic Pickens could be with the ball in his hands until CeeDee Lamb went down with an injury last season. The numbers paint a clear picture of just how different this would be. Among qualifying wide receivers, Pickens had the second-lowest percentage of snaps in the slot across the NFL, according to Pro Football Focus. Moving him inside would represent a dramatic shift in how Dallas deploys its top pass catcher. If Pickens isn’t lining up inside during training camp practices, expectations should come back down to earth quickly—but it wouldn’t be enough to lower the Pickens hype. No.4) What are you hoping to see in Parker’s defense? – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com What will the defense in Dallas look like under Christian Parker in his first year running the show? Tommy: Turnovers. Brian Schottenheimer has consistently harped on how frustrated he was in his team’s turnover ratio last season, where the Cowboys were -9, tied for third-worst in the league with 21 turnovers compared to 12 takeaways. Of course, most of Schottenheimer’s frustration likely comes as the play caller and with the offense, as 21 turnovers isn’t ideal for any good offense. That said, with a good offense you need to give them more possessions. Getting turnovers is the best way to do that and set up Dak Prescott and company in a positive position to go and put points on the board. That is what will go a long way to helping the Cowboys win more games. Of course, you aren’t going to get a turnover on every play and need to be a solid defense in general, but quick changes of possession caused by turnovers turn games on their heads. If those turnovers are able to come from the secondary and through interceptions, that’s a big testament to what Parker has been able to do with the unit that dealt with a plethora of injuries and only had six interceptions total last season. Dallas Cowboys pre-training camp roster projection: Notable cuts, darkhorse candidates and more – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News Diving into what the Cowboys roster could look like in 2026. Quarterback (3) Dak Prescott, Sam Howell, Joe Milton III Notable cuts: N/A Briefly: Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott would probably urge you not to issue causation due to correlation, but still, there is a trend worth noting when it comes to his career. Since 2020, he’s alternated between playing a full season and missing a significant amount of time. This coming season, he’s trying to string together healthy seasons in back-to-back years for the first time since 2019. That makes having a backup quarterback position important. The Cowboys brought in Sam Howell to compete with the raw but talented Joe Milton . Howell has a full season’s worth of starting experience. Could that be enough to win the battle? Wild card: If the Cowboys see enough from Howell or Milton, could they run the risk of having just two quarterbacks on the active roster? It’s something they did a season ago with Milton and former quarterback Will Grier, who spent all of last season on the practice squad but recently announced his retirement. Running back (5) Javonte Williams, Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah, Hunter Luepke, Malik Davis Notable cuts: Israel Abanikanda, Dominic Richardson Briefly: The Cowboys know who their starting running back will be. That’s why you won’t see much of Javonte Williams during preseason. They’ve also been adamant about their optimism for second-year running backs Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah. They expect both to take a big step this season. That probably places Malik Davis on the roster bubble. In this case, however, we keep Davis. He’s someone the Cowboys know they can trust on special teams. He’s the team’s starting personal protector on punt coverage. Will that be enough for him to make the roster? Wild card: The Cowboys signed Hunter Luepke to an extension last season, but he was used on just over 20% of the offensive snaps last season. Could he be on the bubble, especially if the emergence of a run-blocking tight end like Brevyn Spann-Ford continues in camp? Daily…
