title: Patriots mailbag: Will Christian Gonzalez even get a new contract?
summary: The New England Patriots are back at Gillette Stadium and set to hit the practice field for the first day of training camp on Saturday. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. Do you think there is any chance the Pats don’t give Gonzo a new contract? If so, what do you think happens? […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez (0) looks on during minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots are back at Gillette Stadium and set to hit the practice field for the first day of training camp on Saturday. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. Do you think there is any chance the Pats don’t give Gonzo a new contract? If so, what do you think happens? Do you think they could actually get 2x 1sts for him? If Gonzo isn’t on the field this season for whatever reason (holdout, trade, injury), who are the top 3 corners and how good is that unit? How much would the D suffer overall? – Maye The Force Be With You The Patriots have been adamant this offseason that Christian Gonzalez is part of their long-term plans. As of now, there is no reason to believe otherwise. It would not be a surprise to see the Seahawks first extend Devon Witherspoon, then have the Patriots and Gonzalez — who shares an agent with Witherspoon — use that deal as a framework. In the hypothetical scenario that Gonzalez does not sign an extension, a trade package would likely be slightly lower than what the Jets received for Sauce Gardner due to the fact that the acquiring team would immediately need to pay him. New England, however, still controls Gonzalez’s rights for this season and next through his fifth-year option (and then could even franchise tag him), so there should be no urgency to move him. Gonzalez then holding out into the regular season would also be a major surprise, as he would need to play at least six games to earn an accrued season toward free agency. Based on the reporting when Hill, Gilliam, and Vera-Tucker were signed, I was expecting new wrinkles on offense this season. What plans might be abandoned or adjusted as a result of Hill missing the season and the ongoing uncertainty at TE2? – slunkywontergreen While losing Julian Hill is an underrated loss, I would hope the Patriots don’t have to make significant adjustments to their playbook. The goal behind adding Hill, Gilliam and Vera-Tucker was to generate better production out of heavier personnel groupings and make the running game more consistent. Their athleticism and experience also made it easy to envision more zone-run concepts being installed, which would naturally open the door for more play-action boots, moving pockets and other ways to get Drake Maye on the move. New England will need someone to claim the TE2 role — hopefully Eli Raridon — in order to confidently play more 12 personnel groupings, but Gilliam and Vera-Tucker should still help the offense in numerous ways. All the talk has been about AJ and whether or not Boutte will be around. What do you think Romeo Dobbs will bring to the team? – Leatherhelmets I’d would expect Doubs to fill much of the role Stefon Diggs held last season. With A.J. Brown on the outside, Doubs may not see 100-plus targets in the slot role like Diggs did, but the route tree and usage could be similar. Last week, we labeled the 800-yard mark as a realistic target. The free-for-all at backup OL confuses me. Just based on RAS scores the hierarchy is: Lomu and Rizy – 9.88, Gutierrez – 9.44, Bryant – 8.96, Wallace 8.23, Crownover – 7.82 (incomplete, didn’t Bench), Rupcich – 7.76, Butler – 6.11, Hudson – 3.83, Brown, Morgan – no official RAS. But, I’d expect Brown and Crownover to make it over Wallace, Gutierrez and Rizy. I really don’t understand what Hudson, Morgan, and Butler are doing on the roster. Are the Pats committed to getting more athletic at every OL position or not? – WannaBe Pats GM There is definitely an emphasis on getting more athletic up front to better pass protect and move the pocket with Drake Maye at quarterback. But, I believe there is still value to having some bigger bodies up front and it’s hard to fill out an offensive line depth chart with purely athletes. There is always going to be some variety — especially at a position with 10-plus players in the room. Who has the edge at LB, Namdi Obiazor or Khalil Jacobs? – mathblaster97 Like most rookies, neither received much of an opportunity this spring with veterans K.J. Britt and Chad Muma ahead of them. While the team showed plenty of interest in Jacobs pre-draft, I’ll side with Obiazor due to his athleticism (which will help on special teams) and draft status. Are there any concerns about the new turf being installed so close to training camp after natural grass was used for the world cup? Could it increase the chances of non contact injuries while settling or the first time it rains? Will the turf be the same type as before? – DarthVrabel I believe the turf is the same, but the Patriots won’t be practicing inside Gillette Stadium during training camp anyway. They have plenty of time to get it ready for the first preseason game on Aug. 13, so not much worry here. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post or on Twitter using #PostPulpit. Make sure to be following @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots training camp preview 2026: Robert Spillane leads a LB group with plenty to prove
summary: After New England Patriots linebacker Robert Spillane missed four regular-season contests and part of the AFC Championship Game due to injury, the franchise knew it was entering the offseason with a clear need to bolster the position’s depth. While retaining several familiar faces from 2025, New England added veteran K.J. Britt and two rookies, Namdi […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Robert Spillane #14 of the New England Patriots runs onto the field during team introductions prior to an AFC Divisional Playoff game against the Houston Texans at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images After New England Patriots linebacker Robert Spillane missed four regular-season contests and part of the AFC Championship Game due to injury, the franchise knew it was entering the offseason with a clear need to bolster the position’s depth. While retaining several familiar faces from 2025, New England added veteran K.J. Britt and two rookies, Namdi Obiazor and Khalil Jacobs , to create a unit with more stability. In the next edition of our Patriots training camp preview series, we’ll take a look at New England’s linebacker corps in its entirety and discuss the biggest takeaways heading into the summer practices. Veterans will report to the facility on July 24. *Denotes player on the Pats Pulpit 53-man roster projection Depth chart Starters: Robert Spillane (30)* , Christian Elliss (27)* | Backups: Chad Muma (26)* , K.J. Britt (27)* , Otis Reese (28) , Amari Gainer (26), Namdi Obiazor (24/R) , Khalil Jacobs (22/R) , Riley Wilson (24/R) Spillane as the green-dot communicator and Christian Elliss as the quick, physical weakside complement are currently slated to be the starting pair once again in 2026. But behind these starters is a wide-open competition for the rotational spots on the main roster. Veterans Chad Muma and Britt are currently most equipped to take over those roles. Muma considerably repped with the first-team defense during spring practices, while Britt offers extensive special teams experience. Then, sixth-round rookie Obiazor and undrafted free agents Jacobs and Wilson will spend training camp competing for a spot on the final roster. Obiazor, who converted from defensive back to linebacker at TCU, has the 4.53-second 40-yard dash speed to cover a lot of space and the build (6-foot-3, 229 pounds) to finish tackles and be a force against the run. Jacobs is a bit undersized (6-foot-1, 227 pounds) but played with tenacity as a reliable tackler for the Tigers while emerging as a defensive leader. Wilson (6-foot-1, 226 pounds) joined the team just before camp and has on- and off-ball flexibility. All three rookies also bring significant special-teams backgrounds to New England. Finally, Otis Reese and Amari Gainer were each late-season practice squad additions to reinforce the Patriots’ defensive depth over the latter half of 2025; they’ll look to do the same next season. Reese logged 20 total games for the Tennessee Titans over the prior two seasons, while Gainer was primarily a specialist for the Las Vegas Raiders in 2024. Key question: Can Robert Spillane remain fully healthy for postseason play? During Week 15, Spillane suffered a foot/ankle injury in a divisional showdown against the Buffalo Bills, which sidelined the veteran for the remaining four games of the regular season. While Spillane returned for the playoffs and played 96.3% of the defensive snaps against the Los Angeles Chargers and Houston Texans, the injury had been bothering him for some time. The signal caller was a limited participant in the two practices leading up to the Buffalo contest, and he would later reinjure his foot/ankle against the Denver Broncos, forcing him out of the championship game early. Even though Spillane avoided offseason surgery and participated in the spring sessions after following a physical training plan with the franchise, it’s fair to question whether he can remain healthy throughout the entire 2026 season and possibly through another postseason run. Spillane manned the field for 95.4% of New England’s regular-season defensive snaps across the 13 matchups he appeared in. Furthermore, because of the nature of the linebacker position, he’s engaging in contact during almost every play, constantly hitting with force to wrap up running backs bursting upfield. No player currently on the roster can fully replace what Spillane provides to the defense, which further emphasizes the need for rotational pieces to make routine contributions. X-Factor: The rotational committee Replacing Spillane would require a collective effort. An effective committee not only provides stability and strengthens depth behind the starters, but it also reduces their workload over a 17-game season. Based on his involvement during the spring, Muma appears to be the frontrunner for the top substitute role and the leading candidate to step in if Spillane were to miss time. Even at 6-foot-3 and 239 pounds, he also possesses the lateral athleticism to match up against tight ends in coverage. Muma is versatile enough to rotate with either Spillane or Elliss. Britt’s experience lining up for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2024 also makes him a potential option. The 27-year-old played 54.9% of the team’s defensive snaps that season. Additionally, Obiazor is a dark horse candidate to achieve a larger role because of his combination of size and athleticism. If the rookie quickly adjusts to the mental demands on the field, he could increase his opportunities throughout training camp.

title: Final group of Patriots reporting to 2026 training camp on Friday
summary: A first wave of New England Patriots players already reported to this year’s training camp earlier in the week. Now, the rest of the team’s active roster is set to arrive at Gillette Stadium. The team’s veterans — i.e. everybody but quarterbacks, rookies and rehabbing vets — are scheduled to check into the Foxborough facility […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - May 28: New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez runs drills during OTA offseason workouts at Gillette Stadium on May 28, 2025. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images A first wave of New England Patriots players already reported to this year’s training camp earlier in the week. Now, the rest of the team’s active roster is set to arrive at Gillette Stadium. The team’s veterans — i.e. everybody but quarterbacks, rookies and rehabbing vets — are scheduled to check into the Foxborough facility throughout Friday. Veterans arriving on the eve of training camp is standard procedure in New England and across the league. Like those who already arrived earlier in the week, the players in this final group will also go through a medical checkup and the conditioning test to determine their status for the actual start of on-field work on Saturday. This also means that there is a chance the Patriots’ physically unable to perform (PUP) and non-football injury (NFI) lists see some more players added later in the day. At the moment, New England has three players listed . Outside linebacker Harold Landry and tight end C.J. Dippre are on PUP, while running back Terrell Jennings was classified as NFI. Those three, just like any other potential additions on Friday, are eligible to be activated and begin practicing at any point. Also worth keeping an eye on is cornerback Christian Gonzalez, who is currently in a contract stand-off with the club. He was present at mandatory minicamp in June, however, suggesting that he also will report to camp on time and not move into hold-out territory. The Patriots will hold their first practice of the summer on Saturday. Gates will open at 9:15 a.m. ET, with the session set to kick off one hour later.

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for OL Ben Brown
summary: Jerod Mayo’s one-year stint as New England Patriots head coach was mostly forgettable, but there are a few exceptions. One, of course, is selecting Drake Maye third overall in the draft. And while that decision will shape the franchise for years to come, it is not the only one still impacting the roster to this […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - DECEMBER 28: Ben Brown #77 of the New England Patriots warms up prior to the game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on December 28, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jerod Mayo’s one-year stint as New England Patriots head coach was mostly forgettable, but there are a few exceptions. One, of course, is selecting Drake Maye third overall in the draft. And while that decision will shape the franchise for years to come, it is not the only one still impacting the roster to this day. The Patriots’ top interior offensive line backup, for example, was also acquired under Mayo. Hard facts Name: Ben Brown Position: Interior offensive line Jersey number: 77 Opening day age: 28 (5/19/1998) Measurements : 6’5 1/8”, 313 lbs, 10 1/4” hand size, 34 3/8” arm length, 81 3/4” wingspan, N/A Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: Cincinnati Bengals (2022), Seattle Seahawks (2023), Arizona Cardinals (2023), Las Vegas Raiders (2024), New England Patriots (2024-) | College: Ole Miss (2017-21) A three-star recruit out of St. Aloysius High School in Vicksburg, MS, Brown spent his college career in his home state: he joined Ole Miss in 2017, and over the course of his five seasons as a Rebel started all 40 games he appeared in; he lined up at right guard for 30 of those games, and at center for the remaining 10. Despite his versatile experience, he did not hear his name called during the 2022 NFL Draft. Instead, Brown entered the league as a rookie free agent signing with the Cincinnati Bengals. After spending his rookie campaign on the Bengals’ injured reserve with a biceps issue, he joined the Seahawks’ and Cardinals’ practice squads as a sophomore, playing one game in Seattle along the way. He was not retained by Arizona following the 2023 season, and joined the Raiders in 2024. However, he was later signed off Las Vegas’ practice squad by the Patriots. Since joining New England, he has added 31 more games and his first 14 career starts to his NFL résumé. Scouting report Strengths: The 6-foot-5, 313-pound Brown combines good size and length with a proper athletic foundation. He is a fluid mover who has the agility to mirror in the pass game and the speed to climb to the second level or to execute as a pull and reach blocker. His spatial awareness and processing are quite solid, allowing him to recognize his targets even with moving parts around him. He generally is capable of rendering speed rushers and loopers ineffective, in part due to his vision and lateral movement skills, and also because of his active hand usage. Furthermore, his versatility is a plus. Weaknesses: Despite a good athletic makeup, Brown is not the most explosive of blockers. He can be thrown off from a timing perspective on screen and zone plays, and takes time to disengage from double-team blocks to get upfield. He is a competitive player and good mover, who will fight for the dirty yards but also occasionally runs into trouble against power. He does not have the strongest overall makeup extending from his base and anchor in pass protection, to his leg drive in the run game, to his upper body, to his general hand power and grip strength. 2025 review Stats : 21 games (4 starts) | 331 offensive snaps (24.4%), 100 special teams snaps (18.2%) | 10 QB pressures surrendered (2 hits, 8 hurries) | 3 penalties (incl. 0 declined/offsetting) Season recap: Despite joining the Patriots midway through the regular season, Brown started 10 games for them in 2024. However, heading into 2025, the circumstances had changed drastically: with a new coaching staff in town and a different offensive system to be installed, his outlook was unclear entering exclusive rights free agency. Nonetheless, the team decided to tender him and thus allowed him to compete for a roster spot again. Brown did just that, and more. Not only did he make the 53-man roster out of camp as the top interior backup behind starters Jared Wilson, Garrett Bradbury and Mike Onwenu, he also ended up seeing some meaningful playing time in six games — mostly as a replacement for Wilson. The first such game came in Week 3 against Carolina, when the rookie left guard was out with an ankle injury. Brown reentered the lineup in Week 11 versus the Jets as a blocking tight end to help replace an injured Austin Hooper, and again the following week in Cincinnati after Wilson hurt his ankle once more (an injury that also kept him out in Week 13 against the Giants). With a concussion then forcing Wilson out of the Patriots’ final two regular season games against the Jets and Dolphins, Brown was able to add two more starts and his final 125 offensive snaps to his season totals. He did not see the field on offense in the playoffs but continued playing his regular role as a member of New England’s field goal and extra point protection unit. Despite his backup status and resulting uneven playing time, the Patriots’ new staff apparently liked what it saw from Brown in their first few months together. As a consequence, he was signed to a two-year, $5 million contract extension in December. 2026 preview Position: Center/Left guard/Right guard | Ability: Depth player/Role player | Contract: Signed through 2027 (2028 UFA) What will be his role? Brown was the next man up along the Patriots’ interior offensive line in 2025, and he looks like the frontrunner to earn that role again in 2026. This means that he will serve as the backup behind the starting left guard (Alijah Vera-Tucker), center (Jared Wilson) and right guard (Mike Onwenu). While that job ideally comes with no meaningful snaps, the reality of NFL offensive line play is a different one. What is his growth potential? Although some minor strides are within the realm of possibility, Brown making any significant jumps or pushing for a starting role this season is unlikely to happen. That is not necessarily a bad thing, though: a 53-man NFL roster cannot go “Oops! All Starters” and there is a definitive need for readily-available super subs such as Brown. Does he have positional versatility? Brown has the versatility the Patriots are long for from their interior O-linemen. He can play all three spots in the middle of the offensive line, and was even given a handful of reps as a jumbo tight end on both the left and the right side of the line in 2025. Additionally, he saw special teams action as a field goal/extra point protector in all 21 games last year and should be expected to keep playing that role. What is his salary cap situation? As part of last December’s contract extension, Brown is carrying a $1.97 million salary cap hit into the 2026 season. That number consists of a $1.2 million base salary and a $366,666 signing bonus proration, both of which are fully guaranteed, as well as $340,000 in likely-to-be-earned roster bonuses and a $60,000 workout bonus. How safe is his roster spot? Despite not being a starter, Brown’s spot on the Patriots’ roster this year seems fairly secure. After all, he appears to be the next man up at three positions and has not been seriously challenged in a while now. New England does have some young talent along its interior O-line, but the 28-year-old is still the clear frontrunner to win any potential competition. Summary: Brown is not a household name, and likely never will be. What he is, however, is a reliable and versatile player who checks plenty of the boxes the Patriots are looking for. He therefore is an important piece of the puzzle even though his name never getting mentioned would be the best-case outlook for the team’s offensive line. What do you think about Ben Brown heading into the 2026 season? Will the Patriots require his services yet again? And will he remain as the top interior backup? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts.

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for OT Morgan Moses
summary: When the New England Patriots invested the 28th overall pick in this year’s NFL Draft in offensive tackle Caleb Lomu, they very much made their intentions known. Lomu and the team’s 2025 first-round selection, Will Campbell, would eventually become the bookends along the offensive line. But while the plan is in motion, it won’t be […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - NOVEMBER 09: Morgan Moses (76) of the New England Patriots looks ahead during a game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the New England Patriots, Sunday, November 9, 2025 at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Ricky Bowden/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When the New England Patriots invested the 28th overall pick in this year’s NFL Draft in offensive tackle Caleb Lomu, they very much made their intentions known. Lomu and the team’s 2025 first-round selection, Will Campbell, would eventually become the bookends along the offensive line. But while the plan is in motion, it won’t be fully implemented just yet. The Patriots, after all, have a reliable player opposite Campbell at the moment. At age 35, however, the end is near for Morgan Moses. Hard facts Name: Morgan Moses Position: Offensive tackle Jersey number: 76 Opening day age: 35 (3/3/1991) Measurements : 6’6”, 320 lbs, 9 7/8” hand size, 35 3/8” arm length, 84 5/8” wingspan, 5.35s 40-yard dash, 7.93s 3-cone drill, 4.95s short shuttle, 21 1/2” vertical jump, 8’10” broad jump, 2.37 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: Washington Redskins/Football Team (2014-20), New York Jets (2021; 2024), Baltimore Ravens (2022-23), New England Patriots (2025-) | College: Virginia (2010-13) A two-time all-state selection at Meadowbrook High School in North Chesterfield, VA, who later played one year of prep football at Fork Union Military Academy, Moses spent his college career in his home state. He joined the University of Virginia in 2010 and over his four years stint appeared in 48 games with 43 starts — 30 at right tackle, 12 at left tackle, and one at right guard. The one-time third-team All-ACC selection (2013) went onto enter the NFL as the 66th overall pick in the 2014 draft. Starting his career as a backup with what is now the Commanders, he was elevated to a starting position as a sophomore and never looked back: primarily a right tackle, Moses has started all but one game he appeared in since 2015 and missed just six combined contests. Including the playoffs, he now has 192 games as well as 184 starts on his résumé as well as a combined 11,190 offensive snaps. A majority of those came during his seven seasons in Washington, but he also was a reliable player during his two separate stints with the Jets and his two-year tenure in Baltimore. Joining the Patriots in 2025, nothing has changed for Moses — with the exception of playoff success: after going 1-4 to start his career, he went 3-1 in his lone season in New England so far. Scouting report Strengths: Checking in at 6-foot-6 and 320 pounds with long arms and a massive wingspan, Moses checks all the size requirements for an NFL offensive tackle. He uses his arms well to engage pass rushers in pass protection and force them to run a wide arc around the pocket. He also has the hip flexibility to maintain his leverage when opponents try to bend around him, plus the anchor and general core strength to wall off any attacks right at him. His hand fighting also is a plus; he places his mitts well and remains active against counters. As a run blocker, Moses has shown the ability to keep defenders engaged and his legs driving. He has good balance and a plays with a finish mentality without toeing the line to penalization. He furthermore offers good spatial awareness and a natural feel for timing on and disengaging from double-team blocks. Moses also has shown some exceptional durability during his first 12 seasons in the NFL. Since becoming a starter, he never appeared in fewer than 14 games; he only missed noteworthy time (i.e. three games each) in 2023 and 2024. He is a model of consistency not just due to his availability but also his approach to keeping himself ready to play even in his mid-30s. In addition, he has been praised for his leadership and willingness to take younger linemen under his wing. Weaknesses: Moses has never been a top-tier natural athlete, and his game is centered more around size, power and assignment reliability rather than his movement abilities. His first-step explosiveness is underwhelming, as are his change of direction and foot speed. He is not the most fluid mover in open space and has natural limitations as a pull and zone blocker as well as in the screen game. Unsurprisingly, speed rushers have challenged him in the past, which also might have contributed to his five false start penalties in 2025. Moses’ age is also a concern, despite him remaining in good overall physical shape and coming off a 21-game season. However, head coach Mike Vrabel has mentioned the Patriots being mindful of not overworking the veteran entering his 13th season as a pro. 2025 review Stats : 21 games (21 starts) | 1,295 offensive snaps (95.4%), 10 special teams snaps (1.8%) | 34 QB pressures surrendered (2 sacks, 5 hits, 37 hurries) | 7 penalties (incl. 1 declined/offsetting) Season recap: After using natural right guard Mike Onwenu and late-August waiver claim Demontrey Jacobs as their starting right tackles the previous season, the Patriots entered their 2025 offseason with a clear need at the position. It did not take them long to address it: on the first day of the legal tampering period preceeding free agency, they reached an agreement with Moses on a three-year, $24 million contract. The deal very much made it clear that the team intended on starting the veteran, and that is what happened right out of the gate. Moses spent the offseason as New England’s right tackle, allowing Onwenu to remain inside and giving the team an experienced combo on that side of the offensive line. Nothing changed in training camp and heading into the regular season. In fact, nothing changed at all for the remainder of the year. Despite being the Patriots’ oldest player, Moses’ availability was exemplary. He started all 21 regular season and playoff games, and only missed a handful of meaningful snaps all year: he sat out three in Week 12 versus Cincinnati (illness) plus another 20 in Week 16 against Baltimore (knee). Outside of those hiccups, he had a steady season both from an availability and a performance perspective. Accordingly, Moses proved to be the upgrade the Patriots hoped they would get when signing him. Just look at it this way: with him in the lineup, the Patriots gave up 34 quarterback pressures including two sacks from right tackle, a disruption rate of 4.4%. For comparison, that number stood at 7.4% (46 pressures, incl. 6 sacks) the previous season. Moses alone is not the sole reason for that — improved quarterback play and a better overall offensive structure also helped — but his presence also should not be underestimated. The same was true in the run game. Whereas the 2024 Patriots averaged 4.3 yards per carry when running to the general right (i.e. between guard and end), that number jumped to 4.8 in 2025. The number of touchdowns scored in that direction went from four to nine. Again, Moses is not the sole facilitator behind those improvements. However, his insertion into the lineup did help stabilize what was a clear weak point the previous year. Add the fact that he also helped mentor rookies Will Campbell and Marcus Bryant, and almost doubled his number of career playoff games along the way, and you get what can be seen as a rather successful individual first season in New England. 2026 preview Position: Starting right tackle | Ability: Quality starter | Contract: Signed through 2027 (2028 UFA) What will be his role? Despite first-round draft pick Caleb Lomu being added to the mix, Moses’ role will remain largely unchanged heading into 2026. He will remain the Patriots’ starting right tackle and as such rarely leave the field. New England might try to get Lomu some in-game experience at the position, but the meaningful snaps will largely if not exclusively go to Moses again. What is his growth potential? At 35 and with more than 11,000 NFL snaps under his belt, any growth…

title: Patriots training camp preview 2026: Edge stability is a must
summary: The New England Patriots reshaped their defensive edge during Mike Vrabel’s first year as head coach in 2025, signing longtime Vrabel pupil in Tennessee Harold Landry and taking a flier on 2020 first-round selection K’Lavon Chaisson. New England’s sack numbers improved from 2024, with Landry and Chaisson proving to be more effective, but only to […]
full_text: CHAMPAIGN, IL - NOVEMBER 01: Illinois Fighting Illini OLB Gabe Jacas (17) during a college football game between the Rutgers Scarlet Knights and Illinois Fighting Illini on November 1, 2025 at Gies Memorial Stadium in Champaign, IL (Photo by James Black/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots reshaped their defensive edge during Mike Vrabel’s first year as head coach in 2025, signing longtime Vrabel pupil in Tennessee Harold Landry and taking a flier on 2020 first-round selection K’Lavon Chaisson. New England’s sack numbers improved from 2024, with Landry and Chaisson proving to be more effective, but only to an extent. Those totals still placed the defense below the NFL average, so the team decided to make additions. In the next edition of our Patriots training camp preview series, we’ll take a look at New England’s edge-rushing corps in its entirety and discuss the biggest takeaways heading into the summer practices. Veterans will report to the facility on July 24. *Denotes player on the Pats Pulpit 53-man roster projection Depth chart Starters: Harold Landry III (30)* , Dre’Mont Jones (29)* | Backups: Gabe Jacas (22/R)* , Elijah Ponder (23)*, Bradyn Swinson (23)* , Jesse Luketa (27) , Quintayvious Hutchins (23/R) , Xavier Holmes (24/R) Head coach Mike Vrabel and Co. began the offseason by adding hybrid defensive end and linebacker Dre’Mont Jones to aid veteran Harold Landry in his efforts to return from knee surgery earlier this offseason. Jones rushes the passer with power and can line up at multiple spots along the formation. The Patriots then decided the Jones upgrade wasn’t enough and selected an aggressive pass rusher in the second round of the draft, Gabe Jacas. However, the rookie has yet to practice with the team this offseason and sign his rookie deal, leaving uncertainty about how prepared he’ll be for the start of training camp and next season. New England also has two second-year rushers returning in former undrafted free agent Elijah Ponder and 2025 fifth-round pick Bradyn Swinson. Both will look to continue making positive strides throughout summer camp. Local Boston College product and seventh-round selection Quintayvious Hutchins and rookie minicamp tryout Xavier Holmes add further developmental depth as the Patriots try to remain younger at the position with Landry and Jones sitting atop the depth chart. Additionally, after three seasons with the Arizona Cardinals and a practice-squad stint with the Los Angeles Rams, Jesse Luketa also slots in as an experienced and versatile option, rushing the passer, setting the edge in run defense, or helping the special-teams units. Key question: Can the depth provide ample support? With neither Landry nor Jacas participating in practice yet — the former was placed on the active/PUP list this week while the latter remains unsigned — younger players like Ponder and Swinson have seen greater opportunities on the field. In the absence of both players, Ponder, who had four sacks in his final eight games last season, has heavily repped with the first-team defense during the spring sessions. The defensive coaches are seemingly big fans of what he brings to the table. “I’ve got very high expectations for [Ponder]. Very,” outside linebacker coach Mike Smith said ahead of mandatory minicamp practice on June 10. “All these guys have done great all spring, but he really, really looks comfortable out there. It has really slowed down for him. Again, we’re nine or 10 [practices in], but I got high expectations for him.” Vrabel also spoke highly of Swinson at minicamp about his improvement during last season and through the spring, saying he’s “excited” for what the former LSU product can do in training camp. But it remains to be seen the extent of what those second-year jumps will look like and whether they can match the production of players at the top of the depth chart. X-Factor: Gabe Jacas With Landry still rehabbing, drafting Jacas was supposed to provide stability to New England’s room on the defensive edge. That said, Jacas has been absent since his appearance on the sidelines at rookie minicamp on May 7 and 9. It was known that Jacas was dealing with a hamstring injury during the pre-draft process, but ESPN’s Mike Reiss wrote earlier this offseason that the rookie also underwent a “clean-up” knee procedure. Related to Jacas’ absence is his not being given a standard “participation agreement” in his rookie contract, Reiss also noted. That clause financially protects a player if they were to suffer an injury before signing. The team knows what it’s getting from Jones as a player and has seen Landry’s production in a Patriots uniform (3.5 sacks in his first two games). However, Jacas can add a difference-making element to the mix as another pass-rushing body in a group that needed more help in 2025. Jacas has the potential to be a three-down player and an immediate contributor, though missing valuable offseason reps could delay his early development. The same, of course, is true should he remain absent to start training camp.

title: Patriots O-line deep dive: Left guard
summary: When New England Patriots training camp opens at the end of the week, there’s going to be one position group that a lot of eyes are going to be on, and rightfully so. There’s probably not a bigger question mark on the team right now than the offensive line. The possible outcomes for this group […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (75) works with coaching staff during minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images When New England Patriots training camp opens at the end of the week, there’s going to be one position group that a lot of eyes are going to be on, and rightfully so. There’s probably not a bigger question mark on the team right now than the offensive line. The possible outcomes for this group are wildly different, and, depending on who you ask, people either feel a lot better about last year, about the same, or, in some cases, even worse. In this week leading up to camp, I’m going to do a deep dive into each position along the offensive line and let you know whether I think the Patriots improved, and what to expect from the position as a whole. Today is Day 4, so we’re looking at left guard. Let’s get into it. Left guard deep dive 2025 starters: Jared Wilson, Ben Brown Projected 2026 starter: Alijah Vera-Tucker Last season, the Patriots got competent (for the most part, at least) play from Jared Wilson at right guard, but he was clearly playing out of position. With Wilson moving over to center following the trade that sent Garrett Bradbury to Chicago, there was a gaping hole at left guard. With a pick at the end of the first round, the Patriots could have chosen to fill it in the draft. However, they decided to go the free agent route instead, bringing in former Jets first-round draft choice Alijah Vera-Tucker on a three-year, $42 million contract. Vera-Tucker has proven himself to be a solid guard in the NFL, and just turned 27, which means he will be more than just a stopgap at the position. The only problem is that he has suffered multiple injuries throughout his career, and only playing in 43 games in his first five years in the league. If he cannot stay healthy, this will be a position where the Patriots would have to make another investment. His health will be something that Patriots fans are going to want to keep an eye on this summer and into the season, because, as I mentioned in my right guard deep-dive , the Patriots have no proven depth behind him. Caedan Wallace has had another year in the system to improve, and Andrew Rupcich has some NFL experience, but no players behind AVT belong starting on a team that has Super Bowl aspirations. Overall, signing Vera-Tucker should be an upgrade for the Patriots, not only this year, but into the future. His skill and athleticism make him a bonafide stud on the line, and, assuming he can stay on the field, New England might just have one of the best guard combos in the league between him and Mike Onwenu.

title: Patriots 2026 Training Camp Guide: Practice schedule, position battles, practical info, more
summary: After two years of massive organizational change, things have finally started to settle down in Foxborough again. This year’s New England Patriots training camp will be the second under head coach Mike Vrabel, and — in what feels like a blast from a not-too-distant past — see his team try to lay the foundation for […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 13: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots looks on during training camp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on August 13, 2025 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images After two years of massive organizational change, things have finally started to settle down in Foxborough again. This year’s New England Patriots training camp will be the second under head coach Mike Vrabel, and — in what feels like a blast from a not-too-distant past — see his team try to lay the foundation for another Super Bowl run. The process of building that foundation ramps up significantly during camp. Starting with the first practice on Saturday, July 25, the Patriots will gradually increase the intensity and competition to get ready for the start of the regular season in early September. At that point, the reigning AFC champions will also have reduced their roster from currently 92 to 53 players. Before any of that becomes relevant, however, the team will hold 20 total practices this summer — including 13 that are free and open to the general public. To be as best informed as possible heading into those sessions, here is our annual and updated Patriots Training Camp Guide . Practice schedule The Patriots have already announced their full training camp schedule. While dates and times are always subject to change depending on whether or other factors, here is the list at the start of camp: Saturday, July 25: 10:30 a.m. ET Sunday, July 26: 10:15 a.m. ET Monday, July 27: 10 a.m. ET Tuesday, July 28: 10:15 a.m. ET Thursday, July 30: 10:15 a.m. ET Friday, July 31: 10:15 a.m. ET Saturday, August 1: 10:15 p.m. ET Monday, August 3: 10:15 a.m. ET Tuesday, August 4: 10:15 a.m. ET Friday, August 7: 10:15 a.m. ET Tuesday, August 11: 10:15 a.m. ET (joint practice with Colts) Saturday, August 15: 10:30 a.m. ET (exclusive in-stadium practice for season ticket members) Wednesday, August 19: 10:15 a.m. ET (joint practice with Eagles) Thursday, August 20: 10:15 a.m. ET (joint practice with Eagles) In addition to those practices, the Patriots also will hold six others (8/5, 8/6, 8/10, 8/16, 8/17, 8/18) that are closed to the public but open to the media. Each practice will run for approximately two hours. Gates will open one hour before each session (i.e. between 9 and 9:15 a.m. ET for regular sessions) and close about an hour after. Please note that the schedule is subject to change. If a session has to be relocated to the adjacent WIN Waste Innovations Field House because of inclement weather, it can no longer be open to the general public. In case you plan to visit training camp, you therefore need to stay up to date. Besides visiting Pats Pulpit for updates please also call 508-549-0001 or visit patriots.com/trainingcamp . Arrival and parking Directions: Prior to the 2015 training camp, the Boston Globe wrote down directions to Gillette Stadium. Since none of the locations have changed, they obviously still apply and we will just quote them here: From Boston and farther north: Take I-95 South to Exit 9. Follow Rte. 1 south approximately 3 miles to Gillette Stadium (on the left). From Cape Cod: I-495 North to Exit 14A. Follow Rte. 1 north about 4 miles to Gillette Stadium (on the right). From southern Connecticut, Rhode Island: Take I-95 North to I-495 North to Exit 14A. Follow Rte. 1 north about 4 miles to Gillette Stadium (on the right). From northern Connecticut, Vermont, upstate New York: I-90 East to I-495 South to Exit 14A. Follow Rte. 1 north about 4 miles to Gillette Stadium (on the right). Parking: Parking at the stadium facilities’ parking lots is free for all public practice sessions. If you arrive from the north (e.g. Boston), use parking lot entrance P6. If you arrive from the south (e.g. Providence), use parking lot entrance P8. ADA parking can be found in Lot 4 and in Lot 22. Fan services Alumni appearances: Patriots alumni will make special appearances at training camp. While those are always subject to change, the following ex-players are currently scheduled to be present at the Fan Walkway between 9:30 a.m. and 11 a.m. ET on the respective dates. Saturday, July 25: James White Sunday, July 26: Christian Fauria Autographs: Autograph sessions are planned to take place after each day of practice. Concessions: The main concession stands will be positioned behind the bleachers. All will operate cashless, but a cash-to-card machine is available as well. Bringing your own food and/or beverages to camp is permitted. Fan activities: The Patriots will offer various fan activities around the practice area. Participants of physical and interactive activities will not have to fill out any waiver forms beforehand. Signage will be present to make them aware of the team’s terms and conditions. Visitors with disabilities: As noted above, ADA parking lots can be found in Lot 4 and in Lot 22; there are signs leading there. Seating at the facility will be available in all the bleacher sections, located on the western end of the practice fields. For more information, call 508-384-9191 . Prohibited items: The following is a list of things you better leave in your car if you want to watch the Patriots practice: all animals except service animals assisting those with disabilities (leave them at home, not in your car), alcoholic beverages, beach balls, bullhorns and air horns, coolers, fireworks or pyrotechnics, flag poles and tripods longer than 2 feet (shorter ones will be allowed), helium balloons, illegal drugs or any other illegal substance, laser pens, noise makers, video cameras, weapons of any kind (including knives), unmanned aircraft systems, remotely controlled model aircraft, drones, selfie sticks. Additionally, any other items deemed inappropriate by stadium management (e.g. Jets jerseys) are prohibited. Pet Adoption Day: Six different animal shelters — up from three last year — will be on-site on the first day of camp, offering the possibility to adopt dogs on July 25 starting at 10 a.m. ET. Jersey numbers In a break from tradition established during the Bill Belichick era, the Patriots have already handed out regular jersey numbers to all member on their roster. For every jersey number, please visit out our up-to-date Patriots depth chart . The offense will once again wear white jerseys, while the defense will wear blue ones. Quarterbacks and players not to be touched even in full pads — i.e. those recovering from injuries — will be in red. Injury lists The Patriots currently have two players on their active/physically unable to perform list (PUP): TE C.J. Dippre ED Harold Landry III In addition, another player finds himself on the active/non-football injury or illness list at the moment (NFI): RB Terrell Jennings With veterans set to report to training camp on Friday, July 24, there is a chance that more players are added to the respective injury lists. All players on PUP/NFI can return at any time during camp. If such a move does not happen by final roster cutdowns on August 30, however, the players still remaining on the the active/PUP/NFI lists will transfer to reserve/PUP/NFI; they will no longer count against the 53-man roster and would have to miss at least the first four games of the regular season. Position battles There will be multiple position battles throughout training camp, but the five most interesting from our current perspective are the following. Third running back: Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson project as one of the top running back duos in the NFL this season, but the depth spots behind them are up for grabs. Based on the offseason, Lan Larison and the aforementioned Terrell Jennings look like the frontrunners, but rookies Jam Miller and Myles Montgomery are also likely to be in the mix. Depth tight end: Hunter Henry is locked into the starting tight end spot, but who will occupy the other positions in the room is currently TBD. One spot will go to third-round draft pick…

title: Why Drew Brees thinks the Saints end their playoff drought this year
summary: The New Orleans Saints have not made the playoffs since the 2020 season, which also happened to be quarterback Drew Brees last with the team before retiring a couple of months later. Since then, the Saints have undergone a lot of changes with both players and personnel. Now under the leadership of head coach Kellen […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 23: Former quarterback Drew Brees of the New Orleans Saints looks on prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at at Caesars Superdome on November 23, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints have not made the playoffs since the 2020 season, which also happened to be quarterback Drew Brees last with the team before retiring a couple of months later. Since then, the Saints have undergone a lot of changes with both players and personnel. Now under the leadership of head coach Kellen Moore and quarterback Tyler Shough, who went 5-4 last season after being named the team’s starter in Week 9, the Saints have a lot of momentum and fans have plenty of reasons to be optimistic that this is the year the playoff drought ends. It also looks like they aren’t the only one, as Brees, who will be inducted into the NFL Hall of Fame next month, has also weighed in with his opinion. In a recent interview with Heavy Sports, Brees was asked his thoughts on if the Saints can win the division this year. “1,000%,” said Brees. “Last year, it was a three-team race down to the wire. Actually, I guess it was really a four-team race down to the wire. They were all just kind of hovering around .500. Tampa has been kind of the favorite and then Carolina was kind of able to bump them off the top last year. Bryce Young played well. They got three really good receivers, ran the ball well. They got some good young talent on defense. Atlanta has been the one that’s kind of been unpredictable. Michael Penix gets hurt. But they’ve got some weapons on offense, and so we’ll see how he comes back this year.” Brees added why he thinks there is no clear favorite and the division is wide open this season, “Baker Mayfield. I think he’s kind of the one you know real veteran QB in the division. You know, so they kind of they kind of give them the nod as far as just maybe having a bit of the advantage. But look, you know, Saints beat the Bucs. Saints beat the Bucs last year at their place, beat Carolina twice. You know, and so as you as you look at it, it’s pretty wide open.” We will soon see how the 2026 season will shape up for the Saints, as they hit the practice field next Wednesday for the start of training camp and their first preseason game will kick off against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Saturday, August 15, in Caesars Superdome.

title: The best- and worst-case scenarios for the Saints in 2026
summary: Football is the greatest sport on earth. As we sit here in July, we go through our days monotonously running errands, handling responsibilities, and day dreaming about September. The only way to scratch our football itch is hypotheticals and speculation. So, let’s do just that. What is both the best and worst case scenario for […]
full_text: Football is the greatest sport on earth. As we sit here in July, we go through our days monotonously running errands, handling responsibilities, and day dreaming about September. The only way to scratch our football itch is hypotheticals and speculation. So, let’s do just that. What is both the best and worst case scenario for the New Orleans Saints in 2026? Realistically, what can we expect from this Saints team if everything clicks, or if nothing does at all? The best case scenario for this team obviously starts with Tyler Shough. The soon-to-be 27 year old Quarterback is entering his second NFL season. Shough looked borderline incredible in his nine starts as a rookie. Many fans are expecting him to be the Saints new franchise Quarterback. Now that Shough will have a full offseason of being the unrivaled starter under his belt, it is very realistic to expect further development from him. If he does come out on fire, the Saints will be poised to make a run for the NFC South crown with arguably the best quarterback in the division. This is especially true when you factor how much better the offensive situation became around him. A major reason for why Shough’s play in 2025 was so impressive was the lack of offensive fire power he had around him. This certainly included the offensive line which struggled mightily last season. This offseason, the Saints added veteran Guard David Edwards in free agency. Center Erik McCoy will also be coming back from injury. You combine these two interior players with the Saints young tackle duo, Fuaga and Banks, and it’s very easy to foresee a world where this is one of the better units in the NFL providing Shough much needed protection Accompanying Shough in the backfield will be the running back tandem of Travis Ettiene and Alvin Kamara. Ettiene was the biggest name the Saints brought in this offseason and eclipsed 1000 rushing yards in three of his four seasons in Jacksonville. Kamara will be entering his 10th season with the black and gold. Saints fans may recall the “Boom & Zoom” era with Kamara and Mark Ingram in the late 2010s. Although I wouldn’t necessarily say that the best scenario for the 2026 duo would be to reach those heights, I do believe that the Saints rushing attack can provide great balance to the offense. A luxury that was not present in 2025 as the Saints finished at 28th in total rushing offense. The passing attack easily has the highest upside. Chris Olave is coming off a career high 1163 yards and 9 touchdowns in 2025 and displayed a great connection with Shough. The Saints also selected Arizona State Receiver Jordan Tyson with the 8th overall pick in the 2026 draft. When he played, Tyson was a super star at the collegiate level. He possesses elite ball skills, route running, and run after catch ability. In my opinion, there is a world where both receivers each surpass 1000 receiving yards in 2026. This is a feat that the Saints haven’t accomplished in a decade, the last time being the 2016-17 season with Brandin Cooks and a rookie Michael Thomas. Although there are other capable pass catchers on this team, such as Juwan Johnson and Devaughn Vele, the best case scenario for this offense would necessitate both Olave and Tyson becoming an elite receiver duo. It can certainly happen. In six seasons as an NFL offensive coordinator, Kellen Moore produced four top 10 offenses. He achieved this on three different teams with three different quarterbacks (Dak Prescott, Justin Herbert, and Jalen Hurts). Moore has proven that he can adapt his offense to different play styles and find offensive production in a variety of ways. This is the final nail in the coffin for why I believe that the ceiling for this offense is to be near or at the top of the league. If all of the stars align, the Saints will enjoy a hungry Tyler Shough who takes a jump individually while simultaneously being surrounded by talented blockers, pass catchers, and ball carriers. This will all be within a system that is run by one of the best young playcallers in the NFL. The sky truly is the limit. The 2025 Saints defense, no doubt, had some bumps in the road early on. However in the latter half of the season, the unit started to play some great football. Safety Jonas Sanker and Cornerback Quincy Riley both had very promising rookie campaigns in the secondary. Both players will play pivotal roles in 2026, especially with the departure of Alontae Taylor. The secondary also includes third year Cornerback Kool Aid McKinstry, who I believe is nearing a massive crossroads for his career trajectory. His first two seasons have been a mix of up and down moments. This third year could have a crucial effect on his long term NFL and Saints future. I believe that he most likely understands this. It is critical that all three of these players take a jump in order for this defense to reach its full potential. The secondary does have a fair share of veterans however, notable improvement from these three young guys could propel this secondary into one of the premier position groups on the squad. I shouldn’t have to explain how big of a loss it is to lose Demario Davis. His replacement at linebacker will be Kaden Ellis, who is returning to New Orleans after spending the last three seasons behind enemy lines with that team in Atlanta. Ellis has been highly consistent and productive, starting all 17 games and accumulating over 100 total tackles for each of the past three years. I view Ellis as a known commodity, however the key for this linebacking corpse to max out their potential will be second year player Danny Stutsman. The Saints spent the 112th overall pick on Stutsman in the 2025 draft. He didn’t log a single start as a rookie but, at the time of his selection, many people viewed him as a steal in the fourth round. The 6-foot-3, 233-pound linebacker was an absolute problem at Oklahoma. If Stutsman can emerge as any semblance of that player in the NFL, the Saints will have a much easier time adjusting to the post-Demario Davis era. Moving to the defensive line, it is impossible to not start with Defensive End Chase Young. Young is coming off his first career 10 sack season. He began to look like an absolute game wrecker in the second half of the year as Brandon Staley’s defense gained momentum as a whole. Young was selected with the second overall pick back in 2020 to the Washington Commanders. He was one of the most hyped up prospects in recent memory, finishing as a 2019 Heisman finalist (which is absurd to do as a defensive player). His time in D.C. was a bit underwhelming when you consider the expectations that were bestowed upon him. Nonetheless, the raw talent is still undeniably elite and he seems to have begun piecing his NFL game together in New Orleans. If he builds on what he did in 2025, he has a chance to become the superstar that many expected him to be out of Ohio State. Due to this possibility, there is massive upside for this pass rush. Every single defense to ever exist in the history of football objectively gets better when you plop an elite tier pass rusher on it. This scenario would give the Saints an elite player at a top three most important position in the sport. Outside of Young, I would also keep an eye on 2025 third rounder Vernon Broughton. Broughton missed virtually his entire rookie season due to a hip injury in 2025. However, he was a force with the Texas Longhorns and the Saints staff clearly liked him enough to draft him. The best case scenario for the defensive line would be for both of these players to make a name for themselves in 2026, especially Young. In totality, this defense has a realistic shot at finishing as a top 10 to 15 unit. This would be more than good enough to win a weak NFC South, if the offense also hits their ceiling. Brandon Staley’s squad was in a state of constant ascension in his first year. Now that they have continuity going into year two, it is not unreasonable for fans to expect them…

New Orleans has plenty of expectations for the upcoming season. With the breakout […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - OCTOBER 12: Alvin Kamara #41 of the New Orleans Saints runs with the ball against the New England Patriots during the NFL 2025 game at Caesars Superdome on October 12, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana."" (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will report to training camp on July 29th. Training camp is the first big step to preparing for the NFL season, and there is a ton of excitement both within and outside the building for the 2026 Saints. New Orleans has plenty of expectations for the upcoming season. With the breakout of Tyler Shough, the Saints are in a position to win the NFC South in 2026, if they actually complete that feat is another discussion. Alvin Kamara’s role in the offense The Saints officially reworked Alvin Kamara’s contract just a couple of weeks ahead of training camp, putting the narrative that he wouldn’t be a Saint in 2026 to rest. But now that the 30-year-old running back is officially set to play for New Orleans in 2026, what will his role look like? When the Saints signed Travis Etienne to a four-year $47.4 million contract, it was clear he would be the team’s RB1 going forward. Accordingly, New Orleans had to restructure Kamara’s contract, lowering his pay from $11.5 million to $6 million with a chance to make up to $8.5 million with incentives. While Kamara’s pay was lowered, it doesn’t mean he won’t have a pivotal role in the Saints’ offense. The veteran running back is no longer expected to touch the ball 20+ times a game, and while that could be seen as a negative, it gives Kamara a chance to be more explosive in-game. Kamara will be tackled less and be featured more in play designs made just for him. This lowers his chances of getting injured, something he’s dealt with over the past few seasons, and sets him up for the offensive staff to utilize his skill set to its max. Training camp will just be a glimpse of what the black and gold have planned for the veteran running back, but it will be interesting to see what Kellen Moore envisions with the Kamara-Etienne tandem. Who is CB2? There are a lot of questions in the Saints’ secondary, specifically around the cornerback room. New Orleans was surprisingly quiet during the 2026 NFL Draft in terms of adding to their secondary, waiting until the seventh round to finally make an addition with Iowa defensive back T.J. Hall. But the Saints swiftly added cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. shortly after. Second-year cornerback Quincy Riley took over CB2 duties last season as a rookie and showed plenty of promise. But with his promise came glaring mistakes, some you may be able to excuse to him being a rookie, but others that show a clear need to improve. While Riley was the team’s CB2 last season, Emerson was a high-level CB2 during his time with the Cleveland Browns before suffering a significant injury. When asked whether he’ll play in the slot or as a boundary corner, Emerson said discussions with the team while signing pointed towards him being an outside corner. With Emerson being signed as an outside corner, does that push Riley to the nickel? Or is Riley or Emerson starting in front of the other one while another player takes on slot responsibilities? We don’t know yet, but training camp will be a big indicator of who the team believes is more fit for the role. Is Jordyn Tyson healthy enough? The Saints swung for the fences by drafting Arizona State wide receiver Jordyn Tyson. An enticing but risky pick. Tyson has all the talent to be the best wideout in the 2026 NFL Draft, but injuries have plagued his college career. Even after playing in over 10+ games in just one college season, the Saints were comfortable enough to take Tyson eighth overall. The talented rookie wide receiver offers Shough a new weapon on offense and will play a complementary part alongside Chris Olave. But the alarm bells have already rung as Tyson has missed during OTAs and rookie minicamp. Coach Moore has already stepped in and put an end to those conversations, however, saying this was just a precautionary step as Tyson recovers from strains in both his hamstrings that he suffered during his senior year. While Moore has tried to end the injury discussions for Tyson, his availability throughout training camp will tell if he is on track to start and how he is doing during recovery.

title: NY Giants news: Defining success, rookie expectations, good news on Malik Nabers
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about today. Giants WR Malik Nabers is expected to avoid PUP list | Pro Football Talk The question remains about when Malik Nabers will return from rehab on his right knee, with the Giants hopeful he can play the season opener […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about today. Giants WR Malik Nabers is expected to avoid PUP list | Pro Football Talk The question remains about when Malik Nabers will return from rehab on his right knee, with the Giants hopeful he can play the season opener against the Cowboys. The Giants wide receiver, though, is expected to avoid the active/physically unable to perform list to start camp, according to ESPN’s Jordan Raanan. Harbaugh: Real football players play special teams Special Expectations pt2. Banks LT Pepper = Carter Reese Hood? Stay ready.. Want to -Want to! Full @BleavNetwork ep👇🏾 https://t.co/bOq1pSit6a pic.twitter.com/6W0xdvsa4Z — Carl Banks (@CarlBanksGIII) July 23, 2026 8 NFL rookies to watch in training camp and preseason | Yahoo Sports Which offensive and defensive rookies are you most excited to see in training camp and preseason? Defensively, give me Arvell Reese. He was a bit of a surprise pick to the Giants, though his talent is not in question. Reese was a hybrid defender at Ohio State, splitting his time between edge rusher and off-ball linebacker, and it appears the Giants will deploy him similarly. Even with changes up front, Reese could be a monster on a front that features Brian Burns, Kayvon Thibodeaux and Abdul Carter, along with free-agent LB addition Tremaine Edmunds. I’ll be curious to see just how much the Giants put on Reese’s plate. They tried a similar approach with Carter as a rookie, and it took until later in his rookie season for the former Penn State star to really shine. Reese has all the tools to be a star eventually, but his instincts will be put to the test in Year 1. The preseason tape should be fascinating to watch. The Biggest Question for Every NFL Team as Training Camps Begin | The Ringer What will this offense look like if Malik Nabers is sidelined? There’s no certainty that receiver Malik Nabers, who is recovering from injuries to his ACL and meniscus, will be cleared to practice without restrictions at the start of training camp, and we should not assume that the Giants’ best offensive player will be ready by the start of the season. If he can’t go, the Giants will be trying to patch together a passing game with receivers like Darius Slayton, Calvin Austin III, Darnell Mooney, and Odell Beckham Jr. I don’t envision much explosive passing from New York until Nabers is back, and I worry about quarterback Jaxson Dart’s development without him. 2026 NFL training camp previews, projections for all 32 teams | ESPN.com Biggest storyline: How will the Giants handle increased expectations and a new coach? New York added a Super Bowl-winning coach with John Harbaugh to work with a young quarterback in Jaxson Dart. That combination alone has some thinking the Giants will have an immediate turnaround. (Reminder: They won just seven games in the past two seasons combined.) Throw in that they had two top-10 draft picks who are expected to contribute immediately and it’s supposed to instantly produce more wins. But with new schemes offensively and defensively, it might not look so promising right away. How will the organization handle that? The increased workload will also be something to watch, especially when Harbaugh is known as an old-school coach who runs one of the league’s harder training camps. Giants’ 10-step plan revisited: Will New York regret lack of investment in trenches? | The Athletic Cutting Okereke, keeping Thibodeaux, re-signing Eluemunor, letting Robinson walk and taking the best player available with the fifth pick were clear similarities between my plan and the Giants’ actions. There were also some differences, particularly in the lack of investment in the trenches in free agency. The Mauigoa pick mitigates that to an extent, but the Giants couldn’t have known they’d have that pick while making free-agency decisions. The biggest divide was the Lawrence situation. It was impossible at the time of my plan to have a full grasp on the interpersonal dynamics that eroded the relationship. I still wonder whether the Giants, if they had proactively made my extension offer, could have avoided the ugly standoff, but all things considered, they made the best of a tough situation by securing the 10th pick in the trade. Ranking the NFL’s Divisions from Worst to First Entering 2026 | Bleacher Report Biggest Additions: The New York Giants are beginning a new era with young players like Malik Nabers, Cam Skattebo, and quarterback Jaxson Dart. This offseason, they added a Super Bowl-winning coach in John Harbaugh to the equation. As a group, the NFC East has the potential to be a very improved division in 2026. If Harbaugh can get the most out of New York’s roster—and players like Dart, Nabers and Skattebo can get and stay healthy—the Giants could make some noise during the regular season. The Cowboys, meanwhile, could make noise in the postseason if their defense plays up to its potential. From Big Blue View What would a successful John Harbaugh Giants tenure look like? title: NY Giants news: WR Malik Nabers will avoid the PUP list
summary: Wide receiver Malik Nabers (knee) is not expected to start training camp on the PUP list, per a report from Jordan Raanan of ESPN. That is much-needed good news for the New York Giants. As we well know, Nabers suffered a torn ACL with additional meniscus damage in the Giants Week 4 win against the […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers catches a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys | Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images Wide receiver Malik Nabers (knee) is not expected to start training camp on the PUP list, per a report from Jordan Raanan of ESPN. That is much-needed good news for the New York Giants. As we well know, Nabers suffered a torn ACL with additional meniscus damage in the Giants Week 4 win against the Los Angeles Chargers a year ago. In addition to the surgery to repair his torn ACL, Nabers also needed to have his meniscus repaired. He also had a cleanup surgery earlier in the off-season, which raised questions as to his readiness for the 2026 season — let alone training camp. Instead, it does appear that he’s trending toward being ready for Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys. Just how ready remains to be seen, but this is better news than the possibility of missing the first four weeks on the PUP list. Nabers will be ineligible for the PUP list once he practices the first time or plays in a preseason game. Likewise, running back Cam Skattebo will be active to start training camp. While Nabers won’t be on the PUP list to start their training camp, allowing him to practice in some capacity, the Giants have placed three players on the PUP list in advance of camp. DL Sam Roberts (undisclosed) DL Roy Robertson-Harris (Achilles) TE Thomas Fidone II (foot) Defensive tackle Sam Roberts was one of the Giants first free -agent signings, added to beef up their defensive line with Rakeem Nunez-Roches departing, as well as provide more interior pass rush. However, he has missed their off-season program with an undisclosed injury. Tight end Thomas Fidone II, a 7th round pick in 2025, finished his rookie year on the injured reserve after trying to play through a foot injury. He had a cleanup procedure in June and has been expected to return to the practice field at some point in training camp. Defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris is one of a trio of Giants to suffer a ruptured Achilles in OTAs. The Giants believe he could return to the field before the season is out and are trying to avoid putting him on season-ending injured reserve.

title: Fantasy Football 2026: Preliminary RB rankings and tiers
summary: Welcome to the third installment of my preliminary rankings and tiers for each major position for fantasy. I’ve already hit the two big “onesie” positions of quarterback and tight end. I hope you enjoyed those columns, but it’s time to get serious. Today I’m diving into the most important position in fantasy: Running back. You […]
full_text: Skattebo finds the end zone! | Getty Images Welcome to the third installment of my preliminary rankings and tiers for each major position for fantasy. I’ve already hit the two big “onesie” positions of quarterback and tight end . I hope you enjoyed those columns, but it’s time to get serious. Today I’m diving into the most important position in fantasy: Running back. You can find all my preseason fantasy content, including my other rankings and tiers, here . I’ll update rankings in late August. Hopefully, these initial looks will help you to start thinking about player values and draft strategies. Why do I say that running back is the most important position in fantasy? Because it’s the position that’s most detrimental, and hardest to fix, if a poor draft or injuries leave you shorthanded. It’s a question of supply and demand. Running back is a very high scoring position, but the scoreboard spinners are in limited supply. In most leagues you have to start two at the position. Even if you regularly flex a wide receiver, there’s so much more depth at that position that you can always find suitable Flex/WR3 types on the waiver wire, or via trade. Running back? I hate making those trade calls or scouring the wire for a warm body. Workhorse running backs (20+ touches per game) are rare gems — only four backs hit that threshold last season. Even 15 touches is a limited group. Last season, 19 running backs hit that mark. That may seem like a big number, but if you’re playing in a 12-team league where each franchise MUST start two running backs and is allowed to start three, well, you see where I’m going. We’ve all been there – week in and week out, you’re struggling to find a second running back who can give you more than five fantasy points absent a lucky touchdown. So yeah, this position matters. A lot. Before we get to the rankings, here are two quick observations on the position. Backs are back! And have stayed remarkably healthy the last two seasons. We’ve seen a resurgence of RB dominance in fantasy. First off, teams are running a little more, in response to what defenses are giving them. NFL teams averaged almost 34 pass attempts per game in 2023 and that number dropped to 32 last season. In 2023, 26 teams attempted a pass on at least 55% of their plays. In 2025, that number was down to 20 teams. We’re seeing more heavy formations with multiple tight ends. Of greater consequence than those trends, RBs aren’t getting hurt at typical levels. Last season, 24 backs who opened the season as their team’s starter missed two games or fewer due to injury. 2024 was similar. Will we get regression in 2026? Maybe. The top running backs are outscoring the best receivers. This follows a bit from the first observation, and this was not the case for much of the last two decades, when passing exploded. Generally speaking, receivers haven’t enjoyed the same good health luck over the last two seasons. Of the top 14 players in touchdowns last season, 11 were running backs and only one was a wide receiver. And of the top 22 non-QB scorers in fantasy last season, 15 were running backs, six were receivers, and one was a tight end. I’ll talk strategy in a later column, but I’m a big fan of investing early in running back, before they’re gone. I’ve organized the RBs into tiers, as I do at every position. You should do the same. To reiterate, everyone wants the best players, and a tiered approach allows fantasy managers to have a great view of (a) ranges of players who can be expected to have similar fantasy production, (b) where the drop-offs are between those ranges, and (c) how many players in a range remain available at any given time. Tiers really help when position runs come, and they facilitate more effective drafting, regardless of format. My running back rankings and tiers are for Half-Point PPR. Season-long rankings shown are on a fantasy points per game (FPPG) basis and exclude the final week of the season. I’ve ranked 65 players. TIER I – The Absolute Studs J. Gibbs Bij. Robinson There isn’t a lot to say here. These two get bumped up into a tier of their own in part because of the departures of David Montgomery and Tyler Allgeier, who scored a combined 31 rushing TDs the past two seasons. Gibbs is averaging a TD per game across his three years in the league – with Montgomery regularly vulturing him. Both players catch a lot of passes and if Tua Tagovailoa is the starter in Atlanta, the sky is the limit for Robinson as a receiver. De’Von Achane led all backs in receptions over the past two seasons, with Tua finding him early and often. TIER II – RB1s J. Taylor C. McCaffrey J. Cook D. Achane D. Henry C. Brown S. Barkley J. Jacobs K. Walker III There are some question marks in this tier (cue the Josh Jacobs dynasty managers nodding their heads), but generally speaking, these are highly productive workhorses on good offenses (aside from Miami). Cook might be the most underrated back in the league, and Henry just keeps rolling, with Father Time having no say in the matter. Barkley is looking to bounce back from a down year and McCaffrey is, as always, the biggest risk/reward commodity in the fantasy world. Super Bowl MVP Walker has little competition in Kansas City, and is a popular pick for a career year. TIER III – Borderline RB1s A. Jeanty O. Hampton T. Etienne, Jr. J. Love (R) K. Williams J. Williams B. Hall All of the backs in this group have the potential for a Top-10 or even Top-5 finish if things break right, but in most cases, there’s still something to prove, or a concern over workload. Hampton should benefit from Mike McDaniel’s scheme and is a very popular breakout candidate, so you’ll have to pay up. Jeanty too, with Klint Kubiak’s arrival and improvements to the line. Love’s talent is immense but the rookie joins a crowded backfield and there’s no reason for Arizona to overload him in his rookie season, on a team that’s looking to the future. I’m lower on him than most. Can Kyren WIlliams hold off Blake Corum for one more season? I’ve doubted him before and been wrong every time. Javonte Williams is my favorite value in this tier, for now. It’s a high scoring offense and Brian Schottenheimer showed last year that he isn’t afraid to give him a ton of work. TIER IV – Solid RB2s Q. Judkins D. Montgomery C. Skattebo D. Swift B. Irving T. Henderson B. Tuten J. Price (R) I’m OK with any of these guys as my RB2, if for some reason I don’t walk away with two backs from the first three tiers. Each of these players could see a pretty dominant workload, or at least with respect to higher-value touches, but each could also be in a major timeshare. I’m a believer in Montgomery this season, on a team with a great defense and mediocre weapons after Nico Collins. I look at Joe Mixon’s numbers from two years ago and ask, why not? The rookie Price has pretty high volatility, given the uncertainty of Seattle’s backfield. TIER V – The share guys (RB2/3) J. Warren C. Hubbard R.J. Harvey T. Pollard K. Gainwell J.K. Dobbins B. Corum R. Dowdle K. Monangai R. White J. Croskey-Merritt A. Jones, Sr. J. Mason T. Tracy, Jr. C. Rodriguez, Jr. There players in this tier who could have real value as weekly starters this season, either due to an injury to someone else or just by earning more touches. A few of these guys are passing game specialists (Gainwell and White) who have a nice floor and a capped upside, while most of the others are in some kind of backfield share that will reveal its roles and percentages as the season goes along. These players will have similar draft cost as a lot of very good players at other positions, so decisions must be made. TIER VI – Depth and handcuffs T. Allgeier J. Brooks Z. Charbonnet W. Marks I. Pacheco T. Spears D. Sampson K. Mitchell T. Bigsby A. Kamara Bri. Robinson B. Allen E. Wilson E. Johnson (R) M. Washington, Jr. (R) N. Singleton (R) R. Davis J. Coleman (R) M. Lloyd K. Allen (R) J. Wright J. Hill J. Conner S. Tucker I generally like to…
