title: Giants coach John Harbaugh has learned not to ‘blow things out of proportion’
summary: If you expected John Harbaugh to be a bellicose tyrant who ranted about everything and turned the New York Giants into a no-fun team, you are likely disappointed. Harbaugh’s recent reaction to Cam Skattebo’s recent failed backlip was a joking “Dude, at least stick it.” He reacted with a similar blaise attitude to Jaxson Dart’s […]
full_text: John Harbaugh | Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images If you expected John Harbaugh to be a bellicose tyrant who ranted about everything and turned the New York Giants into a no-fun team, you are likely disappointed. Harbaugh’s recent reaction to Cam Skattebo’s recent failed backlip was a joking “Dude, at least stick it.” He reacted with a similar blaise attitude to Jaxson Dart’s leap off a yacht after an impressive long throw to someone on a jet ski. “I was impressed by the yacht. I thought it was pretty nice,” Harbaugh said. “The surroundings looked amazing. It’s like, dude, where are you? Like, I mean, I don’t even know. But more than anything, I just was happy that he threw a dime out there on the on the deal. It was a very accurate throw.” Gary Myers recently asked Harbaugh about his casual responses . “He throws the ball off a yacht to a jet ski. Am I supposed to get mad about that?” Harbaugh told me. “I’m just happy he completed it, to be honest with you.” The jump off the yacht? “It’s just water. He jumped into the water. So, he should be alright if he can swim,” he said. “I guess he can swim. I’m not worried about things that aren’t too important.” Myers got this fantastic tidbit from Harbaugh on why he can seem so unconcerned about things that have some in the fan base up in arms: Harbaugh said the mistake young coaches make is they start thinking everything “is a reflection on them and the program they’re running. It’s not like that. When you start thinking like that, you overreact to things. You make things more important than they are and blow things out of proportion. So I have definitely have learned that lesson over the years.” Valentine’s View I have to love this. Harbaugh worked with these young men all spring. He knows their work ethic, and he knows they care about their profession. He also knows that they are single men in their early 20s doing things single men in the early 20s will do when given the opportunity. It’s just not that big of a deal that people choose to have fun when they aren’t working. Harbaugh, as I have found out in a couple of personal conversations, does not yell, belittle, or issue ultimatums when he isn’t happy. He has a quiet way of letting you know he isn’t happy simply by the fact that you are having a discussion. I won’t be surprised if he has such discussions with Dart and Skattebo to simply remind them that sometimes the optics of things that seem innocent can cause an unintended reaction.

title: What would a successful John Harbaugh Giants tenure look like?
summary: As training camp approaches, the excitement and anticipation among Giants fans is almost palpable with the John Harbaugh Giants era about to begin. Now is a good time to ask: What would a successful Harbaugh tenure look like, and how likely is it to happen? I specifically chose the featured image of Harbaugh above because […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ- JUNE 03: John Harbaugh head coach of the New York Giants speaks at the podium wearing a New York Knicks hat after OTA Practice on June 3, 2026 at Quest Diagnostic Center in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As training camp approaches, the excitement and anticipation among Giants fans is almost palpable with the John Harbaugh Giants era about to begin. Now is a good time to ask: What would a successful Harbaugh tenure look like, and how likely is it to happen? I specifically chose the featured image of Harbaugh above because it shows him wearing a New York Knicks cap after their thrilling (and I mean thrilling, I don’t know how much more exciting you can get than those NBA Finals games) run to the NBA Championship. We all agree, I’m sure, on the answer to my question above: We want Harbaugh to eventually lead the Giants to their next Super Bowl Championship. It’s a tall order. Not only because of the Giants’ dismal history since their last Super Bowl run, but because of league history. Here is a list of all the NFL head coaches who have won Super Bowls with two different teams: … … Anyone? Anyone? That’s right. It’s never been done before. There are seven head coaches who have taken two different franchises to multiple Super Bowls: Don Shula (Colts and Dolphins) Bill Parcells (Giants and Patriots) Dan Reeves (Broncos and Falcons) Mike Holmgren (Packers and Seahawks) Dick Vermeil (Eagles and Rams) John Fox (Panthers and Broncos) Andy Reid (Eagles and Chiefs) None of them won it all at both stops, however. This is obviously relevant to the Giants’ current situation because Harbaugh got a ring in his fifth season in Baltimore. In other sports we don’t see the same thing. For example, four baseball managers have won World Series with two different teams (Bucky Harris, Bill McKechnie, Sparky Anderson, Tony LaRussa), and Bruce Bochy has won it all with three different franchises. It’s not clear whether it’s just luck or whether it’s uniquely difficult for NFL teams for some reason. What got me thinking about this is the great piece Ed published on his interview with Harbaugh last week. SB Nation’s Ravens site, Baltimore Beatdown , republished the piece on their site. This attracted some Ravens fans to comment on the piece and engaged many of you in a spirited discussion about Harbaugh’s bona fides as an NFL head coach. For someone who won a Super Bowl, got his team to the playoffs 11 other times, and only had a losing record three times in an 18-year tenure, it may be a surprise that many Ravens’ fans reactions were of the “Don’t let the door hit you on the way out” variety. Here are a couple. (Aside: Can’t beat SB Nation sites for amusing screen names.) In some sense, Harbaugh can be seen as the safe choice for head coach, given his long experience and the fact that he has one ring (at the expense of brother Jim, who has never won a Super Bowl). He probably sets a floor for competence that the Giants haven’t had since the Coughlin days. The opposing point of view, though, is that three of the past five Super Bowls have been won by young head coaches in their first head coaching jobs (Sean McVay, Nick Sirianni, Mike McDonald), while other young head coaches such as Ben Johnson and Liam Cohen led teams that made an impressive showing last season. So the question is why Harbaugh never got the Ravens back to the Super Bowl. Unlike the Giants, the finger can’t be pointed at the Ravens’ front office, considered one of the best. Part of it is just the bad luck to have been in the same conference as the Chiefs at the height of Patrick Mahomes’ career, and earlier during the heyday of the Belichick-Brady Patriots. There hasn’t been any such dominant NFC team over the same time period – so far – though we’ll see whether Seattle becomes one. Aside from that, perhaps we can take the Ravens fans’ ostensibly legitimate criticisms of Harbaugh to heart and be on the lookout to see whether Harbaugh is able to do the following with the Giants: Maximize a possible elite young quarterback Make the right roster and playing time decisions Devise game plans and call plays that exploit opponent weaknesses Use the clock smartly Use challenge flags wisely Harbaugh will get some mileage just by being an authoritative presence in a locker room that needs that. He can’t help but get better performance from the defense than last year, just from the switch in defensive coordinators, never mind the additions to the roster. On the offensive side, though, the same may not be true. Whatever one thinks of Brian Daboll and Mike Kafka, they did a lot with an offense that had few skilled players for much of the time they were Giants. It is TBD whether the Matt Nagy – Brian Callahan – Greg Roman troika will be as effective. There are precedents for head coaches that did not win it all for a long time but eventually got there. Reid has been a head coach in the NFL for 27 consecutive years. He got to the Super Bowl but did not win it in his sixth year in Philadelphia and never got back again. Eight years and no Super Bowls later, he was gone. He moved to Kansas City and went another six years without even appearing in a Super Bowl. Since then he’s been to the Super Bowl five times and won three. Tom Coughlin was the inaugural head coach of the expansion Jacksonville Jaguars. Amazingly he made them a winning team by Year 2 and led them to a 14-2 record and the AFC Championship Game by Year 5. Three losing years later, he was fired. He took over the Giants in 2004 and after one losing season made them a playoff team, but after considerable player dissatisfaction with his approach, he made changes that finally gave him his first (of two) Super Bowl rings in the 2007 season. All of this is to say that Harbaugh’s past will not necessarily be his future. The two examples above tell us something about what his future actually will be. Reid won when he got Patrick Mahomes as his quarterback. Coughlin won (eventually) when he got Eli Manning as his quarterback. Why Harbaugh didn’t win with Lamar Jackson may not be known until we see whether Jackson finally reaches the Promised Land under Jesse Minter. The likely bottom line, though, is that John Harbaugh’s tenure as Giants head coach will hinge on what Jaxson Dart’s ceiling turns out to be, and whether Harbaugh and his offensive coaches can get him to it.

title: NY Giants training camp: 1 thing each rookie needs to prove
summary: New York Giants rookies report for training camp at The Greenbrier Resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, on Thursday. Veteran players report on Tuesday, July 28. With rookies set to get to work, let’s look at one thing each of them has to prove before the season begins. Arvell Reese Can he handle everything […]
full_text: Arvell Reese speaking to media. | Thomas Salus-Imagn Images New York Giants rookies report for training camp at The Greenbrier Resort in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, on Thursday. Veteran players report on Tuesday, July 28. With rookies set to get to work, let’s look at one thing each of them has to prove before the season begins. Arvell Reese Can he handle everything he is being asked to do? The Giants were clear from the moment they selected Reese No. 5 overall in the 2026 NFL Draft that he would play one position — off-ball linebacker. That, though, doesn’t mean the Giants won’t be asking Reese to handle a wide variety of responsibilities. “He’ll line up next to Tremaine (Edmunds), and he’ll be in the A gap, the B gap, the C gap, the D gap, off the edge,” Harbaugh told media just moments after the pick was announced. “He’ll be moving around with all of our guys. Abdul (Carter) and Brian (Burns) and Kayvon (Thibodeaux) and Tremaine. We’ll be running games and picks and stunts and different things like that on passing situations, and he’s good in coverage as well; he’s a versatile player.” The Giants will align their “off-ball linebacker” in several spots. They will use him in pass coverage. They will use him as a blitzer. Yes, he will play one position. He will, though, have many responsibilities within that one spot. “We’ve gotta be able to take advantage of his physical skill without overloading him as far as the mental thing is concerned,” said inside linebackers coach Frank Bush. “He’s shown an amazing ability to grasp the information, understand the concept, and still flourish within the concepts. “He’s not been a mistake guy. He’s been able to flash and make plays even though we’ve got a lot going on with him. He’s proven that he can handle it, but we as coaches have got to understand where he is, when it’s time to backpedal a little bit and let the kid just use his athleticism.” Sisi Mauigoa Can he adjust to how quickly things happen at guard? Talk to any offensive lineman who has played both guard and tackle, and you hear the same story about the differences in the two positions. You play in tighter quarters at guard, and, consequently, things happen faster. The players on the outside might be more athletic, but the lack of space speeds things up inside. Mauigoa was a collegiate right tackle. He will play right guard for the Giants. “I don’t have that much space to work with [at guard],” Mauigoa said this spring. “Playing at tackle, you have all the space, where at guard everything happens so fast. It’s not something I really need to work on; it’s something that I need to get used to.” Ex-Giant Jon Feliciano, who trained Mauigoa before the draft, has no doubt Mauigoa will adjust . He said Mauigoa will have to adjust to “the timing of throwing your hands and just how fast things happen inside,” but believes he will “hit the ground running when the season starts.” He needs to. Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark of the Dallas Cowboys will be across from him Week 1. Aaron Donald might be lined up against him in Week 2 when the Giants face the Los Angeles Rams. Jeffrey Simmons and John Franklin-Myers are part of the Tennessee Titans’ defensive line. Mauigoa is not going to have a chance to ease into his NFL career. Colton Hood Can he apply the lessons of the spring? During minicamp, there was a rep where Hood trotted out to his cornerback spot on the defense. Across from him was a player who was a world-famous superstar when Hood was just a kid, Odell Beckham Jr. Was Hood a little starstruck in the moment? Maybe. Maybe not. Beckham proceeded to show the young fella that a) there is still some gas in the old man’s tank, and b) Hood still has some things to learn. The ball was snapped, Beckham put a couple of moves on the rookie cornerback, and left him helpless 10-15 yards away as he caught a long touchdown pass. Cornerbacks coach Addison Lynch said there are “little things” Hood needs to improve upon. “He’s picked up the techniques very fast for a young rookie,” Lynch said. “He’s settled into what we’re trying to get accomplished with the scheme, and as far as our technique, and he’s doing a good job applying those skills. “Now it’s just some of the stuff when we get down the field that’s in flight. It’s, hey, we need to stay on top of leverage. We don’t need to undercut some things. And it’s the little things that he’s going to get and get more consistent with, and you’re going to be able to see him take off and play well.” The Giants drafted Hood in the second round, believing he was a late- first-round talent who can be a starter for them. Before they give him snaps ahead of veteran Greg Newsome, though, Hood is going to have to show that he has benefited from the lessons learned from Beckham and others during the spring. Malachi Fields Will his spring production translate? The 6-foot-4, 222-pound rookie had an impressive spring. He showed strong hands, contested catch ability, and usefulness on slants and in the red zone. All of that, though, was done without pads and with defensive backs instructed not to go all-out on 50-50 balls. Will all of that translate in pads, and in game conditions, against NFL competition. Bobby Jamison-Travis Can he hold his ground vs. NFL blockers? Jamison-Travis was the only defensive lineman the Giants drafted, one of their three sixth-round selections. The Giants will need a backup nose tackle for D.J. Reader. Even more than that, they need interior defensive linemen who are stout against the run. They hope the 6-foot-3, 328-pound Travis can be that. “What you have seen in his game is strength in knock-back. In the trenches his hands don’t always work in unison, but that’s coaching,” assistant GM Brandon Brown said this spring. “he has power in his hands, and he can eat double-teams. He doesn’t get moved by side anchor, and he can create knock-back … He’s not a pass rusher, but what he can do is eat two blocks, and he can be firm.” If Jamison-Travis can prove Brown right this summer once the pads come on, that might be a step for the Giants toward fixing their long-troublesome run defense. J.C. Davis Can he handle more than one position? The second of the Giants’ three sixth-round picks in the 206 NFL Draft, I can’t recall seeing Davis play anywhere but left tackle during the OTA and mandatory minicamp practices media had access to this spring. Davis was a left tackle at Illinois. Some analysts speculated that he could have guard flexibility, but the Giants did not seem ready to try him there yet. To make the 53-man roster, Davis likely has to show at least some aptitude to play right tackle. Backup linemen simply have to be able to play more than one position to be active on game days. Jack Kelly Can he consistently tackle NFL-caliber athletes? Considering that he was the 193rd player selected in the 2026 NFL Draft, the last of the Giants’ three Round 6 selections, there is a decent amount of excitement about Kelly. The former Weber State and BYU linebacker seems likely to make the 53-man roster. At least it seemed that way in the spring, when Kelly worked mostly alongside Micah McFadden with the second-team defense. Some analysts think he might be a tweener. He flashed pass rush skills that might be befitting of an edge defender, but there are athletic limitations, and some are concerned about his ability to cover running backs and tight ends. There is, though, one major blemish on Kelly’s resume that should be the biggest concern of all — he struggled mightily to make tackles over the past three seasons. At Weber State in 2023, Kelly missed 16.9% of his tackles. He then transferred to BYU. In 2024, he missed 20.0% of tackle attempts, and in 2025 that rose to an alarming 21.9%. Players who struggle to tackle at the collegiate level do not usually improve that skill in the NFL. The collectively bargained practice rules make tackling something that is rarely done in NFL practices, and make even the…

The former Heisman Trophy winner is knowledgeable. He’s very serious when he needs to be serious, but at the same time he has a light energy about him, a calming essence both on and off the field. There’s also an accountability factor that Winston brings to the practice field and the classroom. He’s unafraid to call teammates out for not carrying out assignments or, say, for dropping passes, even on air during walkthroughs. PFF Tight End Rankings: The top 32 players ahead of the 2026 NFL season | PFF 22. Isaiah Likely, New York Giants. Following an impressive four seasons as essentially the Ravens’ No. 2 tight end behind Mark Andrews, Likely followed head coach John Harbaugh to the Giants and will get his first real chance at being a starter. It was a rough 2025 season for Likely, as he missed three games due to a broken foot and registered a career-low 56.4 PFF grade. But in 2024, he placed seventh among all tight ends with 10 forced missed tackles, and his 75.6 PFF grade was sixth. 32. Theo Johnson, New York Giants. With Isaiah Likely joining the Giants, Johnson will likely get demoted to being New York’s No. 2 tight end. He was a worthy pass-catcher when he did start for the Giants last year, placing 19th with 528 receiving yards. Johnson’s five touchdown catches tied for 13th in the NFL, too. Giants roster bubble breakdown: Odell Beckham Jr., third QB question and draft busts hanging on | New York Post The NFL cliché is that no player’s job is safe after a regime change. Sometimes a new coach — especially one with final say over the roster, such as the Giants’ John Harbaugh — wants to send a message. Other times he just doesn’t care about an inherited hefty contract or high draft status that might have been saving a player on the bubble in the past. Giants legend raves about ‘great’ playoff expectations for Jaxson Dart and Co. | NJ.com The Giants need their prized quarterback, Jaxson Dart, to take the next step in Year 2, as coach John Harbaugh debuts in East Rutherford. And legendary former Giants quarterback Phil Simms thinks that will indeed happen. “I studied him a lot in college. As a pro — I watched him practice during the summer and play — and I just went, ‘Wow. This guy is a lot better than I thought.’ It caught me by surprise,” Simms said. “He really has the team in the palm of his hand. They all like him, they all know he’s really good, and he just has a way about him.” Re-Drafting the 2026 NFL Draft Before Training Camp: Flipping the First Round Upside Down | SI.com 5. New York Giants: Sonny Styles, LB (original selection: Arvell Reese). With Reese drafted by the Cardinals in this scenario, Sonny Styles becomes the straightforward selection for the New York Giants. In fact, with the Giants deciding to keep Reese at linebacker, you could argue choosing Styles, the more natural linebacker of the two, would have made more sense. John Harbaugh’s defense still lands a flexible front-seven defender. 10. New York Giants: Caleb Downs, S (original selection: Francis Mauigoa). We don’t necessarily have an issue with the Giants’ selection of Francis Mauigoa here, but safety Caleb Downs was the better overall prospect. Plus, knowing what we now know, keeping Downs away from their division rival Dallas Cowboys is a sweetener. If this scenario came to fruition, the Giants would feel inclined to sign a veteran starting guard like Kevin Zeitler. 50 days until the 2026 NFL season: Here are 50 under-the-radar players who could shape it | CBSSports.com 10. Darnell Mooney, New York Giants WR. Amid a disappointing 2024 for the Falcons, Mooney quietly impressed with 64 catches for 992 yards and five touchdowns while averaging a career-best 15.5 yards per catch — the seventh-highest mark in the league. Mooney dealt with lingering injuries in 2025, though, and finished with just 32 catches. The Giants would love to see him get back to his 2024 form, when he showed a well-rounded skill set that hadn’t been on display earlier in his career. 30. DJ Reader, New York Giants DT. title: The Top Ten Wackiest Outliers in New York Jets History
summary: Last season’s opener saw Justin Fields put together an impressive performance as he completed 16 of 22 passes for 218 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for 48 yards and two scores. It actually wasn’t his best performance of the year statistically, as he had three other games with more passing yards, one of […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 09: Stephen Hill #84 of the New York Jets jumps over Aaron Williams #23 of the Buffalo Bills for a touchdown during their season opener at MetLife Stadium on September 9, 2012 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The Jets defeated the Bills 48-28. (Photo by Rich Schultz /Getty Images) | Getty Images Last season’s opener saw Justin Fields put together an impressive performance as he completed 16 of 22 passes for 218 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for 48 yards and two scores. It actually wasn’t his best performance of the year statistically, as he had three other games with more passing yards, one of which saw him complete a higher percentage of his passes. However, it was the only time all year Fields played with unflappable confidence and it could have been a signature win if not for an incredible lucky bounce landing right in DK Metcalf’s lap. This set up the long game-winning kick as time expired. Clearly the performance was a significant outlier, but how does it stack up against some of the wackiest outliers in Jets history? Let’s come up with an arbitrary top-10 list and then you guys can tell us what we missed and where we went wrong! 10. Stephen Hill: Rookie Sensation Stephen Hill was one of the final draft busts of Mike Tannenbaum’s tenure as Jets’ general manager. The second round wideout ended up with just 45 career catches as he lasted just two years with the Jets and was soon out of the league altogether. For one game, though, it looked like the Jets had found a difference maker. Hill caught five passes for 84 yards and two touchdowns as the much-maligned Jets offense stunned the Bills 48-28 in Hill’s NFL debut. Hill was injury prone and displayed shaky hands over the rest of his career, although he did actually post a 100-yard game against the Bills in his second season so maybe this isn’t the outlier we remember it to be. Let’s call it the exception that proves the rule… 9. Josh Johnson’s flawless record Josh Johnson has already had one of the wildest careers on record, having played for 14 NFL teams since being drafted in 2008. He was with the Jets in both 2015 and 2021, but only got a shot to play meaningful reps once. He played in the final three quarters of a 2021 game, after Mike White got knocked by the Colts and their head coach, current Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich. However, Johnson passed for 317 yards and almost led the Jets within striking difference after they had trailed 42-10 late in the third quarter. With the Jets down 15, Johnson had the Jets in the red zone with over a minute remaining, and a touchdown would have made it a one-possession game with a chance to go for an onside kick. A deflected pass was intercepted to end the threat but, for three quarters, Johnson had looked the part. He didn’t get another chance with the Jets and then promptly put up another 300-yard game in his only start of the 2022 season with the Ravens. One 300-yard passing performance in zero starts as a Jet is an impressive ratio, though. 8. Brett Favre shows up The Jets made a blockbuster trade to land Brett Favre in 2008, but it was a frustrating season for the Jets who never fully reached their potential. Favre had led the Jets to an 8-3 record but they lost four of their last five to miss the postseason, amid reports that Favre was insisting on playing hurt and wasn’t very coachable. The “real” Favre did show up once, though, in a wild and wacky week four game against the Cardinals. He ended up with six touchdown passes in a 56-35 Jets win. That doesn’t remotely tell the whole story though, as it was really the Jets’ defensive front that dominated the first half. As outliers go, this game was next level, as the score was tied 0-0 after one quarter. However, the Jets took the Cardinals apart in the second quarter to lead 34-0 at the half! The wackiness didn’t end there, though. Kurt Warner, who ended up with 472 passing yards, had the Cardinals back within 13 with three minutes still remaining in the third, so the game was not over, especially considering how easily they were moving the ball. While Favre and the offense kept them at arm’s length, the Cardinals got the ball back with over three minutes to go and a chance to cut it to a one-possession game, but a Jets turnover finally ensured they were out of reach. Despite the six touchdowns, Favre fell short of 300 yards, a mark he never managed to hit with the Jets. In his other 15 games that season, he had just 16 touchdown passes and 21 interceptions. 7. Rex Ryan wins a low-scoring game The Rex Ryan era was characterized by a team with a good defense and a shaky offense. Clearly it was designed to win low scoring games, like when they beat the Bills 19-13 in December 2009, or when the beat the Cardinals 7-6 in December 2012. The crazy thing here is, during the intervening period – which lasted just two days short of three years – the Jets never actually won a low-scoring regular season game. Unless they scored at least 23 points in that intervening period, the Jets lost every time. During those three years, the Jets did win two low scoring postseason games, and the next game after the streak was ended was also a low scoring win, but that Cardinals win was a major regular season outlier, even though it was just the Jets winning exactly the way they were supposedly designed to do. 6. Isaiah Crowell wipes the floor with the competition As false dawns go, this one is tough to beat. After this game, the Jets seemed to have built an unstoppable offensive line, found a great running back tandem and looked to be well on the way to solving their quarterback issue. However, a few weeks later it was like it never happened. The Jets beat the Broncos in week five of the 2018 season as Sam Darnold threw three touchdowns and New York improved to 2-3. The real story, however, was the running game. Gang Green rushed for 324 yards with Bilal Powell carrying 20 times for 99 yards. However, that paled into insignificance compared with Isaiah Crowell’s output. On 15 carries, Crowell racked up 219 yards, setting an NFL record for yards per carry. This included runs of 77, 54 and 36 yards. He did this behind an offensive line that was comprised of Spencer Long, James Carpenter, Brian Winters, Kelvin Beachum and Brandon Shell. The Broncos’ run defense wasn’t even that bad. They held their opponents under 100 rushing yards in nine of 16 games that year. On the basis of this, and another convincing win the following week, the Jets looked to have their offensive line locked up for several years to come. However, their success evaporated almost immediately and all five were off the team by the end of the following season. As for Crowell, he never reached those kinds of heights again either, averaging 3.4 yards per carry over the rest of the season and never playing in the NFL again thereafter. 5. Jaiquawn Polamalu As Sidney Deane said to Billy Doyle in “White Men Can’t Jump”, the sun even shines on a dog’s [posterior] sometimes. (Actually he strictly said “Even the sun shines on a dog’s [backside] some days” which strictly suggests that a variety of items had been shining on this particular dog, the most remarkable of which was the sun. However, such grammatical nuance was rarely a consideration among some of the 1990’s fiercest west coast basketball trashtalkers). Digressions aside, has there ever been a more extreme example of a complete nobody having the game of his life out of nowhere than when Jaiquawn Jarrett took advantage of Calvin Pryor being late to a meeting and won an AFC player of the week award in 2014? Jarrett led the Jets to a win over the Steelers with 10 tackles, a tackle for loss, a sack, two quarterback hits, two interceptions, two passes defensed and a fumble recovery. He was everywhere , and got to start for the rest of the season as a reward. Having ended his career with nine career starts, Jarrett never got close to this kind of game otherwise.…

full_text: Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride (85) is introduced before the game against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium on Sept. 25, 2025. | Joe Rondone/The Republic / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images When and where: Week 13 in Arizona Key additions: HC Mike LaFleur, G Isaac Seumalo, RB Tyler Allgeier, DT Roy Lopez, WR Kendrick Bourne, QB Gardner Minshew Key subtractions: QB Kyler Murray, S Jalen Thompson, DT Dalvin Tomlinson, DL Calais Campbell, LT Kelvin Beachum, RT Jonah Williams Last season: The Cardinals, the franchise with the second worst winning percentage among active NFL teams, lost more games in 2025 than in any season in franchise history The question for this team: Which QB are the Cardinals drafting in April? The Cardinals season is already over. This is a team in a contract dispute with Jacoby Brissett, who led the team to one win in 12 starts in 2025. Brissett isn’t wrong to hold out, he’d probably make more money as a backup on another team, at the least he would have the benefit of no longer being on the Cardinals, a franchise that has charged players for the food they have given them. At the same time, the Cardinals also aren’t wrong to not give Brissett any additional money, they have Gardner Minshew and 3rd round pick Carson Beck to tank with. They don’t need Brissett, nobody does. There’s really no point in discussing the 2026 Arizona Cardinals. This is a team with the 6th most dead money (virtually the same as the Eagles) for 2026, and yet the 5th most cap space for 2026. According to Over The Cap, 24.8% of the Cardinals cap space is from rookie contracts, the most in the league. Over a third of the Cardinals salary cap for 2026 is being used on nobody on the roster. They’re not trying to compete this year. They want to lose this game and as many games as possible and have first shot at a bunch of QBs who a lot of people thought were going to be 1st round picks this past April. Good luck!

title: Philadelphia Eagles Hidden Gems: 3 underrated players on the 2026 roster
summary: Through the Nick Sirianni era, the Philadelphia Eagles have demonstrated an odd, though now predictable, story arc. After Sirianni’s 2022 Eagles barely lost Super Bowl LVII to the Kansas City Chiefs with Shane Steichen as the offensive mastermind, Steichen got the Indianapolis Colts’ head job, and Sirianni promoted quarterbacks coach Brian Johnson to be Steichen’s […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Philadelphia, PA, USA; Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks (13) speaks with the media at minicamp at Jefferson Health Training Complex. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | Bill Streicher-Imagn Images Through the Nick Sirianni era, the Philadelphia Eagles have demonstrated an odd, though now predictable, story arc. Get to the Super Bowl with a great offensive play-caller. Promote the replacement from within with iffy to icky results when said great offensive play-caller gets a head coaching gig, and Subsequently run back to the idea that a constructive offensive identity actually does matter in the NFL . After Sirianni’s 2022 Eagles barely lost Super Bowl LVII to the Kansas City Chiefs with Shane Steichen as the offensive mastermind, Steichen got the Indianapolis Colts’ head job, and Sirianni promoted quarterbacks coach Brian Johnson to be Steichen’s replacement. It didn’t work, and Sirianni then tapped former Los Angeles Chargers OC Kellen Moore to get the job done. Moore got the job done enough for the Eagles’ second Super Bowl win at the end of the 2024 season, and of course, Sirianni replaced Moore with pass game coordinator and associate head coach Kevin Patullo when Moore became the New Orleans Saints’ head coach. We all know how THAT went . Now, with former Green Bay Packers quarterbacks coach Sean Mannion as the new OC, there are a lot of questions to answer. How will the passing game work without A.J. Brown, and how will the run game work without the legend that is Jeff Stoutland? Remarkably for a guy who has done what he’s done, Jalen Hurts still has a lot of uncertainty to his name, and Mannion’s offense — based more on the Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan tree than anything Hurts has run before — makes that uncertainty valid, at least in a short-term sense. If Mannion turns what was a disaster of an offense around, it’s all good. Sirianni surely has enough underqualified acolytes to promote when Mannion becomes a head coach in 2027. If not, for as much as Sirianni has accomplished in half a decade, the questions will land firmly on his head. The Eagles will need more than the right kind of coaching to reach their Super Bowl dreams in 2026; they’ll also need big-time performances not only from Hurts and all the other players of whom such things are expected; but there is also a need for lesser-known guys to step up into new and bigger roles. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Eagles — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent or traded player, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: EDGE Jalyx Hunt With all the offensive agita , there are very few questions about the Eagles’ defense coming into the 2026 season; Vic Fangio had all that on lock as usual. Losing edge-rusher Jaelan Phillips to the Carolina Panthers on a four-year, $120 million contract with $80 million guaranteed was less than ideal, but the Eagles were not going to pay that kind of money for that kind of player. Not over that length of time. Instead, they traded with the Minnesota Vikings for Jonathan Greenard, and signed him to a two-year, $60 million contract with $50 million guaranteed. Greenard can bring a lot when he’s healthy, but the real crucible when it comes to the success of the team’s edge disruption in 2026 falls on third-year man Jalyx Hunt. Hunt converted from safety to EDGE at Cornell, and then showed enough at Houston Christian in the 2022 and 2023 seasons for the Eagles to take him with the 95th pick in the third round of the 2024 draft. Hunt was an athletic project at first, which is one reason he had just 343 defensive snaps in his rookie season. Still, he managed four sacks and 19 pressures, showed up with force in Super Bowl LIX, and displayed enough game-readiness to be more of a factor in 2025 with 722 snaps, seven sacks, and 60 pressures. Hunt reminds me of a young Danielle Hunter in some ways. When Hunter came out of LSU in the 2015 draft, he was far more of an athlete than he was a nuanced football player. But when he matched football acumen with general athleticism, all bets were off. Hunt has filled out his palette of pass-rush moves, and we may see how high his ceiling really is in the new season. Jalyx Hunt with the inside counter, bull-rush, and open-field footwork to get to the quarterback. He's become a complete edge-rusher at the perfect time for the @eagles . pic.twitter.com/lgyIxxcXy6 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) July 13, 2026 “Just keep doing what he’s doing,” Fangio said in May when asked how Hunt can up his game even further. “He’s had a nice progression. I see him growing his game in all aspects. I think he can and will rush better. He’ll play the run better. It’s just the natural progression. He’s had a good progression. In his rookie year, he didn’t play a lot early. Then when BG [EDGE Brandon Graham] went down, he started playing more, and I thought for a guy with his background, it was kind of a perfect year for him. He ended up playing a good bit if you remember in the playoffs, et cetera. Then last year, [he] played a lot, did good. “Yeah, I think he’s just ready to keep getting better and better.” Underrated traded player: WR Dontayvion Wicks Can the Eagles’ offense function without a true X iso receiver? The guy who can beat the opponents’ best cornerback alone to one side of the field? We’re about to find out, because last season, A.J. Brown was that guy. In 2025, Brown lined up as the X iso receiver on 148 snaps , more than twice as often as any other Eagles receiver — DeVonta Smith ranked second with 77 X-iso targets, and then, the whole thing kind of fell off a cliff. Now, with Mannion in charge of the passing game, that might not be as much of an issue. Last season, the Packers ranked sixth in the NFL with a 50% rate of condensed formations, in which no receiver was acting as the X iso receiver, and the Packers have long insisted — for better or worse — that their passing game can function at a high level more through scheme than having that dominant outside guy. (First-round pick Makai Lemon, by the way, lined up outside just 28% of the time in the 2025 season for USC. Just saying). Which is where the trade for former Packers receiver Dontayvion Wicks comes in. Last season, the 6’1”, 206-pound Wicks caught 30 passes on 44 targets for 332 yards and two touchdowns. Calf and ankle injuries, as well as concussion issues, limited his time on the field in 2025, which is why he wasn’t able to replicate his 2024 production, when he caught 41 passes on 80 targets for 454 yards and five touchdowns. Still, when your yards per catch stays exactly the same from one season to the next (11.1), and your catch rate increases from 51.3% to 68.2%, that’s a good thing. “Me and Sean built a relationship, just like [with] Coach Mahaffey,” Wicks said of his new home with Mannion and former Green Bay receivers coach Ryan Mahaffey. “Relationships play a big part in things, so I felt like that was a big part of the reason [for] the trust for me to be here and for them to bank on me.” Howie Roseman explained why Wicks was a consideration before the Brown trade even happened, and why the Eagles gave him a one-year, $10.5 million contract extension with a max value of $12.5 million. “You see his skill set,” Roseman said of Wicks. “He is a physical, explosive player at the top of routes. He can play inside or out, so he is a guy we had our eye on.” Sirianni has admired Wicks’ abilities to a similar degree. Nick Sirianni on Dontayvion Wicks: "I think he has a very unique skill set of being able to get in and out of breaks and be really efficient at the line of scrimmage. For a guy that I've coached, he has some Keenan Allen to him and to his game." …Knowing Sirianni, this is… — Zach Berman (@ZBerm) June 9, 2026 Nick Sirianni has said that Dontayvion Wicks could have a Keenan Allen-style impact on the @Eagles ' offense. Sirianni got to see a few of those traits up close…

title: Cam Heyward, Bud Dupree give brutally honest thoughts on training camp in Latrobe
summary: We are officially less than one week away from having Steelers football back, as players are set to report to Saint Vincent College in Latrobe this coming Tuesday. However, some players may not necessarily be looking forward to staying in Latrobe. Appearing on Cam Heyward’s “Not Just Football” podcast, former Steelers edge rusher Bud Dupree […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - SEPTEMBER 16: Pittsburgh Steelers linebacker Bud Dupree (48) and Pittsburgh Steelers defensive tackle Cameron Heyward (97) looks on during the NFL football game between the Kansas City Chiefs and Pittsburgh Steelers on September 16, 2018 at Heinz Field in Pittsburgh PA. (Photo by Mark Alberti/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We are officially less than one week away from having Steelers football back, as players are set to report to Saint Vincent College in Latrobe this coming Tuesday. However, some players may not necessarily be looking forward to staying in Latrobe. Appearing on Cam Heyward’s “Not Just Football” podcast , former Steelers edge rusher Bud Dupree made it known he was not a fan of living in the dorms at Saint Vincent College. “Nah, they still go to Latrobe?” Dupree asked Heyward. “The best training camp we had was the COVID year. We stayed at our own house. I hated the dorms. I hated it.” Heyward seemed to agree with Dupree that the living situation for players in Latrobe was not ideal. “The COVID year, we were trying so hard to win a Super Bowl so then we could tell Mr. Rooney and be like, Mr. Rooney, we won a Super Bowl, we don’t need to go back to Latrobe,” Heyward said. “It did not work out in that way. We were back in Latrobe the next year.” It was one thing to hear Dupree speak out of the dorms, but for Heyward to echo his opinion was eye-opening. The Steelers have held training camp in Latrobe at Saint Vincent College since 1966. The players stay in college dorms through the duration of camp, making it a unique training camp experience from the rest of the NFL. The Steelers tend to have a fairly rigorous training camp in the heat of August. While this isn’t any different from what any other NFL team does, the living conditions don’t allow for the same freedom that other teams may have available for their players who stay at home throughout training camp, much like they would during the season. It’s hard to imagine Pittsburgh ever leaving Latrobe to have training camp somewhere else, but it is interesting to see former and current players let their thoughts on the Steelers training camp program be known. title: Steelers training camp: Offensive position battles, storylines to follow
summary: NFL football being a weeklong event is almost back. Starting July 28, Pittsburgh will be in training camp, bringing with it the storylines, predictions and everything in between leading into the preseason and regular season. Now less than a week away, Read & React is here to break down the biggest storylines and camp battles […]
full_text: May 28, 2026; Pittsburgh, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. (11) and DK Metcalf (4) participate in OTA drills at the UPMC Rooney Sports Complex. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images NFL football being a weeklong event is almost back. Starting July 28, Pittsburgh will be in training camp, bringing with it the storylines, predictions and everything in between leading into the preseason and regular season. Now less than a week away, Read & React is here to break down the biggest storylines and camp battles before the black and gold head to Latrobe. Today, we’ll be starting off on offense: What changes will Mike McCarthy bring? RB : It’ll probably take some time before we learn if new Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy is better than what Mike Tomlin was in his last few years in the role, but we should get an idea of what’s different early on. Even before training camp, we’ve seen some departures from Tomlin’s “CEO” style of head coaching. McCarthy has been much more hands-on with the quarterbacks, and the Steelers’ offense is expected to be largely his, not based on the schemes or play calling of a coordinator. But training camp should give us an even bigger idea of how the McCarthy era will differ from Tomlin’s. Backs on backers, seven shots and more were all previously staples of Latrobe. Will McCarthy keep those traditions, or bring new ones? Even if they aren’t substantial differences, you could certainly argue that any change should be welcomed given Pittsburgh’s déjà vu season finishes in recent years. Tomlin was the Steelers’ head coach for nearly 20 years — so much of what we expect from the team each year is based on his philosophies. Some things are bound to be different. Focusing on the offense specifically, we should see plenty of new things: more 11 personnel, a more varied run scheme, and new passing concepts, pre-snap motions and tendencies. I’m being purposefully vague just because we don’t fully understand what the McCarthy Steelers will look like yet. But we’ll start getting a good idea come July 28. A new collection of pass catchers RP : Last year, the Steelers were woefully unequipped at pass catcher, exemplified by Pittsburgh’s average of 202.4 passing yards per game (22nd in the league) and -0.04 EPA per pass (17th) according Next Gen Stats. Leading up to the 2025 season, the team made a pair of splashy trades for receiver DK Metcalf and tight end Jonnu Smith, but also traded away the gifted but malcontented George Pickens. Metcalf had moments of brilliance, but was unable to replicate the type of production he had maintained for years in Seattle. He also missed the final two games of the regular season after an avoidable altercation with a fan in Detroit led to a suspension. Behind Metcalf, the depth chart featured a collection of players that more closely resembled a group of Aaron Rodgers’ retired golfing buddies than the depth chart you’d expect of a playoff-caliber team. In particular, Rodgers fruitlessly targeting Marquez Valdes-Scantling on three straight red zone passes late in a loss to the Browns — a game that could have clinched the division with a win, no less — remains seared on my brain like I was trapped in a Stanley Kubrick movie . Smith, meanwhile, might as well have never suited up at all. He produced just 222 yards and two touchdowns, while providing cover-your-eyes level blocking. Worse still, Smith continued to outsnap both Pat Freiermuth and Darnell Washington despite his clear and obvious struggles. With the horrors of last season now behind us, the Steelers should, at least on paper, have a much better-rounded pass-catching group this season thanks to two major additions. Metcalf returns as the team’s primary X-receiver, and his improved supporting cast should better pair with his skill set and set both him and the offense up for success, namely with vertical concepts that can take advantage of his speed. Michael Pittman Jr., the Steelers’ latest offseason trade acquisition, mirrors Metcalf in size (6’4, 223 pounds) but wins his contested catch opportunities at a higher clip (52.6% vs 41.8%) and functions best underneath as either a Z-receiver or power slot. The team also drafted rookie Germie Bernard in the second round. Bernard has already received positive reviews from the coaching staff for the professionalism he’s shown during the offseason program, and he figures to be a Swiss-army-knife for the team, capable of playing all three receiving positions, but most likely to be an interchangeable piece with Pittman. How much McCarthy moves his receivers around, and how well they complement each other — and the tight ends — in the offense will be one of the main things I’m watching for this summer. Three spots, four quarterbacks RB : This is more of a battle between two quarterbacks, Mason Rudolph and Will Howard, as barring injury there’s no way the Steelers enter the regular season without their starter, Aaron Rodgers, or a third-round rookie in Drew Allar. But all four passers have a storyline to follow this summer. Starting with the aforementioned quarterback battle, it’s fair to say Rudolph has the upper hand headed into training camp as he actually has NFL experience — 19 starts, to be exact — compared to Howard’s zero career NFL snaps. With Howard and Allar’s complete lack of NFL experience, there’s a reason why Rudolph is still on the roster. At the same time, Howard is still in the first half of a dirt-cheap rookie deal, and he technically has more upside than Rudolph simply by nature of being a complete NFL unknown. Plus, his college career projects him as the sort of capable, long-term QB2 he was seemingly drafted to be. If he can draw even with Rudolph over the summer, he’ll make a strong case to stick around on the 53-man roster. Of course, the Steelers will also have to think about what their plan of action would be if Rodgers misses time during the 2026 season: See what the young passers can do, or trust that Rudolph can help the team still compete for a playoff spot. Entering the 2026 season, Allar has some stakes as well. He’s largely expected to stay as the QB3, initially at least, but he’ll want to start showing the “it” factor earlier than later as the Steelers are speeding towards having to gamble on their next franchise quarterback in 2027. Rodgers has something to prove as well. His 2025 season showed he could still lead a team to the playoffs and make some bonkers throws, but his diminishing creativity as a passer and quick time to throw have been one of the biggest factors in why the Steelers are still widely considered a member of the league’s middle class. Can a reunion with McCarthy, better receiver play, and maybe an improved offensive line (more on that next), help him look a bit more like the four-time MVP of old? How will the OL starting 5 shake out? RP : Seemingly three positions on the Pittsburgh line appear to be set: center Zach Frazier, Troy Fautanu flipping to left tackle, and guard Mason McCormick following Fautanu in the transition from the right to left side. While that still is subject to change, it is what we saw during OTAs . Assuming that holds, it appears the team is prepared to move forward with 2023 seventh-round pick Spencer Anderson at right guard and 2023 UDFA Dylan Cook at right tackle to open camp. Anderson had a breakout season of sorts in 2025, when he became featured in some of the six-lineman jumbo packages the Steelers deployed. Cook took his first NFL game action last year as well, replacing the injured Broderick Jones. However, the Steelers seem to have plenty of depth along the line this year, and should try to determine what the best combination of players they possess is, regardless of what their initial plans might be. Jones, a former first-round pick, remains on the roster, though it is unclear how soon he’ll be cleared to fully participate as he works back from a serious…

title: Seahawks hold tryout with Australia’s tallest ever National Rugby League player
summary: The Seattle Seahawks hosted tryouts for four players, including a trio of veteran tight ends who’ve bounced around the league throughout their respective careers. That fourth player, however? He’s never played a down of organized football in his life. Ben Te Kura is an Australian rugby player who’s been with the National Rugby League’s Brisbane […]
full_text: BRISBANE, AUSTRALIA - APRIL 08: Benjamin Te Kura takes on the defence during a Brisbane Broncos NRL training session at Clive Berghofer Field on April 08, 2024 in Brisbane, Australia. (Photo by Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks hosted tryouts for four players, including a trio of veteran tight ends who’ve bounced around the league throughout their respective careers. That fourth player, however? He’s never played a down of organized football in his life. Ben Te Kura is an Australian rugby player who’s been with the National Rugby League’s Brisbane Broncos since the 2024 season. A towering figure at 6’9, Te Kura is the tallest player in the history of the NRL. After playing five games for the Broncos, Te Kura set his sights on the NFL, with Brisbane granting him an initial leave of absence to pursue his new career. As of three weeks ago, Te Kura is now out of contract : The Brisbane Broncos have released forward Ben Te Kura from the remainder of his current contract, effective immediately, to allow him to pursue an NFL opportunity in the United States in 2027. The 205cm front rower was initially granted leave from the Club’s NRL squad commitments in April, to attend a six-week NFL training camp. He will now relocate to Arizona to continue his pursuit of a professional career in the sport. There are some highlights of Te Kura with the Souths Logan Magpies, and just look at the big man rumble! Te Kura, who was a “prop” forward in rugby, is listed in the transaction wire as a tackle, so obviously the plan is for him to bulk up a bit given his rugby playing weight was 268 pounds. He could follow in the footsteps of fellow Aussie and current Philadelphia Eagles star Jordan Mailata, who switched from a prop in rugby to eventually becoming one of the premier offensive tackles in the NFL. The Seahawks already have a former rugby player on the roster. Running back George Holani played rugby in high school before going full-time to football at Boise State University. They also have an Australian in superstar punter Michael Dickson, although his sporting background began in Aussie rules football and not rugby. It’s just a tryout for Te Kura, but the thought of the Seahawks going a bit outside the box is intriguing!

title: Seahawks try out 3 tight ends, including a former draft pick
summary: The Seattle Seahawks brought in three tight ends for tryouts, just days after waiving (with an injury designation) Harrison Bryant. One of these names should be familiar to Seahawks fans. Per the NFL transaction wire, Seattle met with the following players: Seattle has invested heavily at the tight end position as a focal point of […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WA - DECEMBER 23: Nick Vannett #81 of the Seattle Seahawks scores a touchdown during the second quarter of the game aganst the Kansas City Chiefs at CenturyLink Field on December 23, 2018 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Otto Greule Jr/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks brought in three tight ends for tryouts, just days after waiving (with an injury designation) Harrison Bryant . One of these names should be familiar to Seahawks fans. Per the NFL transaction wire, Seattle met with the following players: Josiah Deguara , best known for his time with the Green Bay Packers (2020-2023) and most recently of the Arizona Cardinals. Nick Muse , former Minnesota Vikings seventh-round pick (2022) whose last stint was on the New York Jets practice squad. He’s also the brother of former Seahawks linebacker Tanner Muse. Nick Vannett , a 2016 Seahawks third-round draft pick who spent four seasons with Seattle and has bounced around the league. His last team was the Los Angeles Rams, home to fellow former Seahawks TE Colby Parkinson. Seattle has invested heavily at the tight end position as a focal point of the offense. A.J. Barner is the lead tight end who’s coming off a strong second season, as well as a couple of offseason surgeries after playing through some injuries . Elijah Arroyo had an injury-hampered rookie year but figures to be more involved as a receiver in this year’s offense. Veteran Eric Saubert is a blocking tight end whose biggest play of his life was a two-point conversion which more or less won the Seahawks the NFC West . Nick Kallerup deputized for Saubert when he missed time due to injury, and the second-year undrafted player will be battling for a roster spot alongside undrafted rookie Lance Mason out of Wisconsin. We’ll see if any of these tryouts land a contract to essentially replace Bryant on the depth chart.

summary: The Seattle Seahawks begin their 2026 training camp this Saturday, as the Super Bowl champions look to be the first NFC team to win back-to-back titles since Jimmy Johnson’s Dallas Cowboys in the 1990s. Yeah, it’s really been that long since there was an NFC dynasty. There are plenty of intriguing roster battles on both […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JUNE 11: Nehemiah Pritchett #28 of the Seattle Seahawks stretches during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on June 11, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks begin their 2026 training camp this Saturday, as the Super Bowl champions look to be the first NFC team to win back-to-back titles since Jimmy Johnson’s Dallas Cowboys in the 1990s. Yeah, it’s really been that long since there was an NFC dynasty. There are plenty of intriguing roster battles on both sides of the ball, but especially on defense, where the bulk of the Seahawks’ offseason changes occurred. Before camp officially begins, I’m giving it another crack at projecting the initial 53-man roster. Offense (26) Quarterback (3): Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, Jalen Milroe Cut: N/A Notes : Milroe might be competing not to get traded, otherwise it should be the same set-up as last year as long as Milroe doesn’t have a disastrous camp and/or preseason. Running Back (3): Jadarian Price (R), Emanuel Wilson, George Holani Cut: Jacardia Wright , Kenny McIntosh PUP: Zach Charbonnet Notes : Charbonnet is confirmed to be on PUP, while McIntosh is starting camp on PUP. I anticipate the latter being available to practice soon. Jadarian Price, Emanuel Wilson, and George Holani will surely be the top three backs, and it’s up to a numbers game to see if Wright or McIntosh earns a fourth spot while Charbonnet is gone. Most likely, they stick with three and shift one of Wright or Kenny to the practice squad. Fullback (2): Robbie Ouzts, Brady Russell Cut: N/A Notes : Seattle is definitely going to be using full backs, and I hope under Brian Fleury that Ouzts can be something other than a tell that the Seahawks are running the ball. Ouzts had some tight end skills in college, so use it to your advantage! Russell is a “fullback/tight end” hybrid but really he’s there as a special teams beast. Wide Receiver (5): Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Cooper Kupp, Rashid Shaheed, Tory Horton, Jake Bobo Cut: Emmanuel Henderson Jr (R), Cody White, Ricky White III, Velus Jones Jr, Irv Charles, Rashad Rochelle, Montorie Foster Notes : Either Seattle keeps five receivers or six, in which case I’m curious to see if Ricky White III can make good on his second season with the team. Seattle re-signing Shaheed and Bobo in the offseason essentially took away the drama as far as the wide receiver room. Tight End (3): A.J. Barner, Elijah Arroyo, Eric Saubert Cut: Lance Mason (R) , Nick Kallerup Notes : I have a feeling Kallerup is on the bubble, or at least competing with the rookie Lance Mason. Seattle keeping Kallerup on the active roster all of last season is encouraging but doesn’t mean his spot is now guaranteed for 2026. It may make sense to keep four TEs when the team runs so much 12 and 13 personnel, but I’d sooner believe the Seahawks would just make use of Ouzts or Russell when they want to go heavier and stash Kallerup and/or Mason on the practice squad. Offensive Line (10) : Charles Cross, Abe Lucas, Josh Jones, Mason Richman, Anthony Bradford, Olu Oluwatimi, Jalen Sundell, Grey Zabel, Bryce Cabeldue , Beau Stephens (R) Cut: Federico Maranges, Bobby Hart , Amari Kight, Logan Brown, Christian Haynes Notes : Brady Henderson has referenced and at least speculated Oluwatimi possibly being traded on an expiring contract. For now, I think he stays and Seattle will let him walk in free agency. Beau Stephens may eventually challenge or (in 2027) replace Bradford as right guard, but bare minimum I think it’s a wrap for Christian Haynes. I think Seattle may max out at keeping only nine linemen in the long run but the initial 53 could have 10. Defense (24) Defensive Line (5): Byron Murphy II, Leonard Williams, Jarran Reed, Rylie Mills, Mike Morris Cut: J.R. Singleton, Bubba Thomas , Brandon Pili , Uso Seumalo (R) PUP/Injury stash: Deven Eastern (R) Notes : Mills will be one to watch in training camp and preseason now that he’ll have a healthy offseason under his belt. Eastern missing much of OTAs and minicamp has me thinking he’ll just be given the NFL equivalent of a medical redshirt. Seattle lacks a traditional nose tackle—they pretty much have Jarran Reed as the nose—but Seattle may just stash Pili and/or Seumalo on the practice squad and elevate when needed. I’ve had Mike Morris on the bubble for seemingly ever and he’s still here, so I might as well back off until there’s evidence he could be let go. Outside Linebacker (5): Derick Hall, Uchenna Nwosu , Dante Fowler Jr, DeMarcus Lawrence, Aidan Hubbard (R) Cut: Jared Ivey, Connor O’Toole , Marvin Jones Jr (R), Jamie Sheriff, Jalan Gaines Notes : I’ve not changed from the pre-OTAs projection. Hubbard is my lone UDFA to crack the roster. Ivey and O’Toole just miss out and at least one of the two gets put on the practice squad. The only reason I would counter myself to put Ivey over Hubbard is Ivey’s large frame as an edge could provide something of a unique look. Inside Linebacker (4): Ernest Jones IV, Drake Thomas, Tyrice Knight, Chris Paul Jr Cut: Chazz Surratt, Patrick O’Connell, Ja’Markis Weston Notes : ‘Pooh’ Paul is still a great unknown in the Seahawks defense. This is just a pure hunch that could be quickly undone once we get to practices. Surratt was a cheap FA re-sign limited to special teams, but he might get the spot over Paul and others if it comes down to ST value. O’Connell is a perennial “ready squad” guy so I don’t worry about him. Cornerback (5): Devon Witherspoon, Josh Jobe, Nehemiah Pritchett , Julian Neal (R), Noah Igbinoghene Cut: Shemar Jean-Charles, Brandon Johnson, Michael Dansby (R), Tyrone Broden , Andre Fuller (R) Notes : Witherspoon and Jobe are locks, Neal is pretty much a lock, so that leaves Pritchett, Fuller, Johnson, Igbinoghene, and Dansby as five guys competing for two spots. I’ve thought about it some more and for now, I think Pritchett and Igbinoghene have the inside track and that leaves Fuller and Dansby in particular on the outside looking in. Safety (5): Julian Love, Ty Okada, Nick Emmanwori, Bud Clark (R), Rodney Thomas II Cut: Maxen Hook, D’Anthony Bell, A. J. Finley Notes : I think the final spot comes down to Thomas or Bell. Seattle has familiarity with Bell dating back to last season, but Thomas has more experience as a defensive starter while maintaining a high special teams count. Special Teams (3) Kicker (1) : Jason Myers Punter (1) : Michael Dickson Long Snapper (1) : Chris Stoll Cut: No one Notes: There’s nothing to discuss here. It’s like having three free spaces on the giant Seahawks bingo board. There will be more regular roster projections once preseason begins, as by then we’ll have a clearer picture of who has the inside track and whose bubbles are about to burst. We’ll also have a metric ton of signings and waivers during that time frame that will make previous projections obsolete, so it keeps things fresh and exciting. The only thing I’m certain of is that it will be very difficult to predict the bottom end of the roster, which is a testament to the talent level the Seahawks currently possess. full_text: DAYTONA BEACH, FLORIDA - JUNE 07: Jack Plummer #13 of the Orlando Storm throws a pass under pressure from Boogie Basham #90 of the DC Defenders in the second quarter during the semifinal game in the 2026 UFL Playoffs at Daytona Stadium on June 07, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Florida. (Photo by Dustin Markland/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers have often entered training camp with four quarterbacks under Kyle Shanahan. Last year, it was Brock Purdy, Mac Jones, Kurtis Rourke, Tanner Mordecai, and Carter Bradley. There was an extra quarterback in the fold with Rourke recovering from a knee injury. The previous August, it was Purdy, Mordecai, Brandon Allen, and Josh Dobbs. In August 2023, It was Purdy, Allen, Sam Darnold, and Trey Lance. The 49ers have four arms on the roster currently, with Purdy, Jones, Rourke, and Adrian Martinez. According to Aaron Wilson of KPRC 2 Houston, the Niners will work out former UFL MVP Jack Plummer for the Orlando Storm. Plummer led the league with 2,188 yards and had 17 touchdowns with only one interception in 10 games. Plummer went undrafted in the 2024 NFL Draft, but was waived by the Carolina Panthers last August during roster cuts. The 49ers might want to give Brock Purdy rest during the next month, or need a quarterback to throw late in preseason games. To me, the team working out a quarterback is a sign they want to upgrade from Martinez. Plummer’s stat line would suggest he is the kind of quarterback Shanahan would gravitate toward.

title: 49ers news: Apparently, there are 53 players in the NFL better than Fred Warner
summary: Slow news days are about to be a thing of the past, as training camp is underway. It may take a few days for the news to roll in, but we will be back in business in no time. The Feed post of the day that made me laugh: Be sure to sign up for […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 03: San Francisco 49ers' Fred Warner #54 celebrates their 24-9 NFL victory over the Los Angeles Rams at Levis Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif., on Monday, Oct. 3, 2022. (Jane Tyska/Digital First Media/East Bay Times via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Slow news days are about to be a thing of the past, as training camp is underway. It may take a few days for the news to roll in, but we will be back in business in no time. The Feed post of the day that made me laugh: Be sure to sign up for an account if you haven’t. That way you can post your own feeds and participate in the polls listed in The Feed. Onto today’s links… George Kittle Gets Honest About Davante Adams Ahead of 49ers-Rams “He’s fantastic. He’s still such an elite route runner. I try to watch this film and be like, ‘Oh, I could do that. So, I’m just like, ‘Nah, I can’t do that. He’s pretty special,’” Kittle said during the video on X on July 23. “Just to be an elite red-zone threat? Like, ‘Hey, we’re in the red zone. Now, Davante’s going to score.’ To have that confidence from your quarterback, from your team. I don’t think there’s anybody even closer than touchdowns right now. “Share some of those big dog.” 49ers to work out UFL MVP quarterback Jack Plummer ahead of training camp According to KPRC2’s Aaron Wilson, the San Francisco 49ers are set to work out United Football League (UFL) MVP Jack Plummer on Friday, a day before veterans report to training camp. Plummer also has a workout scheduled with the Miami Dolphins. 2026 San Francisco 49ers training camp preview Did the 49ers do enough to contend in football’s toughest division? A 35-point playoff defeat would seem to indicate the Niners have a long road back to the top of their division. But they don’t see it that way, as their many offseason moves can attest. They added wide receivers Mike Evans and Christian Kirk , defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa and linebacker Dre Greenlaw . And they figure to get some of their stars back from injury, including defensive end Nick Bosa , linebacker Fred Warner and tight end George Kittle . Even their top three 2026 draft picks (wideout De’Zhaun Stribling , edge rusher Romello Height and running back Kaelon Black ) are age 23 or older and have extensive college football experience. If all of the above falls into place, the Niners hope they can catch — and potentially pass — Seattle and Los Angeles in the NFC West and reclaim the conference’s top spot. The 10 Most Interesting 49ers in Training Camp This Year 7. Renardo Green | Cornerback Statistically, he was the 49ers’ best cornerback last season. But he got in a shouting match with head coach Kyle Shanahan during their playoff loss to the Seahawks, and the 49ers even benched him for a drive, so you know they’re not completely satisfied with him. Then this offseason, they signed veteran cornerbacks Nate Hobbs and Jack Jones. Clearly, the 49ers want to push Green, who’s a subpar tackler and has intercepted just two passes since high school. If he doesn’t have a lights-out camp, he could lose his starting spot for Week 1. 8. Upton Stout | Nickelback He’s the 49ers’ best young defensive player, but he was a non-factor in the playoff loss to the Seahawks because he hardly was on the field. In fact, he played just 18 snaps. The Seahawks offense used lots of tight ends, and Robert Saleh didn’t feel confident leaving Stout on the field against Seattle’s base offense. Will Raheem Morris find a way to keep Stout on the field all the time this season? He’s too good to come off it, especially given the lack of talent the 49ers have in their secondary. The 49ers’ Biggest Weakness Ahead of Training Camp The glaring flaws in depth were seen at linebacker, wide receiver and along the defensive line. The 49ers have been the most injured team in the National Football League over the last 10 years while fielding some of the oldest rosters during that time frame. Depth should always be an offseason point of emphasis. But the 49ers took a different approach to their offseason moves by doubling down on proven veteran talent. The team opened free agency by signing 32-year-old Mike Evans, who has a reputation as one of the best wide receivers of this decade but has also dealt with injuries over the past couple of years. The 49ers’ next-best move was signing Dre Greenlaw, who has spent the last two years in and out of the lineup because of injuries. The 49ers addressed last season’s positional weaknesses with these moves, but they are not transactions to rely on because of the players’ histories of missing time. If that trend repeats itself, the team will be back where it started this offseason. The 49ers’ front office may understand this reality based on the type of contracts Evans and Greenlaw received, which were low-risk, high-reward deals. 49ers’ Fred Warner has something to prove after catastrophic injury: ‘Toughest times’ His absence from the final 11 games of the year seemingly played a role in Warner’s drastic drop on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026. The list is determined by current players, who vote on their peers based on their performance from the previous year. Warner earned the No. 54 spot on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026 after coming in at No. 16 last season. “I always believed strongly that everything happens for a reason,” Warner told The Athletic in a recent feature. “And it would be wrong to abandon that in the toughest times.”

title: Report: Rams were interested in 49ers top 2026 draft pick
summary: The San Francisco 49ers drew opinions earlier this offseason when they took Ole Miss wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling with the No. 33 pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, with analysts perceiving the pick as a slight reach, given that he was a consensus late second-rounder. However, several reports came out following the draft that Stribling […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers drew opinions earlier this offseason when they took Ole Miss wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling with the No. 33 pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, with analysts perceiving the pick as a slight reach, given that he was a consensus late second-rounder. However, several reports came out following the draft that Stribling was seen higher by the NFL than the media and was expected to be a second-round pick, with the 49ers not wanting to risk losing the wideout with another trade down. Standing 6’2, 210 pounds, Stribling ran a 4.36 40-yard dash and was one of the more physically impressive wide receivers in the draft. San Francisco clearly had an affinity for the wideout, as head coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch revealed after the draft that Stribling would’ve been the team’s pick at No. 27 overall, where the 49ers were initially slated to pick. But the team was able to pick up additional draft compensation and move back to No. 33, where they ultimately still took Stribling. Earlier this week, ESPN’s Adam Schefter revealed that one of the teams interested in Stribling was the Los Angeles Rams, with some even believing the Ole Miss product was the best receiver in the draft. “What’s interesting about this selection is there were some people that wondered if it was too early for De’Zhaun Stribling to go, and yet there were a couple of teams that I spoke to in the draft process leading up to the draft that felt that De’Zhaun Stribling was the best wide receiver in the draft,” Schefter said. “Another team, supposedly the Los Angeles Rams, had eyes on him as well. The 49ers didn’t just come up with this pick out of nowhere. They knew that there were other teams that had a very high grade on Stribling when the 49ers declined to trade out the top draft slot in the second round and take him there.” Of course, while Stribling may have been a surprise for some at his draft slot, he did feel like a good fit with the 49ers with his skill set. “He’s an interesting player,” ESPN’s Mina Kimes added on Get Up. “You can see why it’s possible the 49ers valued him a bit more than other teams in the NFL. That draft pick did take some folks by surprise, but when you dig into the tape, playing at Ole Miss, the route tree is somewhat limited by the scheme. “But you see a lot of the attributes that they want. You mention running that sub-4.4 40. He’s 6’2. That’s a rare combination. He’s also really tough. He’s a good blocker, again very San Francisco 49ers-coded. And he fits in with the players they already have and added. Mike Evans is the true X. Ricky Pearsall, I see as the Z, [and] Stribling playing the slot as like a big slot or just close to the formation.” Stribling’s role in 2026 for the 49ers may not be as big with Christian Kirk and Mike Evans in the fold, but it seems like there was some league-wide interest in him during the draft in the second round.

title: 49ers roster preview: Is this Christian McCaffrey’s final year as a Niner?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers had made the Super Bowl, had deep playoff runs, and had been among the best teams in the NFL before acquiring Christian McCaffrey. McCaffrey playing in a game a few days after the trade says everything you need to know about the player. After that game against the Chiefs, he took […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers gets set during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers had made the Super Bowl, had deep playoff runs, and had been among the best teams in the NFL before acquiring Christian McCaffrey. McCaffrey playing in a game a few days after the trade says everything you need to know about the player. After that game against the Chiefs, he took off. Since then, McCaffrey has consistently found himself in the top-5 of MVP voting. Not many running backs can say that. As we know, McCaffrey is no ordinary running back. The gravity that he commands as a receiver is unlike any player Kyle Shanahan has had in the Bay Area. And Shanahan has taken full advantage of that. After missing all but four games in the 2024 season, McCaffrey played 932 snaps in 2025, which was nearly 83% of the team’s snaps. McCaffrey was the 49ers’ offense last year. He had 10 games with at least 45 receiving yards. He forced a league-high 113 missed tackles, per Next Gen Stats. Understanding that it was a struggle to generate offense, Shanahan went out of his way to target McCaffrey behind the line of scrimmage. CMC had 73 receptions behind the line of scrimmage, which was 35 more than the next-closest running back. McCaffrey still managed 697 receiving yards and 35 first downs. Off a season with 311 rushing attempts and 102 receptions, Shanahan’s hand will be forced to dial back the touches for McCaffrey. Basic Info Age: 30 Experience: 9 accrued seasons Height: 5’10 Weight: 210 pounds Cap Status McCaffrey is under contract through the 2026 season. This is the final year of McCaffrey having a relatively cheap cap number. McCaffrey’s base salary is $1.3 million in 2026. That number spikes to $16.85 million next season. That is in addition to McCaffrey’s annual prorated bonuses. He has a $18.6 million signing bonus that pays out $3.94 million this year and next. Plus a $24.79 option bonus that will be paid out $4.95 in 2026 and 2027.McCaffrey’s base salary is $1.3 million in 2026. That number spikes to $16.85 million next season. That is in addition to McCaffrey’s annual prorated bonuses. He has a $18.6 million signing bonus that pays out $3.94 million this year and next. Plus a $24.79 million option bonus that will be paid out $4.95 million in 2026 and 2027. That’s how you get a cap number of $26 million during McCaffrey’s 31-year-old season next year. If the 49ers were to release McCaffrey after this season, they would save $17.5 million in cap space. The alternative could be restructuring McCaffrey’s contract, which would save $11.7 million in cap space. The latter option does not have any dead money, while the former has $8.9 million. Is this the final year we see McCaffrey in a 49ers uniform? Salary cap and age will have a big say in this. There is no arguing about McCaffrey’s impact and what he means to the 49ers. He’s incredible. But we know how Father Time is with running backs once they hit 30. We also know what history says about players coming off 400-touch seasons. Injuries are as close to inevitable as it gets. If it’s not injuries, it’s the production that falls off a cliff. It’s difficult to imagine McCaffrey not being successful in a Shanahan offense with the weapons currently on the roster. The added speed and WR1 at wide receiver should only make McCaffrey more dangerous out of the backfield. The data tells us McCaffrey has lost a step. That doesn’t mean he’s any less effective, as evidenced by his missed tackle rate. But the 49ers will have to make a decision on McCaffrey with a ballooned salary. The team just used a third-round pick on Kaelon Black. Jordan James is 22. If those two look like they can be the future, the 49ers may turn the page from McCaffrey. If not, a restructure may be in the works.
